sens: One of the valiant warriors of King David
H3300G.detail: Jaasiel-Metsobaja is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:47, among the list of mighty men who joined David at Ziklag and became his trusted warriors. The text provides no details about his personal exploits, but his inclusion in this enumeration shows that he earned a place of honor among the most renowned fighters of the king.
H3300G.origine: The name Jaasiel means "God is the one who does" or "God is the creator." This meaning reflects a trust in the creative and active power of God. Some ancient sources suggest that he may also have been called Jasiel, or that he was a son of Abner, the commander of Saul's army, indicating that he came from a high-ranking military background.
H3300G.emploi: Jaasiel-Metsobaja appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 11:47. He is listed among the "mighty and valiant men" who supported David during his reign. This list enumerates thirty-seven warriors of various origins (Israelites, converted foreigners, sons of prophets) who formed David's military elite. His name is associated with other warriors like Eliel and Obed, without the text mentioning his origins or particular deeds.

sens: Son of Abner and chief of Benjamin
One of David's mighty warriors
H3300H.detail: Jaasiel is an Israelite warrior from the time of the united kingdom, the son of Abner (the famous commander of Saul's army). He appears in 1 Chronicles 27:21, where he is designated as responsible for the tribe of Benjamin, one of the twelve tribes for which David appointed leaders. His name literally means "God is the one who does" or "God creates," reflecting the Hebrew people's trust in God's creative action.
H3300H.origine: The name Jaasiel is composed of two Hebrew elements: "jaa" (God) and "asiel" (the one who does, the one who creates). It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains the name of God, common in ancient Israel. This onomastic construction reflects faith in the creative and active power of God in the daily life of the Hebrew people.
H3300H.emploi: Jaasiel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:21. He appears in the list of the twelve leaders that David established to administer the various tribes of Israel. His appearance in this context indicates that he was a trusted man of King David, chosen to lead the tribe of Benjamin during the period of the united kingdom. This is the only place in Scripture where this character is named, highlighting his administrative and political role rather than a major military one.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H3301.detail: Jiphdeja is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:25. He is presented as one of the sons of Shashak, alongside his brother Penuel and nine other brothers (Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Hananiah, Elam, and Anthothijah). These genealogies in the book of Chronicles record the families of the tribes after the division of the kingdom of Israel.
H3301.origine: The name Jiphdeja means "Jehovah will redeem" or "Jehovah redemption." It is composed of the Hebrew "yiph" (future: "will redeem") and "Jah" (abbreviation of the divine name). This name expresses a trust in God's future intervention, particularly in the redemption or deliverance of the people.
H3301.emploi: Jiphdeja is mentioned only once in the Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 8:25. He appears in the genealogies of Benjamin, which enumerate the descendants of the great families of this tribe. These genealogical lists, while not very narrative, preserve the names of Israel's ancestors and remind us of the importance of family and tribal heritage among God's people.

sens: To possess natural beauty, an attractive and pleasing appearance
To have brilliance, grace, splendor
To adorn, decorate, beautify something or oneself
H3302.detail:
1. Beauty as a primary quality: the word denotes physical beauty, an attractive appearance. In Psalms 45:3, the king is described as "the most beautiful of the sons of men," an image of perfection and royal distinction. It is a quality that stands out and is naturally pleasing.

2. Beauty as charm and seduction: beyond mere appearance, the word expresses charm, irresistible attraction. In Song of Solomon 4:10, we speak of the "charms" of love, meaning what enchants and captivates the heart, not just the eye.

3. The action of beautifying, adorning: the word can also refer to the action of making beautiful, decorating. In Jeremiah 4:30, the woman "beautifies herself" by putting on crimson and gold ornaments—gestures to enhance her appeal. In Jeremiah 10:4, one "beautifies" an idol with silver and gold to make it impressive.
H3302.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to shine" or "to radiate." This image of light and brilliance is at the core of all beauty in Hebrew: something beautiful is something that shines, that attracts the gaze. The same root can also mean "to beautify," showing that beauty can be innate or acquired, natural or cultivated.
H3302.emploi: The word appears eight times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in poetry and in contexts of love or splendor. In the Song of Solomon (4:10, 7:2, 7:7), it praises feminine beauty in the context of desire and marital love. In Psalms 45:3, it honors the beauty of the king as a reflection of his divine majesty. In Jeremiah (4:30, 10:4), it describes vain embellishment—human efforts to adorn oneself or to decorate idols—highlighting a biblical tension: beauty can be a gift from God, but also a temptation to pride.
H3302.portee: This word invites the reader to understand that beauty, in the Bible, is never purely superficial: it often reflects divine blessing, royalty, or love. But it can also become a trap—as in Jeremiah, where beautifying oneself or one's false idols expresses misplaced trust. For the Christian, this reminds us that true beauty, according to Scripture, flows from a relationship with God, not from outward adornment.

sens: Having an attractive and pleasant physical appearance.
Having a harmonious and balanced form or structure.
Remarkable, of good quality, or distinguished in its kind.
Morally or spiritually appealing, worthy of admiration.
H3303.detail:
1. The word primarily describes visible physical beauty: a woman with attractive features (Genesis 12:11), a man without defect from the soles of his feet to the top of his head (2 Samuel 14:25), animals that appear prosperous and healthy (Genesis 41:18). This is the beauty that one sees at first glance.

2. It also qualifies what possesses a beautiful form or structure, such as the mountain of Zion which "is beautiful," or a majestic and well-proportioned tree (Ezekiel 31:3, 31:9). This is the beauty of harmony and balance.

3. The word extends to what is excellent or remarkable in its kind: a woman of good appearance, a beautiful portion. It is less about the physical than about the overall quality and the effect that a person or thing produces.

4. In the Song of Songs, beauty becomes a deep and spiritual attraction: "How beautiful you are, my beloved" (1:16) expresses an admiration that goes beyond the physical, touching on desire and affection of the heart.
H3303.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing brightness and light that attracts the eye. It is from the same family as words meaning "to shine" or "to radiate." Beauty is conceived in Hebrew as something that radiates and captures the gaze: this is why the word can qualify a person, a landscape, an animal, or a moral quality.
H3303.emploi: This word appears 38 times in the Bible, mainly in the accounts of Genesis (Sarai, Rebekah, Joseph), the history of kings (Absalom, Adonijah), and the Song of Songs where it recurs as a leitmotif. In Genesis, the physical beauty of women exposes them to danger or enhances their value in the eyes of power. In 1 Samuel, it characterizes young and vigorous men destined to play important roles. The Song uses it to express mutual romantic admiration. The Psalms apply it to divine creation, particularly Zion. The word can denote fame or distinction rather than purely physical beauty, depending on the context.
H3303.portee: Beauty in the Bible is never purely superficial: it reflects harmony, vitality, and divine blessing. When God creates, He makes beautiful. But the Bible also warns that physical beauty can seduce and deceive (Proverbs 11:22: "Like a gold ring in a pig's snout is a beautiful woman who shows no discretion"). For the Christian, this word invites the search for true beauty: that of the soul, that which comes from love and faithfulness, and especially that which reflects God's creation in our lives.

sens: Having great beauty, remarkable elegance
Shining with splendor and appeal
H3304.detail:
1. This word describes something or someone of striking, radiant beauty. The repetition of the same word ("beautiful beautiful") reinforces the idea and gives a superlative force: not just beautiful, but very beautiful, of striking beauty. In Jeremiah 46:20, Egypt is compared to a "very beautiful heifer," symbolizing a splendid, rich, and flourishing nation.
2. This beauty can also evoke the brilliance, prosperity, or excellence of something considered as a whole. The word emphasizes what shines, what attracts the eye and inspires admiration.
H3304.origine: This word is formed by the repetition of a root meaning "beautiful." In Hebrew, doubling a word or a root is a common way to intensify it, to make it more vivid. It is a poetic device that gives the term a particular strength, as if to say "beautiful in double measure" or "magnificently beautiful." The construction enhances the visual and aesthetic image.
H3304.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 46:20. It describes Egypt in a prophetic oracle, just before the announcement of its judgment: the contrast between its beauty and its imminent downfall makes the message more striking. The use in a poetic and prophetic context emphasizes that this term belongs to the realm of grandeur and elegance, reserved for solemn descriptions.
H3304.portee: This word reminds us that external beauty and earthly prosperity can be fragile. Egypt, despite its splendor, cannot escape divine justice. For the reader, this passage invites us not to place our trust in the riches or appearance of the world, which pass away, but in the word of God that endures.

sens: Seaport on the southwestern coast of Canaan, in the territory of the tribe of Dan
Main port of Jerusalem during the reign of Solomon
City of commerce and transit for building materials
H3305.detail: 1. Joppa is a coastal city located on the Mediterranean shore, to the west of the territory of Israel, in the region that returned to the tribe of Dan (Joshua 19:46). 2. In the time of Solomon and the Second Temple, it became the major port through which precious materials would transit: it is through Joppa that the king brings down the cedars of Lebanon destined for the construction of the Temple (2 Chronicles 2:16, Ezra 3:7). 3. It is also the ordinary trading port, from which merchant ships depart; it is at Joppa that Jonah went down to flee by boat to Tarshish (Jonah 1:3), seeking to board a ship that led to distant maritime routes.
H3305.origine: The name Joppa means "beautiful," which suits a seaport well. In ancient Greek, the city is called Ioppē. It was a natural crossroads for maritime trade in the Mediterranean, a strategic location between Egypt, Phoenicia, and Asia Minor.
H3305.emploi: Joppa appears four times in the Hebrew Old Testament, always as an established and functional geographical location. In Joshua 19:46, it is listed among the cities of the territory of Dan. In the texts of the return from exile (2 Chronicles 2:16, Ezra 3:7), it plays the role of arrival port for the important supplies of wood from Lebanon. In the book of Jonah, it is the starting point of the prophet's flight, an active port from which one can embark towards the Mediterranean. In every instance, Joppa remains the port hub of the southern Levant.
H3305.portee: Joppa reminds the reader that the prosperity of Jerusalem and the Temple relied on commercial infrastructure and diplomatic relations: God provided His people with concrete means to build His house. It is also the starting point for Jonah, the place where one of the greatest stories of divine mercy is rooted: from this port departs the man who will flee from God before being saved and sent to carry divine grace to Nineveh.

sens: To breathe with effort or noise, to gasp
To express exhaustion or anguish through breathing
To manifest distress or moral suffering
H3306.detail: 1. The word primarily describes the physical action of breathing with difficulty, gasping: it is the breath that escapes the body when one is out of strength or shaken by emotion. 2. By extension, to sigh becomes the expression of inner turmoil: one who sighs manifests their exhaustion, deep anguish, their silent cry. In Jeremiah 4:31, the daughter of Zion — an image of Jerusalem facing invasion — sighs under distress: her body breathes poorly, her breath is torn away, while she stretches out her hands in a plea for help. It is the visible and audible sign of one who is defeated, who can only let out their anguished breath.
H3306.origine: The Hebrew verb yaphach comes from a root that imitates the sound of breath: the 'ph' (פ) evokes rough and forced breathing. The grammatical form used here (Hithpael) adds the idea that the subject is itself agitated by this breathing: it does not simply breathe, it breathes itself, it surrenders to this involuntary gasping. It is a verb that paints the body in distress.
H3306.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 4:31. In this dramatic prophetic context, Jeremiah hears the cries of a woman in labor — the image of Jerusalem giving birth in pain under the blows of the enemy. The sigh is not a restrained complaint, but the last breath of an overwhelmed city, capable only of breathing its sorrow and stretching its hands toward God. This hapax (unique word) concentrates all the gasping breath of agony.
H3306.portee: This word makes us hear the silent cry of one who suffers, when words fail and only breath remains. For the believer in distress, it is the reminder that God hears even the unarticulated sigh, the gasping of the heart that cannot find words. It is also the voice of Jerusalem that becomes the voice of the suffering Church: God sees the one who sighs.

sens: To exhale air, to blow
To inhale and exhale air regularly
To desire intensely, to think only of one thing
H3307.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the physical action of expelling air from the lungs, to blow. It is the image of breath coming out of oneself.
2. More generally, to breathe means the natural cycle of inhalation and exhalation that sustains life. It is the quintessential vital act.
3. Figuratively, to breathe something means to be filled with it, to think only of it, to desire it ardently — as if this state or desire were as natural and constant as breathing itself. In Psalms 27:12, the adversaries "breathe only violence": violence is their spiritual breath, what animates them, what they inhale at every moment.
H3307.origine: The Hebrew verb יָפַח (yaphaakh) comes from a root that imitates the sound and action of breath, of the breath that escapes. It belongs to a family of words related to wind, breath, and air. The image is very concrete: it is the sound and movement of breath escaping.
H3307.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Old Testament, in Psalms 27:12. David uses it to describe his adversaries: they "breathe only violence." It is a powerful metaphorical use that transforms physical breathing into an image of what completely animates someone, what defines them entirely. The choice of the verb is striking: violence is not an occasional act for them, it is their very essence, as natural and constant as breathing.
H3307.portee: This word reminds us that our thoughts, desires, and passions define us as deeply as breathing defines life. For the psalmist and for us, the question becomes: what do we aspire to? What do we exhale? Do we breathe violence and hatred, or justice and love? Spiritual breathing reveals the true state of our heart.

sens: Physical splendor of the body or face
Splendor, magnificence of a city or building
Perfection and harmony of form
Attractive and seductive charm
Glory and majesty of a person
H3308.detail:
1. Physical beauty of the face or body: the visible and pleasant shine of appearance. Queen Vashti is presented to show her "beauty" to the peoples (Esther 1:11), meaning her remarkable physical appearance. It is also what seduces: Proverbs 6:25 warns against the danger of coveting a woman "for her beauty."

2. The magnificence and splendor of a construction or city. Tyre is described as "perfect in beauty" (Ezekiel 27:4): all its architectural details and harmony make it radiant. It is the visible order, wealth, and brilliance in proportions and decoration.

3. The perfection and harmony of form — the absence of defect. The king of Tyre was "perfect in beauty" (Ezekiel 28:12), which emphasizes complete perfection in his appearance and composition. Ezekiel 16:14 speaks of the beauty acquired by Jerusalem after its embellishments.

4. The seductive charm and appeal that leads to desire. Ezekiel 16:15 states that Jerusalem "trusted in her beauty" and abused it for prostitution: beauty becomes a power of seduction that is misused.

5. The glory and majesty of a person of high rank. Isaiah 33:17 speaks of the king in his "magnificence," where beauty is inseparable from royalty and authority.
H3308.origine: The Hebrew word יפי (yofi) comes from the root יפה (yafah), which means "to be beautiful, to be pleasant to look at." This root evokes the idea of visible brilliance and harmony. It shares a similar family of meanings with other words of beauty in Hebrew: it designates less inner beauty than outer appearance and its brilliance. The word is common in the biblical text to describe both people (queens, young women) and places (Jerusalem, Tyre, the Temple).
H3308.emploi: The word "beauty" appears 19 times in the Old Testament, especially in the poetic and prophetic books. It primarily refers to the physical beauty of women (Esther 1:11; Proverbs 6:25; Proverbs 31:30), often in relation to seduction and moral danger. It also describes the splendor of cities: Tyre and Jerusalem are praised or blamed for their beauty (Ezekiel 16 to 28). Ezekiel also uses it to speak of the perfection of the king of Tyre. Isaiah 33:17 employs it for royal majesty. Finally, Zechariah 9:17 links it to divine goodness. Beauty in the Bible can be neutral (an object of contemplation), a goal of luxury (Ezekiel 27), or a moral trap (Ezekiel 16:15; Proverbs 6:25).
H3308.portee: Beauty is never presented as a value in itself: it can be a sign of grace, but also an occasion for pride and moral downfall. Proverbs 31:30 asserts that "charm is deceptive, and beauty is vain" — reminding us that outer beauty fades. For Jerusalem and Tyre, beauty becomes a mirror of their prosperity and their distance from God: it draws them into luxury and sin. Contemplating the beauty of the king in his majesty (Isaiah 33:17) points to the worship of God and His glory. This word invites the reader to look beyond appearances.

sens: king of Lachish at the time of the conquest of Canaan by Joshua
H3309G.detail: Japhia is the king of the city of Lachish (also called Lakis) at the time when Joshua conquers Canaan. He appears in Joshua 10:3 as one of the five kings of Lower Canaan who unite against Gibeon and against Israel, and who are ultimately defeated and put to death.
H3309G.origine: The name Japhia means "bright" or "radiant" in Hebrew, from the root that evokes light that shines or glows. It is a proper name borne by at least three different characters in the Old Testament: this king of Lachish, a city in the territory of Zebulun and Issachar, and a son of King David.
H3309G.emploi: Japhia appears only once in the biblical text, in Joshua 10:3. He is one of the five kings of southern Canaan who form a coalition against the city of Gibeon after it has made peace with Joshua. This military alliance fails: the armies of the five kings are defeated, and Japhia is killed along with his companions, signifying the breaking of the resistance of the Canaanite peoples against Israel's conquest.

sens: Location on the border between Zebulun and Issachar
H3309H.detail: Japhia is a small town mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the land distribution among the twelve tribes of Israel. It was located on the border between the territories of Zebulun and Issachar, in the mountainous region of northern Galilee. Its name means "that shines" or "radiant," likely evoking a site visible from afar on the heights (Joshua 19:12).
H3309H.origine: The name Japhia comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to shine" or "to radiate": the image of a bright light. This name likely reflects the characteristic of the place, perhaps a prominent peak or a site built on a height overlooking the surroundings.
H3309H.emploi: Japhia appears only once in the canonical Bible, in Joshua 19:12, at the time when God assigns the territories to the twelve tribes. This passage lists the cities and boundaries of the territory of Zebulun, and Japhia is mentioned as a landmark on the border between Zebulun and Issachar. This cadastral mention shows that it was a fairly well-known locality at the time, significant enough to serve as a boundary between two tribes.

sens: son of David
name of a city on the border of Zebulun and Issachar
name of a king of Lachish at the time of the conquest
H3309I.detail: 1. Japhia is a son of King David, born of one of his concubines. He appears in the lists of David's children enumerated in 2 Samuel 5:15 and 1 Chronicles 3:7 and 14:6, alongside his brothers Shobab, Nathan, Solomon, and other sons of the king. 2. A city also bore this name, located on the border between the territories of Zebulun and Issachar, probably present-day Yafa. 3. A king of Lachish named Japhia fought against Joshua at the time of Israel's conquest of Canaan.
H3309I.origine: The name Japhia means "radiant" or "that shines," evoking brightness and luminosity. The biblical context emphasizes its connection to the royal house of David.
H3309I.emploi: Japhia appears three times in the Old Testament, exclusively in the genealogical lists of David. In 2 Samuel 5:15 and 1 Chronicles 3:7 and 14:6, he is mentioned among the children born to David in Jerusalem. These genealogical lists enumerate the king's sons to establish the succession and continuity of the house of David. The name Japhia also designates a city in Canaan and a king of Lachish, showing the versatility of the name in Israel's history.
H3309I.portee: Japhia reminds us that the royal lineage of David included many sons and that the promise of the throne did not always come with unquestioned authority. His mention in the genealogies shows that God kept a faithful account of the chosen people and their descendants.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher during the time of the Judges
Son of Heber and brother of Shomer, Hotham, and Shua
H3310.detail: Japhleth is a man of the tribe of Asher mentioned in the genealogies of Israel before the monarchy. He is the son of Heber (1 Chronicles 7:32) and has brothers Shomer, Hotham, and Shua. He himself is the father of three sons: Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath (1 Chronicles 7:33).
H3310.origine: The name Japhleth means "he will deliver" in Hebrew, formed from the root of the verb "to deliver." It is a common theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing confidence in God's liberating action.
H3310.emploi: Japhleth appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles 7, in the genealogical list of the tribe of Asher. These verses place him in the lineage of Asher through Beriah and Heber, and enumerate his three sons. He embodies a branch of the tribe of Asher at a time prior to the establishment of the Israelite monarchy.

sens: Descendants of Japhlet, a man of the tribe of Asher
Inhabitants or clans of the southwestern border region of Ephraim
H3311.detail:
1. The Japhléthiens are the descendants of a family of Asher whose ancestor was named Japhlet. Japhlet himself was a man of the tribe of Asher who lived before the establishment of the monarchy in Israel, and his children Pasach, Bimhal, and Ashvath founded this family line.

2. The name also designates a region or territory: in Joshua 16:3, the Japhléthiens appear as a population occupying a specific area, on the southwestern border of Ephraim, between Lower Beth-Horon and Gezer, towards the sea. This territory marked an important geographical boundary during the division of the promised land among the tribes.
H3311.origine: The word comes from Japhlet (meaning "he escapes" or "one who escapes"), which was the name of a family of Asher. In Hebrew, the addition of the suffix -i creates an adjective of filiation or belonging: those who belong to the family of Japhlet. The Japhléthiens are thus identified by their genealogical link to this ancestor and by their location in the territory of Asher-Ephraim.
H3311.emploi: The Japhléthiens appear only once in the Bible, in Joshua 16:3, in the context of the division of the promised land among the tribes of Israel. The passage describes the borders of the tribe of Ephraim, and the Japhléthiens are mentioned as recognized local inhabitants or a clan in this border region. They are descendants of Asher who, while belonging to this tribe, occupied territory on the margins of Ephraim, reflecting the complex realities of settlement in Canaan after the conquest.

sens: father of Caleb
a Kenizzite
man of faith who entered Canaan
H3312G.detail:
1. Jephunné is the father of Caleb, one of the two spies that Moses sent to explore the promised land (Numbers 13:6). His name means "He will face" or "He will look," an image of one who confronts the future with confidence.

2. Jephunné was a Kenizzite, meaning a man from the clan of Kenaz, integrated into the people of Israel. This particular origin is recalled several times to accurately identify his son Caleb (Joshua 14:6, 14:14).

3. Jephunné is best known for being the father of Caleb, this man of faith who, alone with Joshua among the Hebrews who left Egypt, entered the land of Canaan (Numbers 14:30). His son maintained faith in God when all the others lost courage.
H3312G.origine: The Hebrew name יְפֻנֶּה (Yephunné) literally means "He will face" or "He will look," formed from the root פנה (panah) which evokes the action of turning, facing, directing one's gaze. This name evokes someone turned towards the future, ready to confront what comes. Jephunné also appears as the son of Jether and a descendant of Asher (according to 1 Chronicles 4:15), showing that there were several men with this name in Israel's history.
H3312G.emploi: Jephunné appears 15 times in the Bible, almost always as "father of Caleb." He is first encountered when Caleb is chosen as a spy for the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6). Then, his name appears in references to the promise that God made to Caleb alone to enter Canaan, while the entire generation of rebels would perish in the desert (Numbers 14:30; 26:65). After the conquest, Caleb recalls his genealogy — "Caleb, son of Jephunné, the Kenizzite" — when he claims Hebron as his inheritance (Joshua 14:6, 14:14). The name Jephunné thus becomes a symbol of the familial bond between a father and a son whose faith was exceptional.
H3312G.portee: Jephunné reminds us that faith is transmitted: his son Caleb became the quintessential man of trust and perseverance, alone with Joshua in believing that God would keep His promise. The fact that Caleb's genealogy is repeated throughout the narrative underscores the importance of this ancestry and invites the believer to see how God's promises are fulfilled in faithful families across generations.

sens: Man of the tribe of Asher, son of Jether
H3312H.detail: Jephunné is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the genealogical list of the tribe of Asher during the time of the divided monarchy. He is presented as the son of Jether and the brother of Pispa and Ara (1 Chronicles 7:38). His name literally means "he will face" or "he will be in front," evoking the idea of confrontation or presence face to face.
H3312H.origine: The name Jephunné comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of turning towards, facing, or presenting oneself before. This root suggests an active and direct presence. It is noteworthy that this name also designated another well-known character: the father of Caleb, the explorer of Canaan and man of faith from the tribe of Judah (Numbers 13:6). However, the character described here is a different man from the tribe of Asher.
H3312H.emploi: Jephunné appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 7:38, in the genealogical record of Asher established during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel. He is listed among the descendants of this tribe, with no other historical or personal information provided about his life. His limited appearance in the genealogical context indicates that he played no remarkable role in biblical history.

sens: To shine with a brilliant light, with strength and brilliance
To emit light or rays of light
To make appear, to manifest through clarity
To show oneself in splendor, to radiate
H3313.detail:
1. Resplendir means to shine brightly, like light that bursts forth with strength. It is the image of something that shines so intensely that one cannot look at it without being struck. When God shines from Sinai in Deuteronomy 33:2, we see the divine majesty manifested through glorious light.

2. The word also describes the emission of rays or beams of light. This is particularly clear when speaking of light that radiates or spreads. Job 37:15 states that God makes his sparkling cloud shine, as if rays of light are coming out from it.

3. Resplendir can also mean to manifest or make something known through light or clarity. When Job says in Job 10:3 "make your favor shine upon the counsel of the wicked," he is asking God to manifest his kindness and make it visible.

4. In the broadest sense, resplendir means to radiate, to show oneself in all one's splendor and beauty. Psalms 50:2 states that God shines from Zion as perfect beauty: he manifests himself in his absolute glory.
H3313.origine: The Hebrew verb יָפַע (yapa') comes from a root that evokes light that shines and spreads. The word family carries the fundamental idea of clarity and brightness. The Hebrew word is primarily used in the poetic and majestic passages of the Old Testament, particularly in the Psalms and Deuteronomy, to describe divine splendor or brilliant light.
H3313.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic books and majestically theological texts. In Deuteronomy 33:2, it describes the glorious appearance of God at Sinai. The Psalms use it to speak of divine radiance: Psalms 50:2 and Psalms 80:2 show God shining with his perfect beauty. In Job, the word takes on a broader nuance: it refers to both the physical light that radiates and the manifestation of divine favor. In Job 10:3, Job asks God to make his favor shine; in Job 37:15, he speaks of God making his cloud shine. The context of the Psalms and Deuteronomy reveals that resplendir is the prerogative of God and his sovereign majesty.
H3313.portee: This word invites the believer to contemplate the glory and beauty of God. Resplendir speaks of God who manifests himself with splendor and power, who cannot remain hidden. It is an invitation to recognize that God is luminous, pure, magnificent, and that his presence illuminates all that surrounds him. Meditating on this word helps to develop awe before the divine majesty and the certainty that God reigns with brilliance.

sens: Brilliant light, radiance that catches the eye
Resplendent beauty, apparent magnificence
Glory or prestige that inspires admiration
H3314.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes intense light, a brilliance that manifests visually: it is the radiant splendor of something that shines and captures attention. In Ezekiel 28:7, this "éclat" characterizes the wisdom of the king of Tyre, as if his knowledge were clothed in dazzling beauty.
2. It also evokes beauty in its most seductive and visible form: an external perfection that attracts gazes and enchants. Ezekiel 28:17 shows how this character became proud precisely of this shining beauty, confusing his magnificent appearance with his own worth.
3. By extension, it designates glory, prestige, everything that makes something or someone shine in the eyes of others and rise above the ordinary. It is less about substance than the visible brilliance that impresses and seduces.
H3314.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of standing out, radiating, shining on the surface. It is related to the image of something that emanates, that flows outward like visible light or splendor. The root evokes what appears, manifests, becomes apparent to the eyes.
H3314.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in Ezekiel 28, a passage that addresses a judgment against the king of Tyre. In verse 7, éclat is associated with the king's wisdom: it is a beauty that makes him remarkable. In verse 17, the same word describes the beauty of which the king became proud, leading to his downfall. In both cases, the context emphasizes the spiritual danger: this external éclat can become a trap, as it leads to self-deception and the sin of pride. Ezekiel thus opposes this apparent éclat to inner spiritual corruption.
H3314.portee: This word reminds us that external beauty, visible magnificence, and brilliant appearance should never be confused with true inner greatness. For the believer, it invites us not to be seduced by the deceptive éclat of appearances, especially worldly prestige or human honors, which can mask deep corruption. It calls us to seek true beauty, that of the heart and integrity before God, rather than that which dazzles the eyes.

sens: Third son of Noah
Ancestor of the peoples of the northern and eastern Mediterranean
H3315.detail:
1. Japhet is the third son of Noah, born before the flood. He enters the ark with his family (Genesis 7:13) and comes out after the flood with his brothers Shem and Ham (Genesis 9:18). During the incident of Noah's drunkenness, Japhet and Shem honor their father by covering him with modesty, unlike Ham (Genesis 9:23).
2. Japhet receives a special blessing from Noah: "May God enlarge Japhet's territory" (Genesis 9:27). His descendants—Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, Meshech, and Tiras—scatter after the flood and occupy the lands of the north and east, extending towards the Mediterranean, Europe, and Asia.
H3315.origine: The name Japhet means "he has opened" or "opening." This etymology refers to the idea of expansion and extension: God "opens" the territory of Japhet, his descendants spread and extend widely. The name thus evokes the destiny of his lineages: a geographical radiance that contrasts with the intention of Canaan, son of Ham, destined to serve.
H3315.emploi: Japhet appears 11 times in the Old Testament, primarily in Genesis (5:32; 6:10; 7:13; 9:18; 9:23; 9:27; 10:1; 10:2; 10:21) and in 1 Chronicles (1:4; 1:5). He is first presented as one of the three sons of Noah born before the flood. After the flood, the Bible recounts his respectful attitude towards his father and the blessing he receives. Genesis 10 lists his seven sons, who become the fathers of distinct nations and peoples, establishing his lineage as a major line of post-flood humanity.
H3315.portee: Japhet embodies filial kindness and respect towards parents: unlike Ham, he honors his father in his vulnerability. His blessing shows that God promises not only survival but also expansion and prosperity to those who live in fear and righteousness. For the believer, Japhet reminds us that God blesses integrity and that the descendants of the righteous fill the earth.

sens: City of the tribe of Judah
H3316G.detail: 1. Jiphtach was a city located in the territory that had been assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the Promised Land. It appears in the list of cities that Joshua enumerates to delineate the inheritance of this tribe (Joshua 15:43).
H3316G.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "he opens" (from the root פתח, pataḥ). It is a theophoric name, common in Israel, which perhaps expresses the idea of a city being "open" or of doors wide open, or entrusting to God its "opening" towards prosperity.
H3316G.emploi: Jiphtach appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:43, where it is mentioned among the cities that Joshua lists to describe the land inheritance of the tribe of Judah. It held a modest place in this territory, in the region of the lowlands of the south.

sens: A judge of Israel during the time of the Judges, son of the Gileadite
A warrior who defeated the Ammonites
A man who made a vow to the Lord before battle
H3316H.detail:
1. Jephthé is a judge of Israel mentioned in the Book of Judges. He is presented as "a mighty warrior" (Judges 11:1), the son of a prostitute and the Gileadite, which immediately places him on the margins of his own family.
2. Jephthé is best known as the warrior whom the elders of Gilead called to lead the battle against the Ammonites. He decisively defeated this people, as reported in Judges 11:32: "Jephthé went against the Ammonites."
3. Jephthé is the biblical character whose bold vow forever changed his destiny. Before entering battle, he promised the Lord: "If you give the Ammonites into my hands, whatever comes out of the door of my house to meet me... I will offer it as a burnt offering" (Judges 11:30-31). This vow, fulfilled after the victory, determines his entire place in biblical history.
H3316H.origine: The name Jephthé means "he opens" in Hebrew, perhaps evoking the idea of opening or beginning. It is a name that does not carry any explicit religious connotation, unlike many other Hebrew names, which may highlight the humility of his origins or the particular place he occupies in the history of Israel.
H3316H.emploi: Jephthé appears in the Book of Judges almost exclusively (27 occurrences out of 29), notably in Judges 11-12, where his story occupies a chapter and a half. He is seen once outside of this context, cited by Samuel as one of the great deliverers of Israel (1 Samuel 12:11). His actions follow a dramatic arc: family rejection (Judges 11:2), call to power (Judges 11:6), diplomatic negotiation (Judges 11:14), the fateful vow (Judges 11:30), the victory (Judges 11:32), and finally the painful fulfillment of the vow (Judges 11:34-40). He dies after judging Israel for six years.
H3316H.portee: Jephthé embodies the tension between faith in the Lord and the unpredictable consequences of our promises. His story reminds us that God uses imperfect and even despised men to accomplish His plans, but it also warns against rash vows. For the Christian reader, it teaches the importance of carefully considering commitments to God and understanding that the Lord prefers mercy over sacrifice.

sens: Valley between the territories of Zebulun and Asher
Region in northern Palestine, at the borders of the territory of Asher
H3317.detail:
1. Jiphthach-El is a valley located in northern Palestine, used as a landmark to delineate the borders of the lands assigned to the tribes of Israel during the division of Canaan. Its name means "God opens," evoking the idea of an opening or passage in the mountainous terrain. It appears in the descriptions of the borders of the territory of Asher (Joshua 19:27) where it serves as the northern boundary.
2. This valley marked an important point in the tribal geography of Israel, serving to precisely identify the contours of the promised lands. Although mentioned twice in Joshua, its exact location in Palestine remains uncertain for modern geographers, but it was clearly recognized as a significant landmark during the establishment of Israel in the land of Canaan.
H3317.origine: The name Jiphthach-El is formed from two Hebrew elements: "yiphthach" ("he opens" or "God opens") and "el" ("God"). This composition reflects a common practice in the Old Testament of giving places theophoric names (containing the divine name) that celebrate the action or characteristic of God. The term evokes the idea of an opening created by God, perhaps to symbolize the access or passage that God granted to His people in this region.
H3317.emploi: Jiphthach-El appears only twice in the Bible, both in the Book of Joshua, chapter 19, where the borders of the tribal territories are enumerated. It is mentioned as a boundary of the territory of Asher in Joshua 19:14 and again in Joshua 19:27, where it serves as a landmark to describe the precise contours of this region. Its role is purely geographical and administrative: it allows for the exact location of where one tribe's territory ends and another begins. No particular biblical event is attached to this place.

sens: To go or come outside, to cross a threshold or boundary
To head towards, to set out, to depart
To emerge, to spring forth, to escape
To be produced, to originate, to come forth
To bring out, to extract, to pull outside
To lead outside, to conduct, to extract
H3318G.detail:
1. The simplest and most common meaning: to leave a closed or limited place to go outside. The raven that Noah releases "goes out" of the ark (Genesis 8:7); Ehud "went out" from the king's chamber (Judges 3:23). It is the physical action of crossing a door, a threshold.

2. To set out, to depart for a journey or direction. Abram "went out" from the land of Chaldea and Lot "went out" with him (Genesis 12:4); the children of Israel "went out" of Egypt at the time of the Exodus (Exodus 13:3). The word here denotes the act of beginning a journey.

3. To spring forth or escape: the branches of the lampstand "go out" from the central trunk (Exodus 37:19), or the entrails that "come out" of the body (2 Chronicles 21:19). It is what emerges or comes forth from its place of origin.

4. To originate from, to be derived from. When the Hebrew definition speaks of what comes from a source or a person, it means the origin or production: what is born, what emanates.

5. In causative forms (Hiphil), the verb changes: the one who acts brings someone else out. The Lord "brings out" the children of Israel from Egypt with power (Exodus 13:3). It is the action of extracting, liberating, leading outside.

6. To bring outside, to pull from, to extract. Pharaoh "brings out" (sends away) the people of Israel (Exodus 12:31); the Lord "pulls" His people from slavery.
H3318G.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצָא (yatsa) has at its root the basic idea of crossing, surpassing a limit. It is linked to the image of passage and exit. In the Hebrew Bible, it is a simple and universal verb; it is found in many concrete contexts (going out of a house, departing on a journey, springing forth, being produced). Its natural opposite is בּוֹא (bo'a), "to enter." The verb has active forms (Qal: I go out) and causative forms (Hiphil: I bring out), allowing the Bible to describe both free action and action imposed by another.
H3318G.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Hebrew Bible (575 occurrences). It is found everywhere: in Genesis to describe the movements of people and animals, in Exodus to recount the liberation from Egypt (a central theme), in Judges and Kings for the movements of warriors and kings. In the simple form (Qal), it describes the own movement: someone goes away, something flows out. In the causative form (Hiphil), it is God or a king who "brings out," "liberates," "sends away." The context changes the nuance: to go out can be a simple movement, an escape, a liberating exodus, or an expulsion. The French translation varies (sortir, aller, partir, venir) depending on whether the movement is viewed from the inside or outside.
H3318G.portee: For the believing reader, this verb is loaded with theological meaning. The Exodus is not just an exit from Egypt: it is God's liberation, the moment when He "brings out" His people from slavery to freedom and the promised land. This verb reminds us that God acts, that He leads, that He saves. It also invites reflection on our own exit from sin and our walk towards God: just as the people of Israel had to "go out" of Egypt, the believer is called to come out of the world of sin.

sens: To go out from a place, to leave a location
To manifest, appear, emerge
To be produced, to result from something
To lead someone out, to take them out of a place
To draw something from a set for use
H3318H.detail:
1. To go out from a place, to leave a location: this is the primary image of the word — physically leaving a space to go elsewhere. When Noah "brings out" the animals from the ark (Genesis 8:17), he opens the doors and the animals go out onto the land. It is a simple movement: to depart, to leave, to distance oneself.
2. To manifest, appear, emerge: the word takes on meaning when something moves from the invisible or from the inside to the visible or to the outside. When God says "Come out" to Abraham while showing him the stars (Genesis 15:5), He invites Abraham to step outside his tent to see. It is to make appear, to show, to reveal.
3. To be produced, to result from something: to go out also means what comes from, what is derived from. When one "draws" horses from Egypt (2 Chronicles 9:28), these are horses that one obtains by drawing from the Egyptian stock. It is an act of extraction.
4. To lead someone out, to take them out of a place: in an active sense, "to bring out" someone means to take them outside, often with authority. When Pashhur "brings out" Jeremiah from prison (Jeremiah 20:3), he frees him by leading him outside. It is an act of liberation or dismissal.
5. To draw something from a set for use: it is to extract something from its reserve. When one "brings out" horses, one takes them from a herd for use. It is the idea of taking, making available.
H3318H.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that appears in several words of the family: "exit," "seed" (that which comes out of the earth or the body), "origin." The basic image is the movement outward, the passage from inside to outside. It is a very concrete verb, rooted in the observation of daily life: leaving a building, going to war, letting out animals, giving birth. The Bible also uses it in a figurative sense: a word "comes out" of the mouth, a curse "comes out" from a person, a judgment "comes out" from a court.
H3318H.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (253 occurrences in Hebrew). It appears in all the books, from the Pentateuch to the Prophets. From Genesis, it denotes the movement from one place to another. But above all, it becomes a key word of the Exodus: God "brings out" Israel from Egypt, which occurs 40 times in the cited usages. It is a foundational event that Moses recalls to Pharaoh (Exodus 3:10), that the Law commemorates (Exodus 13:3, 13:14), and that God Himself states as His signature (Exodus 20:2: "I am the Lord your God who brought you out of Egypt"). The verb is also used for concrete acts: sending away a son (Judges 6:30), freeing a slave (Leviticus 25:54), producing a harvest (Leviticus 26:10). It can also mean "to give life" or "to give birth" in certain contexts.
H3318H.portee: This verb encapsulates the history of salvation: God is the one who "brings out" His people from slavery, who delivers them, who frees them. That is why the Bible asks believers to remember the day when God "brought them out" (Exodus 13:3) — it is a promise kept, a commitment to freedom. For the Christian, this word reminds that God acts, that He intervenes in history, that He breaks the chains of oppression and gives a future to His people. It is the biblical image of a God who does not remain distant, but who manifests and acts to save.

sens: To move from one place to another, to leave a location
To advance in a direction, to head towards
To extend from one point to another (for a limit, a boundary)
To go forward, to progress
To come out of, to be derived from
To be delivered, to be released (passive sense)
H3318I.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: to leave a place to go elsewhere. Jacob "departed" from Beer-Sheba (Genesis 28:10): he left that place and set out for Haran. It is the simple movement of departure.
2. To actively advance in a specific direction, with intention. After turning south of the ascent of Akrabbim, the boundary "will continue" by Hazar-addar (Numbers 34:4): the boundary line progresses, extending from one point to another.
3. To gradually extend in space, particularly for boundaries and territorial limits. The "portion" of the sons of Joseph extended from the Jordan and "continued to the Jordan" (Joshua 16:7): it is a progression that leads to a limit.
4. To go forward, to proceed continuously. The boundary line "continued" towards Rimmon and then extended to Neah (Joshua 19:13): continuous movement of a line in geographical space.
5. To come from, to be derived from something. Related to the idea of "going out," this meaning expresses origin or emergence.
6. To be led, brought, delivered (by an external authority). The passive form of the verb expresses the act of being taken outside or being released.
H3318I.origine: The root יצא (yts) fundamentally expresses the idea of movement outward, crossing a boundary. It likely has as its primary image the act of exiting a closed space. The verb also covers figurative uses related to the idea of progression or spatial extension. The forms of the verb (Qal for simple action, Hiphil for the causative action "to bring out") show the richness of this movement: to act by oneself or to be acted upon by an external force.
H3318I.emploi: This verb appears 21 times in the provided usages, almost exclusively in the books of Joshua dedicated to the delineation of the lands of Israel. The original meaning "to depart, to go" (Genesis 28:10) is the starting point. But the dominant usage concerns the drawing of boundaries: the verb describes how a boundary line "continues," "extends," or "stretches" from one geographical point to another. Translations vary ("to depart," "to continue," "to extend") depending on the context, but the idea remains that of directed spatial progression. In 2 Chronicles 21:19, the verb seems to apply to the end of an illness, as an extension towards the end. The Bible thus uses this word for both the action of leaving and the idea of advancing, progressing, extending.
H3318I.portee: This word invites reflection on the biblical notion of territory and promise. The lands of Israel are not vague or indefinite: they have precise boundaries, "carefully continued." This shows that God gives His people a defined and secure inheritance. The verb "to depart" also reminds us that faith in action means moving towards the promise, as Abraham and Jacob did. It is to move, to progress, not to remain stagnant.

sens: To go out, come outside, depart
To go toward a place or in a direction
To produce a result, to end up
To be designated by lot, to fall to someone
To be delivered, to be handed over to someone
H3318J.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: "to go out" or "to go outside." It is the action of leaving a place, crossing a boundary or an opening. Joshua 18:11 speaks of a "portion" that "fell" in the sense of "came to rest" — literally, the lot "went out" and designated Benjamin.

2. The verb also describes a directional movement: to go toward, to head toward, to advance toward a destination. In Numbers 33:54, the families receive portions according to the lot that "goes out" — it is the result of an action that progresses.

3. The word means "to result in" or "to have as a result" — the idea that something "comes out" of a decision or an act. The lot "goes out" and someone receives an inheritance.

4. Specifically here: to be designated by drawing lots, to receive by lot. Joshua 19:1 says that the second "portion" "fell" to Simeon — the lot designated him. It is the image of chance or divine verdict that "comes out" and determines who receives what.

5. To be delivered or handed over: Joshua 21:4 speaks of the cities that "fell" to the Levites — they were assigned to them or placed in their possession.
H3318J.origine: The root יצא expresses the action of going out, going outside, crossing a boundary — the basic image of an exit, an emergence. In Hebrew, it is very common and very ancient. The word conjugates in different modes: in the simple mode (Qal), it means "to go out"; in the causative voice (Hiphil), it means "to bring out, to lead outside." In the context of drawing lots, it is the causative or passive sense that dominates: something or someone is "brought out" of the urn or the drawing, designated by divine will.
H3318J.emploi: This verb appears about 11 times in the provided biblical usages, almost exclusively in the context of the division of the land of Israel (Book of Joshua, Numbers, 1 Chronicles). Each time, it describes how the lot designates a portion of territory or a city. Numbers 33:54 states the principle: they divide "by lot," meaning they let the lot (or God by the lot) "bring out" the name of each family or tribe. Joshua 18:11, 19:1, 19:17, 19:24, 19:32 repeat the same formula: "the (n-th) portion fell [by lot] to (such tribe)." Joshua 21:4 and 1 Chronicles 24:7, 25:9, 26:14 apply the same verb to the division of Levitical cities or priestly service rotations. The word thus designates a process ordained by God, where apparent chance conceals a divine will.
H3318J.portee: This verb reminds us that in the Bible, the lot is never truly chance: it is God who "brings out" the results and distributes to each their portion. For the believer, this teaches that the circumstances of our lives — even those that seem due to chance — are ultimately in God's hands. The repetition of this verb in the division of Canaan affirms that the possession of the land is not human conquest, but a divine gift distributed equitably according to His wisdom.

sens: To appear above the horizon, speaking of the sun or a celestial body
To begin to shine, to show oneself with strength and clarity
To occur, to arrive (in the sense of becoming visible or manifest)
H3318K.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning: the sun rises on the horizon, emerging from the earth to illuminate the sky. It is the image of morning being born. In Genesis 19:23, the text says, "The sun was rising on the earth" at the moment Lot enters the city of Zoar: it is the beginning of the day, the moment when light appears.

2. Beyond the physical rising, the word evokes the manifestation of power and strength. In Judges 5:31, those who love God are compared to the sun "when it appears in its strength": the image is no longer just the appearance, but the dazzling brilliance that dominates everything. The sun does not merely rise; it shows itself in all its power.

3. The word can also designate anything that becomes visible or manifest, anything that emerges or arrives. In Isaiah 13:10, the "rising of the sun" is mentioned to indicate that it will appear: the moment it becomes visible. It is a passage from the invisible to the visible.
H3318K.origine: The Hebrew root יצא (yassa) fundamentally means "to go out, to go outside." The rising sun is the sun that "comes out" from under the horizon, that emerges. This root is also used for going out of a city, leaving a place, or figuratively for "coming" or "occurring." In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this Hebrew verb is often rendered by a Greek verb meaning "to rise" or "to appear," hence the translation "to appear" found here.
H3318K.emploi: This Hebrew verb appears three times in the provided passages, but only in the context of the rising of the sun or celestial bodies. In Genesis 19:23, it simply marks the moment of day when Lot arrives at Zoar — a time marker. In Judges 5:31, the context is more poetic and spiritual: the image of the rising sun becomes a metaphor for the victory and strength of those who serve God. In Isaiah 13:10, in a context of divine judgment, the darkened sun will no longer be able to rise — its light ceases to appear. In these three usages, the word describes the appearance of celestial light as a significant and visible moment.
H3318K.portee: For the believer, the rising sun reminds us that each day is a new gift from God, a moment when His creation manifests. When Scripture compares the righteous to the rising sun (Judges 5:31), it invites us to shine with justice and the presence of God to others. It is an invitation to be a visible, manifest light, like the sun that rises and cannot be hidden.

sens: To move out of a place, to leave a location
To gush, to escape from a source or a hearth
To emerge, to push, to grow outward
To flow or occur as a result, a consequence
To bring out, to take outside, to release (in the causative form)
H3318L.detail:
1. To go out or leave a place: this means to leave one location to go elsewhere. For example, a river "goes out" of Eden (Genesis 2:10) by flowing out of its source. This is the most common and concrete meaning of the verb.

2. To gush or escape: this is when something bursts forth forcefully from a place. The water that "comes out" of the rock struck by Moses gushes to quench the people (Numbers 20:8). The fire that "comes out" of the burning bush escapes in flames (Judges 9:15).

3. To emerge or push: this is particularly for plants and branches that extend outward. The branches of the lampstand "come out" from the central trunk (Exodus 37:21). A flower "comes forth" or "emerges" from the ground before withering (Job 14:2).

4. To be produced or result: this is when something proceeds from a source or cause. The words that "come out" of the mouth come from the heart. This is a more figurative sense, related to the idea of origin or emission.

5. To bring out, to take outside: this is the active form where someone else causes the exit. Moses must "bring out" the water from the rock. God "brings out" the people from Egypt with power and authority.
H3318L.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצָא (yatsa) is a very ancient root that evokes the fundamental idea of movement outward, crossing a boundary. The image of departure is that of passage, of going out. This root is related to the idea of emergence: something that was hidden or enclosed becomes visible and manifest. It is very frequent in biblical Hebrew and is used for both physical movements and more abstract realities.
H3318L.emploi: The verb "to go out" appears 49 times in the Old Testament. It is used in all registers: historical (the exodus from Egypt, departure to war), descriptive (river that goes out of Eden, branches that come out of the lampstand), and even prophetic. Its meaning varies slightly depending on the context. In creation and descriptive narratives, it describes what emerges naturally (water, fire, plants). In action narratives, it evokes a voluntary or provoked departure. The causative form (to bring out) emphasizes authority and power: this is how God "brings out" Israel from Egypt. The word is also used for violent or unexpected phenomena: a disease that "comes out" of the body (2 Chronicles 21:15), a fire that "comes out" of the sanctuary (Leviticus 9:24).
H3318L.portee: This verb invites the believer to meditate on the idea of liberation and emergence. When the Bible speaks of God "bringing out" His people from Egypt, it affirms that He breaks chains and manifests His power. Conversely, "to go out" oneself can mean accepting God's will and moving forward in faith. The word also carries a promise of fruitfulness: God "brings out" water from the rock, plants from the soil, life from situations that seem dead. It is a call to trust in God's creative power.

sens: To go or come outside, to leave a place
To manifest, to appear
To be born, to come into the world
To emanate, to originate from
To produce, to give birth to (plants, fruits)
To be derived from, to descend from
H3318M.detail:
1. To go or come outside, to leave a place: the most basic meaning of the verb, that of a movement of exit. The word evokes someone or something that crosses a threshold, a door, a boundary (Exodus 32:24).
2. To manifest, to appear: what was hidden or retained becomes visible and known. It is the moment when something is revealed to the open, like light that bursts forth (Job 12:22).
3. To be born, to come into the world: the image of exit applies to the child who is born, who leaves the mother's womb or the entrails of his mother. Examples: Genesis 25:25-26 (Esau and Jacob come out of Rebekah's womb), or 2 Chronicles 6:9 (the son born from David's loins).
4. To emanate, to originate from: what springs forth from a source, a person, or a will; what has its origin in something else. Thus, children "come out" from a father’s loins (Genesis 35:11) and kings "will come out" from his descendants.
5. To produce, to give birth to (plants, fruits): used for the creation or appearance of living things. The earth "produces" greenery and trees (Genesis 1:12), and this also includes what comes from a tree or a vine (Judges 13:14).
6. To be derived from, to descend from: to establish a lineage or origin. This meaning emphasizes that a person or group derives its existence from an ancestor (Exodus 1:5: "the souls that came out of Jacob's loins").
H3318M.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצָא (yatsá) comes from a very ancient root that expresses the idea of crossing, traversing, bringing out. The basic image is that of movement outward, of passing from a closed space to an open space. This same root also produces words to designate a door or a portal (the place from which one goes out). It is a very common verb in Hebrew, and it carries within it all the richness of movement: to go out can mean fleeing, being born, emanating, or appearing.
H3318M.emploi: The verb appears 41 times in the provided usages, mainly in historical and poetic books (Genesis, Exodus, Job, Psalms). It primarily carries a physical and literal sense: to go out of a place, to leave (Exodus 32:24). But its usage quickly expands to the realm of generation and descent: children "come out" of their mother's womb or their father's loins, which is the dominant usage in Genesis (Genesis 25:25-26, 35:11, 38:28-30). It also applies to natural production, that of plants and the earth (Genesis 1:12, 1:24), or to what emanates from a source or will. In some contexts, it carries a nuance of deliverance or manifestation (Job 12:22). The context determines the exact meaning: a pregnant woman giving birth, the earth producing herbs, an ancestor from whom kings descend—these are variations around the fundamental theme of exit and emergence.
H3318M.portee: This rich verb teaches the reader that everything that exists proceeds from a source: creatures are born, plants grow, peoples descend from their fathers. The Bible uses יָצָא to show the chain of generations and the continuity of life according to God's plan. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize his origin and that of everything around him: everything "comes out" from God in the ultimate sense, and everything that is born in our lives comes from His creative will.

sens: Who has the strength and age required to fight
Fit to serve in the army
Able for war
H3318N.detail:
1. This word designates one who possesses the physical capacity and age to fight — literally "fit" to bear arms and march into battle. In the census of Israel, those "fit to bear arms" are counted (Numbers 1:3), meaning men aged twenty and older, deemed strong and mature enough for war.
2. The term thus qualifies a valid warrior, capable of wielding the sword, bow, and shield. Texts refer to "men fit to go to the army" (1 Chronicles 5:18), distinguishing those who can serve from those who are too young, sick, or weak.
H3318N.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that primarily means "to go out, to go outside" — the basic image is that of one who "goes out" to fight or accomplish a mission. In Hebrew, to say someone "goes out" for war means they are mobilizable, able to act. The military context (bearing arms, going to the army) has specialized the word towards the idea of capacity to fight.
H3318N.emploi: The word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the military census texts of Numbers and Chronicles. It is used to qualify men fit to form an army: during the first census of Israel (Numbers 1), the men "fit to bear arms" are counted twelve times by tribe. The same usage appears during other military recruitments (1 Chronicles 5:18; 2 Chronicles 25:5). It is an administrative and military term that sets the objective criteria for mobilization.
H3318N.portee: This word reminds us that strength and capacity for service are not given to all in the same way — they depend on age, health, and equipment. It invites the reader to recognize their own limits and those of others, and to accept that God calls each according to what they are truly capable of doing, not according to pretensions.

sens: To move out of a place, to leave
To emanate, to originate from somewhere
To be pronounced, to escape from the mouth
To be produced, to manifest, to spread
H3318O.detail:
1. To move out of a place, to leave: the physical movement of leaving a location. This is the most basic sense of the verb. For example, in Numbers 32:24, the Gadites and Reubenites must go out of their lands to enter Canaan.

2. To emanate, to originate from somewhere: that which comes from a source, originates from a place or person. Thus in Isaiah 51:4, the Law goes out from the Lord, proceeding from His will and authority.

3. To be pronounced, to escape from the mouth: the words that leave a person's mouth, what has been said. This is very common: in Numbers 30:3, a word "that has gone out" from a man's mouth means a word he has spoken and for which he is responsible. In Esther 7:8, a word comes out of the king's mouth with authority and immediate effect.

4. To be produced, to manifest, to spread: that which emerges or unfolds, like a feeling, a cry, or a message. In Proverbs 29:11, passion comes out of the mouth of the fool, escaping without restraint. In Psalms 19:5, the voice of the heavens goes out and spreads throughout the earth.
H3318O.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצָא (yatsa) comes from a root expressing the fundamental idea of "leaving a closed space, crossing a boundary." The different forms of the verb (simple, causative) reflect this idea: the Qal (simple form) means "to go out" oneself, while the causative form (Hiphil) means "to cause to go out, to bring outside." This root appears in many words of the same family in Hebrew. The meaning has naturally extended from physical movement to speech, as speech also "goes out" of the body, crossing the barrier of the lips.
H3318O.emploi: The verb יָצָא is very frequent in the Hebrew Bible (about 1000 occurrences). It appears in virtually all types of texts: historical narratives, poetry, wisdom, prophecy. Its meanings nuance according to context: it first means "to depart, to set out" (Numbers 32:24), then "to emanate, to originate" (Isaiah 51:4), and especially "to be pronounced" when it comes to words (Numbers 30:3, Esther 7:8). The word that "goes out" is particularly important: it engages the one who pronounces it (a vow, a promise, a judgment). In biblical poetry and wisdom, the word also designates what escapes from the heart or mind — a feeling, a desire, an expressed thought (Proverbs 29:11).
H3318O.portee: This word invites the believer to take responsibility for their words. In the Bible, the word that "goes out" of the mouth is not empty: it engages the one who pronounces it, it carries weight and consequences. This is why Ecclesiastes advises to "guard" one's words (Ecclesiastes 5:1). The believer must also understand that their words reveal what is in their heart — what comes out of the mouth exposes the inner disposition. It is an exhortation to vigilance, wisdom, and the fear of God in the use of words.

sens: to go or come outside, to leave a place
to head towards, to move towards (with a purpose)
to manifest, to appear
to surrender, to capitulate (referring to a person)
to faint, to lose courage (of the heart)
H3318P.detail:
1. To go out means to move towards the outside, to leave a closed or confined place to go outside. This is the most direct and common sense of the verb: to go outside, to leave, to depart. In Jeremiah 38:21, the prophet asks the king if he refuses to go out, meaning to leave the besieged city.

2. The verb can also express the idea of advancing in a direction, moving towards something with a goal. This includes the act of going to a place or presenting oneself before someone, as when Jeremiah tells the king: "If you go to the leaders of the king of Babylon" (Jeremiah 38:17).

3. To go out can mean to appear, to manifest, to emerge — the image of something coming outside, becoming visible or known.

4. In a context of conflict or siege, to surrender means to present oneself to the enemy to capitulate, to abandon resistance and give one's life to the one being faced. It is an act of submission: the king must choose between going out to surrender or staying and perishing (Jeremiah 38:17-18).

5. Finally, the word can denote a fainting of the heart, a loss of courage, an impression of fainting. In Genesis 42:28, the hearts of Joseph's brothers "failed" when they discovered the money returned in their sack: it is as if their hearts "went out" of place, collapsing from fear.
H3318P.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצָא (yatsa) comes from a root expressing movement towards the outside. Its primary image is that of going out, crossing a threshold, leaving a closed space. This root is found in many Hebrew words related to departure, passage, and appearance. The verb has two main forms: a simple form (Qal) that simply means "to go outside," and a causative form (Hiphil) that means "to cause to go out, to lead outside, to conduct." This flexibility allows the word to express both the physical movement of a person and the action of someone else pushing them outside.
H3318P.emploi: The verb יָצָא is one of the most frequent verbs in the Hebrew Bible. It primarily expresses physical movement: to go outside, to leave a place. But it acquires particular nuances according to context. In the prophet Jeremiah, especially during the siege of Jerusalem, the word takes on a martial sense: to surrender then means to go out of the fortified city to deliver oneself to the enemy. It is a choice that determines life or death (Jeremiah 38:17-18, 38:21). In Genesis 42:28, the heart that "goes out" or "faints" expresses a sudden loss of courage, an intense fear — the idea is that the heart, the seat of life and courage, escapes from the body. The word illustrates how the same root can describe very different realities: physical movement, military surrender, and an emotional state.
H3318P.portee: This verb invites the reader to reflect on two levels. First, it speaks of concrete choices, decisions that force us to "go out" of our apparent security: to flee, to surrender, to face the unknown. Secondly, it reveals the link between our actions and our emotions: the heart that faints (loses courage) and the actions we take (surrendering, fleeing) are intimately connected. For the believer, this verb reminds us that trust in God is stronger than fear, and that sometimes obeying God requires us to "go out" of our human refuges.

sens: Bring a project to its conclusion, carry it through to the end
Finish, completely complete
H3319.detail:
1. This Aramaic verb primarily means to bring an action or work to its conclusion: to complete it, to carry it to its final outcome. In Ezra 6:15, it describes the completion of the temple rebuilt after the exile: "the house was completed," meaning that the reconstruction work was brought to its full conclusion.
2. The meaning extends to the idea of finishing, of completing: bringing to an end what was in progress. The emphasis is on the outcome, not just the stopping, but the effective realization to the end.
H3319.origine: This Aramaic verb derives from the same root as the Hebrew verb "yatsa" (יָצָא), which means "to go out" or "to come." The Aramaic strengthens it with a prefix (Shaphel) that conveys the idea of causation and completeness: not just to go out, but to bring out, extract, and by extension, to bring to completion. The family of words shares the idea of movement toward a goal, transformed here into completion, into conclusion.
H3319.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 6:15, a text written in Aramaic. It describes the moment when the exiled Israelites complete the reconstruction of the second temple under the reign of Darius. The context shows a people mobilized to finish this holy work. It is a rare word, characteristic of biblical Aramaic, used to express the accomplishment of a great collective endeavor.
H3319.portee: This word reminds the believer of the importance of perseverance and faithfulness until the end of a task. The rebuilt temple symbolizes the restoration of the people's relationship with God after the exile. To complete means here not to abandon, even when the task is long, but to persevere until the work is established.

sens: To place oneself in a location, to stand up
To remain in one place, to wait
To be present before someone or something
To oppose, to resist
To persist, to endure, to be established
H3320.detail:
1. To place oneself in a location, to stand up: the word primarily means to take a physical position, to stand in a specific place. When Moses' sister "stood at a distance" to watch the child (Exodus 2:4), she was taking her position of observation. The angel of the Lord "stood on the way" (Numbers 22:22) to block Balaam's path.
2. To remain in one place, to wait: the word also describes the act of staying fixed, without moving. When Samuel tells the people, "Wait here still" (1 Samuel 12:16), he uses this verb to ask the people to remain in place.
3. To be present before someone or something: it also means to appear or present oneself before someone, especially before God. Moses and the elders "presented themselves" before the Lord (Exodus 19:17), standing in His presence.
4. To oppose, to resist: the word can express resistance, the act of facing without retreating. No one will "stand" before Joshua (Joshua 1:5) means that no one will be able to resist him. Job asks, "Who then could stand before me?" (Job 41:1), using this verb to speak of opposition.
5. To persist, to endure, to be established: the verb can finally mean that something remains in place, established, durable. When God promises, "No one will stand before you all the days of your life" (Joshua 1:5), it speaks of a stable and persistent situation.
H3320.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצַב comes from a root that expresses the idea of taking a position, of standing firm. It belongs to the same family as words meaning "base," "foundation." In Aramaic, a very similar form is found (יְצַב). The verb always describes a subject that intentionally takes a position or persists in a position; it is a verb of action and establishment.
H3320.emploi: This verb appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical narratives (Exodus, Numbers, 1 and 2 Samuel, 2 Chronicles) and in poetic books (Job, Psalms). It describes very varied situations: soldiers standing ready for battle (2 Samuel 23:12: "He stood in the midst of the field"), servants presented to the king (1 Samuel 10:23), elders gathered by Moses (Numbers 11:16), or even heavenly creatures "standing" before God (Job 1:6: "The sons of God came to present themselves before the Lord"). The meaning varies slightly according to the context: passive waiting, active resistance, or simple presence. The form used in all these passages is the Hithpael (reflexive), emphasizing that the subject takes his position himself.
H3320.portee: This word reminds the reader that faith is not about fleeing, but about standing firm in the face of what God calls. When God tells Joshua, "No one will stand before you" (Joshua 1:5), He assures him that the position of the faithful believer is unshakeable. Conversely, the refusal to "stand" — that is, to present oneself before God or to resist evil — shows human fragility. Meditating on this verb invites the Christian to examine where he truly stands: before God, or turned away from Him.

sens: Establish firmly, make stable
Acquire certainty about something
Truly know, grasp the truth of a matter
H3321.detail:
1. The verb evokes the idea of making something firm and stable, like holding up what threatens to fall. That is why it also means "to establish" or "to affirm" strongly.
2. Hence comes the meaning of "to gain certainty": to understand something in a solid and definitive way, without doubt or hesitation. In Daniel 7:19, the prophet desires to "know for certain" (to truly know) what the fourth terrifying beast means: he wants a firm and assured understanding of his vision.
3. It is therefore "to know the truth" — not just a simple opinion, but a stable and certain knowledge, established like on rock.
H3321.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the Hebrew root יָצַב (yatsav, "to stand firm," "to remain firm"). The basic image is one of stability: what is standing does not move, does not waver. The verb in the Pael form (the intensive form in Aramaic) transforms this idea: "to make stand" becomes "to make certain" or "to establish as true." That is why the word designates both the action of making something stable and the act of acquiring an unshakeable certainty.
H3321.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Daniel 7:19. Daniel receives a vision of the four great beasts that represent the empires that will dominate the world. Terrified by the fourth beast — the most horrible of all — he desires to "know the truth" about it, that is, to understand its true and certain meaning. It is in this context of prophetic vision and the search for divine understanding that the verb takes on its full force: Daniel is not seeking vague knowledge, but established and unwavering certainty.
H3321.portee: This verb reminds us that knowing God and His truths is not a vague opinion, but a certainty that is firmly established. Just as Daniel desires to "know the truth" about future mysteries, the believer is called to seek firm and assured knowledge of God, not changing impressions. It is an invitation to trust: what God reveals is established as something stable and definitive.

sens: To put something in a specific location, to install it
To leave, to maintain something in a state or at a place
To present someone or something before someone else
To expose, to show, to highlight
H3322.detail:
1. To put something in a location: this is the physical action of placing an object somewhere. In Genesis 30:38, Jacob "placed the peeled branches in the troughs, in the watering places" so that the sheep would see them while drinking. It is a material and intentional positioning.
