2. To leave or maintain: the word expresses the idea of allowing something to remain or permitting it to stay. In Exodus 10:24, Pharaoh says that the sheep and the cattle "will remain" in Egypt while the people leave. It is a form of retention or detention.
3. To present or hand over: this is putting someone in front of someone else, in a relationship of exposure. In Genesis 43:9, Judah promises to "present" Benjamin before his father’s face, meaning to present him in person.
4. To expose or show: the word can also mean to bring to the forefront, to make visible or manifest. In Judges 6:37, Gideon "places" a fleece in the threshing floor for God to cover it with dew: it is positioned to receive a divine action.
H3322.origine: The verb יָצַג (yatsag) comes from a root that evokes the idea of placing upright or fixing. In Hebrew, it belongs to the family of verbs of position and placement. The main form (Hiphil) carries the idea of causing something to be placed or fixed. This verb expresses less movement than the resulting state: the establishment or final arrangement of something.
H3322.emploi: The verb יָצַג appears 16 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narratives of Genesis and Judges, but also in the historical and prophetic books. It denotes very concrete actions: placing objects (branches, fleece), allowing a situation to persist (the herds in Egypt), presenting a person (Benjamin). Its meaning varies slightly depending on the context: it can be purely physical (installing something), legal or relational (presenting someone), or even temporal (to remain, to persist). The context determines whether the subject acts for itself or if something is highlighted by a divine or human action.
H3322.portee: This verb reminds us of the concrete reality of biblical faith: God acts in time and space, placing people and things in their rightful place. Understanding how He "places" or "presents" circumstances helps the reader recognize the divine hand in events, and to accept that what is "presented" to us by God serves His purposes, even when it is not initially pleasing to us.

sens: Olive oil, a precious agricultural product
Substance used for anointing and consecrating
Holy substance of worship and piety
H3323.detail:
1. The oil is primarily olive oil, a fundamental agricultural product in Israel alongside wheat and wine; it is a concrete wealth that farmers produced and stored (2 Chronicles 32:28), which priests received as tithe and first fruits (Numbers 18:12), and which enemy nations sought to steal or destroy (Deuteronomy 28:51).
2. Oil is used to anoint kings, priests, and prophets to consecrate them to God, thus marking the one who receives this anointing as belonging to the Lord; it is a ritual gesture loaded with significance.
3. Oil also burns in the lamps of the sanctuary and symbolizes the presence of God, divine light, and spiritual abundance; in Zechariah's vision, the two olive trees pour oil into the lamp as an image of the Spirit's power (Zechariah 4:14).
H3323.origine: The Hebrew word yitshar specifically denotes fresh and shining oil, pure and of the highest quality — that which flows naturally from the olive or is obtained by the first pressing. It comes from the agricultural and pastoral world of Israel, where the olive tree was one of the three pillars of economic and religious life alongside wheat and the vine.
H3323.emploi: The word appears 23 times, always in the Old Testament, mainly in the texts of the Law (Deuteronomy), the history of Israel (2 Chronicles, Nehemiah), and the prophets (Jeremiah, Hosea, Joel, Zechariah). It is used in two major contexts: first as a material good, an agricultural resource for which tithes are paid or that enemies ravage (Deuteronomy 28:51 in times of famine, Joel 1:10 in times of plague). Secondly, as a substance of worship and consecration, linked to the anointing of kings and priests. It is also associated with eschatology, with the hope of future blessing (Jeremiah 31:12: oil is part of the goods of the Lord to which restored men rush).
H3323.portee: For an Israelite, oil was life: daily food, nighttime light, a mark of well-being and health. Losing it meant famine and ruin. Spiritually, it teaches that God blesses His people not only with an invisible blessing but also with concrete and tangible goods. The anointing oil finally reminds us that to consecrate someone is to set them apart for God to dwell in them and act through them.

sens: Son of Kehath, grandson of Levi and uncle of Moses and Aaron
Leader of one of the Levitical families, progenitor of the Jitscharites
H3324.detail: Jitschar is a Levite of the generation that lived in Egypt and during the wilderness. He is the son of Kehath (himself the son of Levi, one of the ancestors of the Israelite people) and the brother of Amram, Hebron, and Uziel. He is therefore the uncle of Moses and Aaron, who were sons of Amram. Jitschar had four sons: Korah, Nepheg, Zichri, and Shelomith (Exodus 6:18, 6:21). His descendants, called the Jitscharites, form one of the important branches of the priestly tribe of Levi. Although Jitschar himself is not at the center of biblical narratives, his son Korah becomes famous for his rebellion against Moses and Aaron (Numbers 16:1).
H3324.origine: The name means "the oil that shines" (in Hebrew, yitshar = oil). It is an image of wealth and blessing. The word belongs to the genealogy of Jacob's sons, which structures the religious organization of Israel.
H3324.emploi: Jitschar is mentioned nine times in Scripture, always in genealogical lists or texts of worship organization. He first appears in Exodus 6:18 as one of Kehath's four sons. Numbers 3:19 mentions him again in the enumeration of the Levites. The most dramatic moment is in Numbers 16:1, where his son Korah is presented as the leader of the great rebellion against Moses in the wilderness. The texts of Chronicles (6:2, 6:18, 6:38, 23:12, 23:18) revisit his genealogy and that of his descendants to show how the tribe of Levi was organized and how it was distributed in the temple worship.
H3324.portee: Jitschar reminds us that every Levite, even obscure, has a place in God's plan for worship and adoration. The story of his son Korah teaches us that proximity to the divine does not automate obedience: even in the priestly family, pride and rebellion can arise. It is a lesson on the necessity of submitting to the order that God has established.

sens: Descendant d'Itsehar, fils de Kehath et petit-fils de Lévi
H3325.detail: The Jitseharites are members of a Levitical family descended from Itsehar. Itsehar was the son of Kehath (who was himself the son of Levi) and lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. His descendants formed one of the four major families of the Kehathites, alongside the Amramites, the Hebronites, and the Uziélites (Numbers 3:27). In the religious and civil organization of Israel, the Jitseharites held important roles: some served in the temple service, such as Jachath son of Shelomoth (1 Chronicles 24:22), while others held civil responsibilities, such as Kenaniah and his brothers who were magistrates and judges in Israel (1 Chronicles 26:29).
H3325.origine: The name comes from Itsehar (יִצְהָר), which means "oil." Itsehar was the son of Kehath and the brother of Amram (the father of Moses and Aaron), Hebron, and Uzziel. The term "Jitseharite" simply refers to the descendants of this man.
H3325.emploi: This term appears four times in the Bible, always to designate the members of this Levitical family. Numbers 3:27 lists them among the four main families of the Kehathites during the census in the desert. The other three occurrences are found in 1 Chronicles and describe the role of the Jitseharites in the organization of worship and administration: some are responsible for the service of the tabernacle or temple, while others hold civil positions as magistrates and judges. This role illustrates how the Levitical families fulfilled their religious and administrative responsibilities in the life of Israel.

sens: Meuble pour se reposer ou dormir
Relation conjugale ou sexuelle
Lieu de repos figuré, notamment face à la mort
H3326A.detail:
1. A piece of furniture intended for rest and sleep, as in Psalms 132:3 where the psalmist says, "I will not go up to the bed where I lie": it is the place where one lies down to sleep.
2. An intimate relationship between spouses, particularly the sexual act or its rights: Reuben "went up to his father's bed" (Genesis 49:4) in a serious violation of family honor and the order established by God. Similarly, "to defile the bed" means to commit adultery or incest.
3. A metaphorical place of rest in the face of spiritual realities or death: Job says, "It is in darkness that I will make my bed" (Job 17:13), referring to his expectation of the abode of the dead. Psalms 63:7 shows a "bed" where one meditates on God during the watches of the night, an intimate place of prayer.
H3326A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of stretching out or lying down. It primarily designates the concrete piece of furniture where one rests lying down, and by extension, everything related to rest, marital intimacy, or the abode of death. The connection between the physical meaning (the piece of furniture) and the figurative meanings (the sexual relationship, eternal rest) comes from this primary image of the horizontal extension of the body.
H3326A.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is mainly used to evoke the marital bed or its violations: Genesis 49:4 and 1 Chronicles 5:1 mention it in the serious context of Reuben's sin, who violated his father's bed. In the Psalms, the word takes on a more intimate and spiritual tone: the psalmist meditates and prays there (Psalms 63:7), or associates it with the expectation of eternal rest (Job 17:13). The bed thus becomes the place where major moral, intimate, and spiritual issues are intertwined.
H3326A.portee: This word invites the Christian to recognize the holiness of the marital bond and the seriousness of its violations. The examples of transgression (Reuben) show how carnal desire, when it becomes disobedience to God, compromises the destiny of a life. Conversely, the psalmic usages remind us that the bed can be a place of prayer and meditation on God, a legitimate space of intimacy transformed by the presence of the Lord.

sens: Niveau ou plancher d'une construction
Étage particulièrement disposé autour d'un édifice central
H3326B.detail:
1. The word designates a floor or horizontal level of a construction. It is a flat surface intended to support weight and create a separation between superimposed floors, as in any building. In 1 Kings 6:5, the "circular floors" that Solomon built around the temple of Jerusalem are mentioned, meaning a succession of levels surrounding the sanctuary.
2. In architectural context, the floor can have variable dimensions depending on its position. Thus, in 1 Kings 6:6, the lower floor measured five cubits wide, the middle one six cubits, and the upper one seven cubits: these progressive retreats allowed the framework not to enter the walls of the temple, creating a visible offset from the outside.
H3326B.origine: The Hebrew word יָצִיעַ comes from a root meaning to extend or be flattened, evoking the image of a flat surface. It belongs to the family of words describing what is extended horizontally or laid solidly. This architectural vocabulary was common in biblical Hebrew to describe the structures of large buildings in the ancient Near East.
H3326B.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Bible, exclusively in the detailed description of the temple built by Solomon in 1 Kings 6. It serves to designate the three levels of floors that formed an annex surrounding the central sanctuary. Each floor had its own height and dimensions, and they were connected to the main house by cedar beams (1 Kings 6:10). It is a purely technical term used to clarify the precise structure of the temple.
H3326B.portee: This word reminds us that the temple of Jerusalem was an extraordinarily well-planned and constructed edifice, reflecting divine magnificence. The progressive dimensions of the floors show thoughtful and organized architecture, worthy of the presence of God. For the believer, these construction details invite admiration for the wisdom and order that God inspires in His servants.

sens: son of Abraham and Sarah, patriarch of the Covenant
husband of Rebekah and father of Esau and Jacob
man of faith tested by God in sacrifice
figure of the heir of the divine promise
H3327.detail:
1. Isaac is the son that God promises to Abraham and Sarah in their old age: "You shall call his name Isaac" (Genesis 17:19). His name itself means "he laughs," evoking joy and astonishment at this miracle. He marries Rebekah and becomes the father of the twins Esau and Jacob (Genesis 25:19-26), thus passing on the promise made to Abraham.
2. Isaac lives as a patriarch in the land of Canaan, digging wells and building altars (Genesis 26:12-25). He is a man of prayer and meditation: "One evening Isaac went out to meditate in the field" (Genesis 24:63), which shows his quiet piety.
3. Isaac is subjected to the supreme test when God asks Abraham to sacrifice him (Genesis 22:2-19). Although the provided text does not detail this event, Isaac embodies obedience and trust in the divine promise in the face of the ultimate trial.
4. Isaac remains the central figure of the Covenant between God and the patriarchs, invoked alongside Abraham and Jacob: "God of my father Abraham, God of my father Isaac" (Genesis 32:9).
H3327.origine: The name Isaac (Hebrew יִצְחָק yitshaq) derives from a root meaning "to laugh." It is a theophoric name celebrating the miracle of his birth: a supernatural joy linked to the fulfillment of the divine promise. In the Old Testament, Isaac is the indispensable link in the genealogy of salvation, the quintessential son of the promise, the one who perpetuates the Abrahamic Covenant toward Jacob-Israel.
H3327.emploi: Isaac appears about 101 times in the Bible, first in Genesis (from 17:19 to 50:24), where his entire life is recounted: his miraculous birth, his sacrifice test, his marriage, his life as a shepherd and farmer, and his death. He also figures in the solemn invocations of the Pentateuch: "Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel" (Exodus 32:13). Each mention of his name emphasizes his central role in the transmission of the divine promise, and the incidents of his life (digging wells, being confused with his brother Esau) illustrate how God protects and guides this unique heir.
H3327.portee: Isaac teaches the believer about God's faithfulness to His promises, even when they seem impossible or challenged by circumstances. His life shows that spiritual inheritance is passed on not by force or cunning, but by divine blessing. For Christians, Isaac foreshadows the one who will be offered in sacrifice and will rise for the salvation of humanity.

sens: Child or descendant born of a person
That which comes from a source
Progeny, lineage
H3329.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a child or descendant in the literal sense: one who is born of a parent and comes from them. It conveys the idea of life continuing through generations.
2. More broadly, it applies to anything that "comes out" or "originates from" something: a consequence, a result, a natural production. In 2 Chronicles 32:21, the word describes the sons of the king of Assyria who were killed — they are presented as what comes from him, his progeny.
3. Figuratively, the term can refer to a lineage, a descent, or even a spiritual posterity: those who inherit and continue someone's work.
H3329.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to go out," "to come forth." It expresses the idea of what emerges, what is born and goes away. The family of this root includes terms for "exit," "issue," "departure." The basic image is that of movement outward, applied to birth and descent: the child who "comes out" of the parent.
H3329.emploi: The word is very rare in the preserved biblical text (only one occurrence in the Segond). In 2 Chronicles 32:21, it designates the sons of King Sennacherib of Assyria, presented as his progeny who perished. The context is one of military defeat and divine judgment. Although infrequent, this term powerfully expresses the idea that a person's descendants or fruits can be annihilated by the hand of God.
H3329.portee: This word reminds us that our descendants and what comes from our actions do not belong to us definitively: only God has control over all life and all progeny. It is a call to humility before the divine sovereignty over our works and our children.

sens: What is true, what corresponds to reality
What is reliable, trustworthy
Solemn affirmation or absolute certainty
H3330.detail:
1. The word first designates truth as an established reality, what truly exists and cannot be contradicted. When King Nebuchadnezzar speaks about the dream he had: "The dream is true, and its interpretation is sure" (Daniel 2:45), he affirms that what has been seen and announced corresponds to reality, to what will truly happen. It is the opposite of a lie or illusion.
2. The word then expresses reliability, the solidity of what one can count on: a true word, a certain promise that will not fail. When the king says, "The thing is certain, according to the law of the Medes and Persians, which cannot be altered" (Daniel 6:12), he emphasizes that the decree is established in a stable and definitive manner.
3. Used as an adverb or interjection, it becomes a solemn affirmation, a strong assurance: "Certainly, O king!" respond the advisors (Daniel 3:24), confirming with conviction what the king has just said. It is a way of affirming without any doubt.
H3330.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to fix," "to establish firmly." The starting image is that of something set, planted firmly, from which the idea of stability and certainty derives. The word belongs to the vocabulary of wisdom and justice: what is true is what holds firm, what withstands the test. In biblical Aramaic (the language of the Book of Daniel), this word retains its fundamental meaning of established and reliable reality.
H3330.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Bible, only in the Book of Daniel, which was written in Aramaic. It occurs in official and solemn contexts: King Nebuchadnezzar recognizes a revealed truth (2:45), advisors confirm an event (3:24), the king asserts the firmness of a law (6:12). The word is never used to speak of a mere opinion or supposition, but always of what is established, recognized, or promulgated with authority. Daniel himself uses it to question an angel (7:16): it is a word used in the face of what is undeniable.
H3330.portee: This word reminds the believer that God alone is the source of absolute truth and unshakeable certainty. In a world filled with uncertainties, the visions and revelations of God possess this quality of solid truth that does not change. For us, recognizing the truth of God's word means resting on something stable and reliable, capable of guiding and saving us.

sens: To lie down on the ground or a bed
To recline, settle down to sleep or rest
To be laid out, to rest (passive sense)
To lie, to be buried or dead
H3331.detail:
1. The verb describes the physical action of lying down on a surface: one "lies down" on sackcloth and ashes (Esther 4:3, Isaiah 58:5), a gesture of mourning and humiliation where the body stretches out on the ground. It is the concrete image of a person lying down.
2. When one "lies down" in the realm of the dead (Psalms 139:8), the word takes on the meaning of resting or dwelling somewhere, as one lies down to sleep or remains in place.
3. In the passive form, "a bed of worms" (Isaiah 14:11) means that a layer is laid out, placed beneath someone: that which rests, that which lies. It is the state of being laid out or being covered.
4. For a corpse or a dead person in the realm of the dead, "to lie down" evokes the final state: to lie, to rest in death, the idea of eternal rest or the mortal remains.
H3331.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצַע comes from a root that means to extend, to spread out, to lay flat. It evokes the image of something being spread or arranged on a surface. The word is related to the simple and concrete idea of placing or flattening.
H3331.emploi: This verb appears 4 times in the Hebrew Bible provided here, mostly in contexts of mourning, supplication, and death. In Esther 4:3 and Isaiah 58:5, it describes the act of penitential fasting: lying down on sackcloth and ashes, an act of prostration that expresses humiliation and distress. In Psalms 139:8, it means to remain or dwell in the realm of the dead, showing that God is present even where the dead rest. In Isaiah 14:11, the word (in the passive form) speaks of the bed of worms that covers the corpse of the king of Babylon, an image of decomposition and dishonor. The meaning oscillates between the action of lying down voluntarily (in penitence) and the state of being laid out (in death).
H3331.portee: This word reminds the reader that humiliation before God—lying down in dust and ashes—is a biblical gesture of repentance and sincerity. It is also a reminder that death equalizes us all: kings and powerful people lie down like the humblest, a truth that should temper pride and turn us toward divine mercy.

sens: To pour a liquid from a container
To spill a liquid on something or someone
To flow, to run naturally
To serve food or drink
To be overwhelmed, submerged (figurative)
H3332G.detail:
1. To pour means to make a liquid flow: one pours it from a pot, a pitcher, or a vial. In Leviticus 2:6, the priest pours oil on the cake offered to God. It is the action of transferring a liquid from one place to another.
2. To spill refers to the action of pouring a liquid on a person or thing for a specific purpose. When Samuel pours oil on Saul's head (1 Samuel 10:1), he consecrates him as king: the act of anointing fulfills what is promised. It is pouring with intention and meaning.
3. To flow or run: the word can also describe the natural movement of liquid that flows. Water flows, rain falls, everything that is poured follows its course.
4. To serve food or drink: in 2 Kings 4:40, one "served" food, meaning one presented or offered. The meaning expands to the action of providing, presenting.
5. To be overwhelmed or submerged in a figurative sense: in Psalms 41:9, the one who is "dangerously afflicted" is like poured out, emptied of strength, overwhelmed by evil. The image of flowing liquid evokes exhaustion here.
H3332G.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצַק comes from a root that evokes flowing and melting. The same word also describes what is poured and then solidified—what is cast in a mold becomes firm and stable. Hence the underlying idea: what flows becomes established. Related words in Hebrew share this family of flowing and forming.
H3332G.emploi: This verb appears 28 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in accounts of worship and anointing. It is very frequent in Leviticus and Kings, where it describes the rituals of offering: oil is poured on bread, on priests, on kings to consecrate them. In 1 Samuel 10:1, Samuel pours oil on Saul to designate him as king. In 2 Kings 9:3, Elisha commands the young prophet to pour oil on Jehu. The word also extends to liquids in general: water, blood poured on the altar. Sometimes it describes the act of serving (2 Kings 4:40). In poetry (Psalms, Job), it takes on a figurative hue: to be poured out means to be cast down, struck down, overwhelmed.
H3332G.portee: For the believer, this verb indicates that God acts through concrete gestures: the poured oil is not a mere abstraction, but a visible sign of an invisible reality—the consecration, the anointing of the Spirit. Understanding the meaning of the verb sheds light on why the Bible emphasizes these rituals: the body, the gesture, the material matter count in the relationship with God. It also prepares one to receive the teaching of the New Testament on the Spirit poured into our hearts.

sens: To pour a liquid metal into a mold to create an object
To cast molten metal, to create a shape by melting
To be cast, molded in metal
To be firmly established, immutably
H3332H.detail:
1. To pour a liquid metal: the verb describes the action of casting molten metal (gold, silver, bronze) into a mold to make a finished object. Thus, for the Ark of the Covenant, "four gold rings were cast for it" (Exodus 25:12): gold is poured into molds to create these rings.
2. To manufacture by casting: the result of this action, the object shaped by molten metal. The "bases of silver" of the sanctuary were "cast": each was a solid block of silver poured for this purpose (Exodus 38:27).
3. To be cast in the mold: the passive state of the metal that has taken its final shape. The "sea of cast metal" of the temple was a massive round basin of molded bronze, which was "ten cubits from one edge to the other" (2 Chronicles 4:2).
4. To be firmly established: in a figurative sense, to be immutably fixed, like a metal that has cooled in its form. This rare sense broadens the image of the word: what is cast does not move anymore, it is established forever.
H3332H.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצַק (yatsaq) primarily evokes the act of pouring, of casting. The root suggests a flow, a stream of liquid that one controls to give it a shape. It is close to other terms in the same family expressing flowing or placing. In biblical Hebrew, the verb is mainly used for precious metals or melted alloys of the temple and cult furniture.
H3332H.emploi: The verb appears 14 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the chapters of Exodus and 1-2 Chronicles that describe the temple furniture. It applies to the making of rings, bases, feet, and metal pieces of the sanctuary or royal temple. Three major uses: (1) to cast the pieces of the tabernacle and altar (Exodus), (2) to manufacture the elements of Solomon's temple and especially the "sea of cast metal," this gigantic basin of bronze (1 Kings and 2 Chronicles), (3) rarely, to describe what is firmly established (Job 41:14). The context is always that of sacred architecture, revealing the importance of the casting work in ancient Israel.
H3332H.portee: This verb reminds the reader that the sanctuary and its cult pieces were not fragile assemblies, but enduring works, founded with care and skill. The image of casting suggests solidity, permanence, and order: each piece was made to last, just like the covenant itself. For the Christian, meditating on these cast metals of the temple can evoke how God builds His spiritual temple, an object of durable and precise creation.

sens: To pour a liquid from one container to another
To drop or deposit something
To place or install firmly
H3332I.detail:
1. To pour means to cause a liquid to flow from one container to another: in 2 Samuel 13:9, the servant "pours" the pancakes from the pan in front of Amnon, meaning she slides or drops them from the hot container.
2. The word also refers to the action of depositing or dropping something in a place: in Joshua 7:23, the stolen goods are "deposited" before the Lord, meaning they are placed on the ground to be exposed.
3. In a more stable sense, it means to place or install something firmly and durably: in 2 Samuel 15:24, the ark of the covenant is "set down," meaning it is placed securely in a location.
H3332I.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצַק comes from a root that evokes the act of pouring or flowing. The basic image is that of liquid flowing freely. By extension, the word applies to any action of depositing something, and then to that of establishing or installing it durably. This range of meanings reflects the transition from movement (flowing, falling) to stability (placing, fixing).
H3332I.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Segond. It is used in concrete contexts: pouring food (the pancake pan), depositing objects (the loot), or placing important elements (the holy ark). The three uses show the same root of physical action, from the simple gesture to the solemn act. The word only appears in these three passages of the Old Testament provided.
H3332I.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of physical gestures in biblical life: pouring, depositing, placing are not insignificant acts. Depositing the loot before the Lord, placing the ark solemnly, shows how the Israelites honored God through their concrete actions. This invites us to recognize that our ordinary gestures can become acts of worship and obedience when done with an awareness of His presence.

sens: To pour liquid, to make it flow
To cast molten metal to shape an object
To be firmly established, solidly
H3332J.detail:
1. To pour means to cause a liquid to flow from one container to another or to spill it. This is the basic image of the word: water, oil, or any fluid that flows. The word also applies to the action of flowing freely, like a liquid that flows without obstruction.

2. To cast metal involves pouring molten metal into a mold to create a solid object. In Job 37:18, the sky is compared to a "mirror of cast metal": it is metal that has been cast and hardened, becoming firm and shiny. This image evokes solidity and perfection.

3. To be firmly established means to have an unshakeable foundation. The Hebrew verb, when it describes what has been "poured" and has solidified, comes to mean what is stable and secure. In Job 11:15, being "firm" before God means having a clear conscience and a steadfast heart. In Job 41:15, the heart of the sea monster is "hard" like a millstone: unshakeable, fearless, frozen in its raw strength.
H3332J.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצַק comes from a root that depicts the action of pouring, of letting flow. Its primary image is that of liquid in motion. The Hebrew language also names "casting" (the action of pouring metal) and the resulting "firm" state: the verb thus naturally glides from the movement of what flows to the solidity of what has hardened. This progression from fluid to solid is characteristic of the figurative thought of Hebrew.
H3332J.emploi: The verb appears three times in the Bible, and each occurrence is found in Job, the book of the problem of evil and divine justice. In Job 11:15, the wise man advises Job: if you set your heart right with God, you will be "firm," meaning unshakeable in your integrity. In Job 37:18, Elihu describes the heavens as solid as cast ice: the image of the hard and perfect sky reinforces the idea that God has established everything with admirable order and firmness. In Job 41:15, the Leviathan has a heart "hard" like stone or a millstone: this contrasts with man, who could become firm in God (as in 11:15), but who, faced with this monster, can only recognize God's incomprehensible work. The word thus evolves between "to pour" (physical sense) and "to establish" (spiritual and moral sense).
H3332J.portee: This word invites the reader to see that firmness is not brute inflexibility: it is a solidity given by God. In Job 11:15, the firmness of the heart comes from justice and integrity towards God. The path to this firmness passes through trust. Contemplating the firmness of the heavens (Job 37:18) or recognizing God's unshakeable power before His creatures (Job 41:15) teaches the believer that he can seek his own liberation from fear by relying on this divine order established since the beginning.

sens: An object of cast metal made in one piece
A set of elements cast together without seams
A work or creation formed in one go
H3333.detail:
1. Casting is an object shaped by pouring liquid metal into a mold and then allowing it to cool and solidify into a unique and continuous piece. In 1 Kings 7:24, the sea (large basin) of the temple is described: the ornamental gourds that decorated it all around "were cast with it in one piece," meaning they were not added or welded afterward, but cast at the same time as the basin, in one movement, forming an inseparable whole.
2. By extension, the word refers to the harmonious whole of what has been created or formed in the same operation, without addition or demarcation. Integrity and uniqueness are essential: it is a complete creation, not assembled from different pieces.
3. Figuratively, this evokes the idea of a perfectly united work, where each part holds its place in a comprehensive design, without rupture or disparity. Casting suggests strength and stability: what has been cast together does not separate.
H3333.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root (צוק, tsuq) meaning "to pour, to flow, to pour a liquid." It is a feminine noun that designates the action of pouring molten metal and its solid result. The same root is found in other Hebrew words related to pouring and casting. The mother idea is that of the fluid movement of molten metal solidifying to take shape.
H3333.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in 1 Kings 7, in the precise description of the furniture of the temple built by Solomon. In 1 Kings 7:24 and 7:30, it qualifies different parts of the large basin (the sea) in bronze: the gourds that adorn the edge and the supports of the basin are explicitly described as being "cast" with the main piece, rather than added or fixed afterward. It is a technical term, architectural and artisanal, used to emphasize the excellence of the work: nothing is assembled in a rudimentary way, everything comes from a single controlled casting.
H3333.portee: This word reminds us that God asked Solomon for a temple built with perfection and beauty. Every detail, even in the technique of making the furniture, had to testify to excellence and unity. For the believer, this evokes the importance of integrity and harmony in our service to God: a Christian life or work worthy of the name can only be a coherent whole, where faith and actions are one, never hastily assembled or disparate.

sens: State of affliction, anguish caused by danger, fear, or misfortune
Feeling of being pressed, constricted, in a place or situation that suffocates
Oppression or persecution inflicted by an enemy or authority
H3334.detail:
1. It is primarily the anguish that seizes someone at the moment of danger or fear — an affliction that paralyzes. Jacob, seeing Esau approaching with his men, is seized with anguish (Genesis 32:7); David, hunted by his own soldiers who want to stone him, finds himself in great distress (1 Samuel 30:6). The word evokes that feeling of tightness in the heart, the impression that one can no longer breathe.
2. The word also conveys the idea of being cramped, pressed, constricted — like a person trapped in a shrinking space. Amnon is tormented by his impossible desire for Tamar, as if caught in the trap of his own thoughts (2 Samuel 13:2).
3. Finally, it designates the oppression inflicted by an enemy who besieges or dominates you. Israel experiences great distress when the Ammonites fight against it (Judges 10:9); the hands of the Lord weigh upon Israel to make it suffer (Judges 2:15). It is the distress of a people crushed by its enemies, who cry out to God for deliverance (Nehemiah 9:27).
H3334.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that means to embrace, to squeeze, to confine — the basic image is that of a hand that grips, of a space that closes in. The same Hebrew verb also takes on the meaning of forming, shaping (God forming man from the dust), like a hand that shapes — a similar image of compression and formation. Distress is therefore what constricts, confines, torments you like a vise.
H3334.emploi: The verb appears ten times in the Hebrew Bible. It is especially found in crisis narratives: when Jacob fears Esau, when David flees from his enemies, when Israel is invaded by its neighbors, or when Amnon is consumed by desire. Distress can be physical — an army encircling you, enemies oppressing you (Judges 2:15, Nehemiah 9:27) — or psychological — fear, moral anguish in the face of danger (Genesis 32:7, 1 Samuel 30:6). It is always a situation where one sees no way out and where only God's help can save us.
H3334.portee: This word reminds the Christian that distress, anguish in the face of trials is a reality that the Bible does not hide. It invites one to cry out to God, as Israel and David did: not to stifle one's fear, but to entrust it to the One who listens. Distress becomes a pathway to faith when one turns to the Lord instead of despairing.

sens: To give a shape, a figure to something
To shape, work a material to make an object
To create, produce (particularly by the action of God)
To establish, foresee, or predestine according to a divine plan
H3335G.detail: 1. The verb "to form" primarily refers to the action of giving a shape, a figure to a material. It is the concrete gesture of the potter or sculptor who molds his material. Isaiah 29:16 illustrates this: the vessel receives its shape from the hands of the potter, just as the clay is shaped by the worker. 2. It more precisely describes the artisanal work of transformation: taking a raw material and giving it a use, beauty, a new existence. It conveys the idea of shaping, the patient modeling of a form from nothing or little. 3. In the vocabulary of creation, "to form" denotes God's creative action: He forms man from the dust of the ground (Genesis 2:7), He forms the eye and the ear (Psalms 94:9), He forms every day and every creature. This includes the original creation and the formation of each person at conception (Jeremiah 1:5: "I formed you before your birth"). 4. The word takes on a figurative meaning when it expresses God's plan or will: to form a people, to form Israel as His servant (Isaiah 44:2, 44:24), is to predestine it, to establish it according to a prior design. God also "forms" events and situations according to His wisdom (Isaiah 45:7: "I form the light and create darkness").
H3335G.origine: The Hebrew root yatsar literally means "to mold" or "to shape," as one molds clay. It evokes the image of the potter in turn, of the sculptor facing his material. The word belongs to a rich semantic family: it is close to "potter" (yotser) and "formation" (yetsirah). The Old Testament uses this verb mainly to speak of God's creative action, particularly in the prophetic passages of Isaiah where the potter becomes a major metaphor for God the creator.
H3335G.emploi: The verb "to form" appears about 35 times in the Old Testament, especially in the poetic and prophetic books. In Genesis, it describes the original act of creation: God forms man and animals. In the Psalms, it asserts that God forms the physical world and each creature. Isaiah makes massive use of it (over 20 occurrences): the prophet continually returns to the image of the potter and clay to show that God forms Israel, individuals, and even historical events according to His sovereign will. Jeremiah uses it in the same way for the formation of the prophet and the nation (Jeremiah 1:5). Amos and Zechariah use it in contexts of revealing divine power. The meaning remains consistent: whether it is the creation of the world or the formation of a people, the verb always emphasizes the sovereign and intentional action of the One who forms.
H3335G.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate God as the wise and powerful potter, who does not create by chance but according to a deep intention. Meditating on the formation of man from dust shows the intimacy of the bond between the creator and His creature: God does not manufacture from the outside; He molds. For the believer, knowing that he is "formed" by God before his birth (Jeremiah 1:5) becomes a source of trust and meaning: my existence is not an accident, but a work of divine wisdom. This also establishes the humility of man: just as clay cannot contest the potter's shape, we cannot contest God's plans.

sens: To shape, mold a material (clay, earth) like a potter
To create, establish something new
To create a human being, give it form
To elaborate, conceive a plan or design
H3335H.detail:
1. To form is primarily the work of the potter who shapes the clay on his wheel: in Jeremiah 18:3, we see the potter "working at the wheel," and the earthen vessels can break "like the potter's vessel" (Psalms 2:9).

2. In a figurative sense, to form means to create and establish something durable: God "forms" the people of Israel to make them His instrument, like the clay in the potter's hand (Jeremiah 18:6).

3. To form also applies to the creation of a person: God has "formed" us from the womb, giving us our shape and identity (Isaiah 64:7: "We are the clay, and it is you who has formed us").

4. In a more abstract sense, to form means to conceive, elaborate, order: God forms His plans and prepares in advance what is to happen (Isaiah 41:25: God has "formed" the one who is to come).
H3335H.origine: This verb comes from a root that evokes the image of the potter working the clay. The Hebrew potter (yâtsâr) is the one who "forms": it is, moreover, a very common profession in Israel, where pottery, lamps, and vessels are made. The image has enriched itself: to form is no longer just a technical act, but the quintessential creative act, the act of God who gives form to creation and to each creature.
H3335H.emploi: This verb is used 15 times in the Old Testament. In the Pottery Workshop (Jeremiah 18:2-6), it first describes the ordinary work of the clay modeler; but immediately the scene becomes symbolic: God treats Israel as the potter treats the clay, with absolute authority. Isaiah powerfully takes up this image (Isaiah 29:16, 64:7): we are from nothing that God has formed, from the clay that cannot dispute with the one who shapes it. The verb also applies to the original creation (the formation of beings), to the conception of a child, and to the elaboration of God's plans, who "forms" in advance what will happen. It is a key word to express God's creative and sovereign authority over His creation.
H3335H.portee: This word teaches us that we do not belong to ourselves: we are God's handiwork, formed by Him like clay by the potter. This should inspire us with two feelings: trust in the One who has so carefully formed us, and humility before His sovereign hand. We too, with our gifts and limitations, have a given shape, a design traced in advance by God.

sens: Part of the human or animal body (arm, leg, hand, foot, etc.)
Figuratively: a constituent part of a whole, a group, or a community
H3338.detail:
1. The word concretely refers to the members of the body — arms, legs, hands, feet, and other parts — that enable movement and action. Job 17:7 illustrates this: when a man suffers deeply, his members weaken and fade like a shadow, so profoundly does pain affect the whole body.
2. Figuratively, a member is a person or part that belongs to a larger whole: a part of the social body, the Church, or a community. This meaning naturally derives from the first: just as an arm or leg is worthless alone and exists for the body, a member of a group is an indispensable part of the whole.
H3338.origine: The Hebrew word יְצֻר (yetsur) comes from the root יצר (ytsr) which literally means "to form" or "to shape." Members are thus what has been formed and shaped in the body. This root sheds light on the image: the human body is like a creation, a deliberate form where each part has its place and role.
H3338.emploi: This word appears rarely in the Hebrew Bible (only one instance attested here). It is used to speak of the members of the body in their physical fragility, especially in a context of suffering or diminishment. In Job 17:7, the context is that of illness and spiritual depression: the members, like the rest of the being, lose their strength. The word can also apply to members of a community or a collective body, although this usage is less frequent in the Old Testament.
H3338.portee: This word reminds us that our body is not a spiritual prison, but a creation of God, and that every part of ourselves — our physical strength, our sensitivity, our capacity to act — matters in the eyes of God. The mention of the members weakening in Job also invites the reader to recognize that suffering affects the whole person, body and spirit, and that God sees this fragility.

sens: Levite from the time of the united monarchy, leader of one of the choirs of the sanctuary
H3339.detail: Jitseri is a musician from the tribe of Levi who lived during the time of the united kingdom of Israel. He was one of the sons of Jeduthun and one of the brothers of Obed-Edom, Mattithiah, Gedaliah, and Hashabiah. He led the fourth of the Levitical choirs of the sanctuary, each composed of twelve musicians (1 Chronicles 25:11). His name also appears in the form Zeri in other lists.
H3339.origine: The name Jitseri means "my form-giver" or "the one who shapes me." It is derived from the root צר (tsur), which means "to form" or "to shape." This name expresses the idea that God shapes or forms the one who bears it, which is common in Hebrew names: they often confess the divine action in the life of the one who receives them.
H3339.emploi: Jitseri is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the passage where David organizes the Levitical musicians who will serve in the temple. Among the sons of Jeduthun, he is given the charge of the fourth choir. He is the only Levitical musician whose name appears with the rank "fourth" (1 Chronicles 25:11), indicating his importance in the organization of the sanctuary worship.

sens: member of the family of the Jitsrites, descendants of Jetser
H3340.detail: 1. The Jitsrites are the descendants of Jetser, a man from the tribe of Naphtali. Jetser was the son of Naphtali and lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. His name means "form" or "intention," evoking the action of shaping. The Jitsrites appear only once in the Bible: during the census of the tribes of Israel in the desert, in the book of Numbers, where they are counted as a distinct family among the children of Israel.
H3340.origine: The Hebrew word יִצְרִי (Jitsri) is formed from the name יֵ֫צֶר (Jetser, H3337), son of Naphtali. The root יצר (tser) means "to form," "to shape," or "to imagine," the image being that of a potter shaping clay or of the mind forming an intention. The suffix -י (-i) marks belonging to a family or clan: the Jitsrites are therefore "those who come from Jetser." It is a classic patronymic in the manner of Israelite genealogical lists.
H3340.emploi: The Jitsrites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:49, during the second census of the people of Israel in the desert, after the exodus from Egypt. They are listed among the families of the tribe of Naphtali, alongside the Jahzélites, the Gunites, and the Shillemites, all descendants of the four sons of Naphtali. This context shows how Israel was organized into tribes and family clans, each counted for conscription and the religious organization of the people.

sens: To light a fire, to burn something
To be on fire, to catch fire
To be consumed, to be devoured by flames
To devastate, to destroy by burning
H3341.detail:
1. To light a fire, to burn something: this is the action of deliberately setting fire to an object or place. In Joshua 8:8, the Israelites are commanded to set fire to the city of Ai to destroy it. This is an act of war or judgment.
2. To be on fire, to catch fire: the fire spreads, igniting by itself. In Jeremiah 21:14, God declares that He will set fire to the forest (the king's forest) and that this fire will consume all around it — the image of destruction that spreads.
3. To be consumed, to be devoured by flames: what remains after the fire has done its work. Nehemiah 2:17 speaks of the gates of Jerusalem consumed by fire during the destruction of the temple — nothing remains.
4. To devastate, to destroy by burning: figuratively, to cause ruin. In Jeremiah 9:10, the plains of the desert are burned, emptied of their inhabitants and flocks — the fire symbolizes divine judgment that annihilates everything.
H3341.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצַת (yatsat) comes from a root that evokes fire and intense heat. It has a close connection with the idea of a bright flame. Its usage in the Old Testament always carries the image of destructive fire: whether it is a human act (setting fire to a city in wartime) or the action of God (the fire of divine judgment). The root suggests a quick, intense, and irrevocable action.
H3341.emploi: The verb appears 28 times in the Old Testament, especially among the prophets (Jeremiah very frequently, then Ezekiel and Amos) and in historical narratives (Joshua, 2 Samuel, 2 Kings). In war narratives (Joshua 8:8, Judges 9:49), it is the concrete action of burning a city or refuge. Among the prophets, and especially Jeremiah, the verb becomes a threat or a word of God's judgment: God will set fire to the cities, temples, and forests of Israel and neighboring nations (Jeremiah 21:14, 49:2, 49:27). Sometimes it designates the resulting state: to be burned, consumed, defenseless (Nehemiah 2:17, Lamentations 4:11). Fire is always a sign of catastrophe, never of blessing.
H3341.portee: This verb reminds us of the reality of divine judgment in the Old Testament: God is not indifferent to evil; He intervenes to punish, and this judgment is described with terrible intensity — the fire that devours everything. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation to meditate on the holiness of God and the gravity of sin. It also sheds light on the Gospel: in Jesus, judgment is satisfied; His death absorbs the divine wrath that this Hebrew verb expresses so forcefully.

sens: a reservoir carved in stone or built of masonry to receive the must of crushed grapes
a basin or vat where wine ferments
the action of crushing grapes in the winepress, symbolizing the harvest and the feast of the vintage
an image of destruction, of divine judgment pouring out its wrath
H3342.detail:
1. The winepress is primarily a concrete piece of agricultural equipment: a vat or basin carved from rock or built of stone, where the crushed grapes release their must. Isaiah 5:2 mentions it alongside the vineyard's tower, as an essential element of any vineyard operation.
2. This vat also becomes the place of fermentation for wine, the reservoir that preserves and transforms the must into wine. In Jeremiah 48:33, the empty vats mark the complete cessation of agricultural work and desolation.
3. The word can also extend to the entire operation of harvesting: crushing grapes, gathering, celebrating the feast. In Numbers 18:27, the must taken from the vat is part of the tithes owed to the priests, a sign of prosperity.
4. From a broader theological perspective, the winepress becomes an image of judgment: God crushes the wicked as one crushes grapes, pouring out His wrath like the juice from the winepress. This image appears especially in the prophets announcing the punishment of nations.
H3342.origine: The Hebrew word yéqev comes from a root that evokes the idea of crushing, pressing. The winepress was part of the everyday life of farmers and was a precious possession: it was passed down from generation to generation, as shown in the lists of goods in Deuteronomy 15:14. It is a typically rural word, tied to the rhythms of the Promised Land.
H3342.emploi: The word appears sixteen times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Law (Deuteronomy), the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Joel), and in the wisdom literature (Job, Proverbs, Haggai). In legal contexts, it appears in enumerations of goods or tithes (Numbers 18:27, Deuteronomy 15:14): the winepress is a wealth to be shared with the priests or with freed slaves. In prophetic contexts, Isaiah 5 and Jeremiah 48 lament the silence of the emptied vats: this is a sign of ruin. Joel 3:13 uses the winepress as a metaphor for eschatological judgment: "The sickle has come, for the harvest is ripe." The word thus oscillates between concrete agricultural prosperity and the spiritual image of judgment.
H3342.portee: The winepress reminds the believer that God blesses work and the land, and calls to share the fruits with the poor and servants. It is also a powerful image of judgment: divine wrath crushes injustice as surely as the winepress crushes grapes, reminding that God does not leave sin unpunished. For the Christian, this invites both gratitude for material goods and fear of the Lord.

sens: City in the south of Judah, at the border of Edom
H3343.detail: Jekabtseel is a fortified city located at the southernmost tip of the territory of Judah, near the border with Edom. Its name literally means "God gathers," which evokes the divine action of bringing together or protecting this border place. In Nehemiah 11:25, it is listed among the cities where the sons of Judah settled during the repopulation of the Promised Land after the exile, attesting to its strategic importance and its concrete reality as an inhabited center.
H3343.origine: The name Jekabtseel is composed of two Hebrew elements: *Ye-* ("God"), formed from the verb *qavatz* ("to gather, concentrate"), and *-el* ("God"). The literal meaning "God gathers" expresses the idea that God protects and gathers His people in this place, particularly significant for a border city. This type of theophoric name is common in Israel.
H3343.emploi: Jekabtseel appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 11:25, during the account of the repopulation of Judah and Benjamin after the return from exile. It is mentioned alongside other cities where the Judeans settled, confirming its role as an important city in the occupation system of the Judean territory. Its location in the south of the country, at the edge of the Negev desert and near Edom, explains its strategic and defensive importance for the restored community.

sens: to be on fire, to be consumed by flames
to remain lit, to continue burning without going out
to ignite, to suddenly catch fire
to manifest with intensity, like a flame (anger, judgment)
H3344.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: something is on fire and is being consumed. At the altar of the Tabernacle, the fire continually burns the offerings: "The fire shall burn on the altar, it shall never go out" (Leviticus 6:6). It is an active flame that devours whatever it reaches.

2. The word also refers to a fire that persists, that does not stop. Each morning, wood must be added to keep it burning: "The fire shall burn on the altar continually" (Leviticus 6:6). It conveys the idea of sustained, enduring combustion.

3. The word can express a flash or sudden eruption, as when it is translated "will burst forth." In Isaiah, judgment "will burst forth like the blazing of a fire" (Isaiah 10:16): a violence that erupts suddenly.

4. Figuratively, to burn signifies divine anger and judgment. The Lord's anger "has been kindled, and will burn to the depths of Sheol" (Deuteronomy 32:22): it is a destructive power that spreads everywhere, an intensity that persists.
H3344.origine: The verb comes from a Hebrew root that paints the image of active, consuming fire. The same root produces words for fire and combustion. In Hebrew, this root first evokes the concrete experience of flame that consumes wood and turns everything to ash, before applying to invisible realities like anger or judgment.
H3344.emploi: The verb appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mainly to describe the fire of the altar (Leviticus 6:2, 6:5, 6:6), which must burn without interruption according to the Law. It is also used for divine judgment: God's anger burns against sinners (Deuteronomy 32:22), and judgment will burst forth violently (Isaiah 10:16). In a few rarer passages, it takes on a nuance of inwardness: the heat of a passion that consumes from within (Jeremiah 15:14, 17:4). The context determines whether it refers to physical fire, passion, or judgment.
H3344.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate the holiness of God, represented by this perpetual fire that purifies and consumes. It reminds that divine judgment is not a fleeting threat, but a reality that persists. Finally, it serves to express how intense and inevitable God's anger is for those who turn away from Him — a tender warning that calls for repentance.

sens: extremely hot oven or furnace
place of punishment by fire
intense trial or suffering
H3345.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to an oven or furnace, meaning a place where fire burns intensely. In the story of Daniel, it is the furnace where King Nebuchadnezzar orders those who refuse to worship his statue to be thrown: it is a real place, likely intended for the production of bricks or metals, but heated to an extreme temperature (Daniel 3:6).
2. The furnace becomes an instrument of punishment and death: it represents divine or royal punishment inflicted by fire. The three young men Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego are thrown alive into it for their refusal of idolatry (Daniel 3:20, 3:21).
3. Figuratively, the term evokes a terrible and purifying trial, a suffering that consumes but can also reveal faithfulness to God. The story shows that those who remain faithful go through the fire and come out unharmed, transforming punishment into a sign of divine power (Daniel 3:17).
H3345.origine: The Aramaic word yeqad comes from the same root as the Hebrew yaqad (יָקַד), which means "to burn." This root expresses the action of fire that consumes and destroys. It is close to words describing fire and heat in other Semitic languages. The underlying image is that of a blaze or incandescence, hence the development of the meaning of "furnace": a place where fire burns intensely.
H3345.emploi: This Aramaic word appears 8 times in the Bible, all in chapter 3 of the book of Daniel. It describes the furnace in which King Nebuchadnezzar threatens to throw anyone who refuses to bow down before the golden statue he has erected. The term constantly returns to evoke both the threat (Daniel 3:6, 3:11, 3:15), the execution of this threat (Daniel 3:20, 3:21), and the miracle by which God delivers His servants from the flames (Daniel 3:17, 3:23, 3:26). The furnace thus becomes the heart of the story: it symbolizes the conflict between human power and divine power, between idolatry imposed by force and faithfulness to God.
H3345.portee: This story reminds the believer that remaining faithful to God may lead to terrible trials, but that the divine promise of deliverance is stronger than any human danger. The furnace represents any trial that seems destined to consume us, and it invites radical trust in God: "Our God can deliver us... and He will deliver us." For the Christian, it is a powerful image of victory over the persecutions and sufferings of the world.

sens: destruction by fire
consumption by flames
total annihilation
H3346.detail:
1. Burning refers to the action of burning, the moment when something is consumed by fire and reduced to nothing. In Daniel's vision, the horrible and arrogant beast is killed, and then its body is thrown into the fire "to be burned" (Daniel 7:11): it is the image of a definitive and complete destruction.
2. By extension, this word evokes the total annihilation of something, its radical elimination. The fire leaves nothing behind, reducing it to ashes.
H3346.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same verbal universe as the Hebrew word for "burning" or "combustion." It is a concrete word: it describes the physical process of fire that devours and consumes. The underlying Hebrew root is found in other biblical passages to evoke the action of fire, notably in images of divine judgment.
H3346.emploi: This word appears only once in the Aramaic New Testament (Daniel 7:11). It is used in the context of a famous prophetic vision: Daniel sees four terrible beasts symbolizing enemy kingdoms of God. The fourth beast, the most arrogant and threatening, is ultimately judged, killed, and delivered "to the fire to be burned." The term "burning" emphasizes the irrevocable and total nature of its destruction: nothing escapes it.
H3346.portee: This word reminds the reader that divine judgment is real and unappealable. The earthly powers that oppose God, however impressive they may seem, will be annihilated without remission. Daniel's vision invites the believer to an unwavering trust in God's sovereignty over history.

sens: mountainous city in the south of Judah
H3347.detail: Jokdeam is a small city located in the mountains of southern Judah, in the mountainous region of southern Israel. It appears in the list of cities in the territory of Judah, mentioned between Jezreel and Zanoach. Its exact location remains difficult to pinpoint today, but it was probably situated in the mountainous area south of Hebron, a dry and rocky region.
H3347.origine: The Hebrew name Yoqde'am literally means "burning of a people" or "fire of the people." It combines elements evoking fire or burning and the people. Like many names of ancient cities, this one may carry the memory of an event or a geographical feature (the arid region of southern Judah resembles a "burning" land), although its exact origin remains obscure.
H3347.emploi: Jokdeam appears only once in the Bible: in the list of cities located in the territory of the tribe of Judah at the time of the conquest of Canaan, in Joshua 15:56. It is among the many cities listed to mark the boundaries and tribal possessions. This unique mention suggests that it was a minor locality, with no major biblical event associated with its name.

sens: father of the wise Agur
H3348.detail: Jakeh is the father of the wise Agur, author of the words of Proverbs 30. This is all the Bible tells us about him: he appears only once, at the beginning of chapter 30 of Proverbs, solely to place Agur in his genealogy. His name means "without guilt" or "innocent," which may suggest moral integrity, although the Bible recounts nothing else about him.
H3348.origine: The name Jakeh comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be exempt" or "to be innocent," formed from the verb that expresses the absence of guilt. It is an uncommon name in Israel, attested only here in the entire Bible. Its meaning evokes a purity of conscience, a life without reproach in the eyes of God and men.
H3348.emploi: Jakeh appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 30:1, where he is presented as the father of Agur. Agur is the author of a collection of wise sayings, a remarkable section of Proverbs known for its spiritual depth and enigmas. Although we know nothing else about Jakeh himself, his mention alongside Agur suggests that he was a respected figure, perhaps a man of wisdom or integrity whose son continued this spiritual legacy.

sens: The act of submitting to an order, an authority
The disposition of the heart to listen to and follow the one who commands
H3349.detail:
1. Obedience is the act of submitting to an order or instruction from someone who has authority. It is doing what is asked of us, without resisting or refusing. In Genesis 49:10, the peoples "obey" Shiloh, meaning they submit to his authority and accept his guidance.

2. Beyond the external action, obedience also refers to an inner attitude: the willingness to listen, the respect towards the one who commands. In Proverbs 30:17, "obedience to a mother" speaks of this disposition of the heart to honor and follow parents, not just mechanically executing their orders.
H3349.origine: This word comes from a Hebrew root that fundamentally means "to listen" or "to hear." Obedience arises from listening: to obey, one must first hear and welcome the word of the one who commands. This is why in Hebrew, the same word expresses both the action of hearing and that of submitting — they are inseparable. To obey is truly to listen.
H3349.emploi: This word appears twice in the Bible according to the Segond. In Genesis 49:10, it describes how the peoples will accept the authority of the Messiah (Shiloh) — an obedience that will be universal and definitive, the sign of his reign. In Proverbs 30:17, it concerns filial obedience to parents, which is placed at the heart of morality and blessing: he who despises this obedience incurs a serious curse. In both cases, obedience is linked to deep respect, not to forced submission.
H3349.portee: Biblical obedience is not a servile fear, but a heartfelt response to the one who leads. For the believer, it reminds us that the Christian life begins with listening — hearing the voice of God and voluntarily submitting to it. It also shows that true authority (that of the Messiah, that of parents) deserves a respect that comes from the heart, not just from constraint.

sens: action or state of that which burns intensely
visible manifestation of a fierce fire, brilliant flame
H3350.detail:
1. The word describes the action or state of that which is engulfed in flames, in an intense and destructive manner. It is a fire, a vigorous combustion. In Isaiah 10:16, God sends the "blazing" among the warriors of the king of Assyria, compared to a devouring fire: it is the image of destruction by fire, of rapid and total devastation.
2. The word emphasizes the spectacular and luminous aspect of fire: its brilliant flames, its visible and striking manifestation. It is what shines, what radiates. The repetition in Isaiah 10:16 ("a blazing, like the blazing of a fire") insists on the intensity and irreversibility of the phenomenon.
H3350.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to burn" or "to be consumed." The Aramaic equivalent יְקֵדָא (ye.qe.da) has the same meaning and etymological family. The word evokes the visceral image of the flame that consumes, of the fire that devours everything in its path.
H3350.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 10:16, where God promises judgment on the Assyrian army. In this prophetic context, "blazing" refers to the fire of divine judgment, a sudden and total destruction. The repetition of the term emphasizes its weight: not only will there be a fire, but this fire will be a true blazing, inevitable and devastating. It is strong, poetic language that reinforces the certainty of the announced punishment.
H3350.portee: This word reminds the reader of the reality of divine judgment in the face of pride and iniquity. For the believer, it illustrates how God does not allow evil and injustice to prosper unpunished, even under the appearances of power and magnificence. It is also an invitation to take seriously the holiness of God and his prophetic warnings.

sens: That which subsists, that which remains alive
That which persists after destruction
Substance or essence of that which exists
H3351.detail:
1. The word designates that which lives and subsists — life itself or that which possesses the capacity for it. In Genesis 7:4, it speaks of "everything that has the breath of life" that God will cause to disappear: it is every living being, everything that "stands up" or actively exists on the earth.
2. It is used for that which persists, that which remains after an event. In the same flood narrative (Genesis 7:23), it describes what survives or conversely what remains nothing — the idea of a presence that continues or ceases.
3. More broadly, the word evokes the substance or essence: that which gives a creature or thing its character of real existence. In Deuteronomy 11:6, it speaks of that which "stands" in the midst of the assembly — a tangible presence, a living and visible reality.
H3351.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to stand" or "to rise." It expresses the idea of stability and persistence — that which remains in place, that which does not collapse. This root is active in biblical Hebrew: it produces very common verbal forms, but the noun "yéqoum" is a precise nominal form, concentrating the meaning on the durable and living reality of that which "stands up."
H3351.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in dramatic contexts related to life and death. Two occurrences are in the flood narrative (Genesis 7:4 and 7:23), where it designates all living beings that will breathe, then everything that will perish. The third (Deuteronomy 11:6) uses it to evoke what "stands before" the Lord at the time of engulfment. In all these passages, the word carries a solemn tone: it speaks of life in its most elementary and fragile dimension, confronted with death or divine judgment.
H3351.portee: This word reminds us that life is not an acquired right, but a presence that entirely depends on God. It invites us to recognize the fragility of our existence and the greatness of the gift of life. For the reader, these passages teach to measure the seriousness of sin and the reality of divine judgment, but also the grace that preserves those whom God chooses to save.

sens: one who sets traps for birds
one who uses cunning to capture
person who traps or leads into hidden danger
H3352.detail:
1. The fowler is a tradesman who captures birds by setting nets or traps. He is a specialized hunter, armed with his know-how and tools. In Hosea 9:8, the prophet literally speaks of a "fowler's net" — the image of the bird caught in the trap evokes the condemnation that awaits.
2. By extension, the fowler becomes the image of one who traps others by cunning, without resorting to brute force. He prepares his trap in silence, waiting for his prey to engage in it willingly. In Hosea 9:8, the prophet's ways are surrounded by these traps: he is targeted by enemies who lie in wait for him.
3. Spiritually, it is the image of invisible danger, of evil that progresses in secret. The fowler does not shout: he acts in secret. Thus Ephraim, the northern kingdom, is unaware of the nets being prepared around him, and the prophet who warns him finds himself at the heart of this web of snares.
H3352.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to bind" or "to tie" — the primary image is that of a knot, the link that captures. The fowler is literally one who "ties" his nets. This root appears in words designating traps or snares. The profession of fowler was known in the ancient Near East: it is an ordinary trade that Hosea chooses to symbolize danger and cunning.
H3352.emploi: The word appears only once in biblical Hebrew, in the prophetic word of Hosea against the northern kingdom (Hosea 9:8). Hosea denounces Ephraim as a corrupted spiritual watchman: instead of guarding the people, the prophet himself (or those acting as prophets) becomes an instrument of destruction. The fowler's nets symbolize here the dangers that close in on the people, a consequence of their unfaithfulness. The context shows how cunning and scheming replace justice and covenant.
H3352.portee: This word reminds the reader that spiritual danger often acts in secret: evil does not always strike visibly. It invites vigilance and discernment of the nets laid around us — not only the obvious temptations, but those that hide in darkness. For Hosea, it is a warning against the moral decline that precedes judgment: Ephraim does not see his trap coming.

sens: one who hunts birds by setting traps or nets
one who lays snares, who traps
one who seeks to capture or dominate someone by cunning
H3353.detail:
1. The birdcatcher is literally a hunter of birds who uses nets, traps, or bait to capture them alive. This was a profession practiced in antiquity (Proverbs 6:5 contrasts the bird that escapes from the hands of the birdcatcher with one that remains caught).
2. Figuratively, the birdcatcher becomes the image of one who sets snares to trap others: Jeremiah 5:26 describes the wicked who "watch like the birdcatcher," laying nets and capturing men, acting with cunning and malice.
3. In the prayer of Psalm 91:3, God "delivers from the snare of the birdcatcher," evoking spiritual danger: the believer is threatened like a bird by traps (sickness, evil), and God protects him from these hidden dangers.
H3353.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to trap" or "to set a snare." The birdcatcher is literally "one who traps," particularly birds. This image of the trap set discreetly reflects hidden and malicious action: one does not catch a bird by force, but by cunning and patience.
H3353.emploi: The word appears 3 times in the Hebrew Bible, always in a negative or dangerous tone. In the Psalms and Proverbs, it serves as an image of divine protection (God protects us from traps) and caution (one must escape these traps like the bird escapes). In Jeremiah, it describes the behavior of the wicked who plot schemes. Each time, the emphasis is on the hidden and treacherous nature of this threat.
H3353.portee: This word reminds us that evil often acts through cunning rather than direct violence. It invites the reader to remain vigilant against the hidden traps of this world and to trust God for protection. It is also a call not to act as a birdcatcher towards others, that is, not to seek to trap or deceive one's neighbor.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah mentioned only once in the Bible
H3354.detail: Jekuthiel is a character from the Old Testament belonging to the tribe of Judah, being a descendant of Caleb. He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:18, where he is presented as the father of Zanoach. He is part of a complex genealogy: he is the son of Mered and the Jewish woman (a wife from the Hebrew people), and the brother of Jered and Heber.
H3354.origine: The name Jekuthiel means "God's purification" or "God's cleansing" — it combines the idea of purity (a root related to the verb "to make pure") and the divine name ("God"). It is a typical theophoric name in Hebrew onomastics, expressing a blessing or divine action.
H3354.emploi: Jekuthiel appears exclusively in 1 Chronicles 4:18, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Judah likely dating from the divided monarchy period. He is presented as one of the sons from a mixed marriage between Mered, a Judean, and Bithiah, the daughter of the Pharaoh of Egypt. This genealogy shows how some Judean families allied with foreigners, including Egyptians, and how these children integrated into the official genealogy of God's people.

sens: Son of Eber and brother of Peleg, patriarch living in the time of the Patriarchs
Ancestor and father of several ancient Arab peoples and tribes
H3355.detail: 1. Jokthan is a character from the Old Testament who appears in the genealogy of Noah's descendants through Shem. He is the son of Eber and the twin (or fraternal) brother of Peleg, whose name means "division" because it was during his time that the earth was divided among the peoples (Genesis 10:25). 2. Jokthan is best known as the father of thirteen sons who became the ancestors of Arab peoples: Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, Jerah, Hadoram, Uzal, Diklah, Obal, Abimael, Sheba, Ophir, Havilah, and Jobab (Genesis 10:26-29). These descendants populated and dominated the Arabian Peninsula and surrounding regions.
H3355.origine: The name Jokthan comes from the Hebrew verb meaning "to be small" or "to diminish," hence the meaning "smallness" or "one who has become small." This name may reflect the lesser importance attributed to Jokthan compared to his brother Peleg in the patriarchal lineage. Jokthan descends from Shem, one of Noah's three sons, thus representing an important branch of post-flood humanity.
H3355.emploi: Jokthan is mentioned six times in the Bible: three times in Genesis (chapters 10:25-29) and three times in the Book of Chronicles (chapter 1:19-23). Genesis presents him in the context of the dispersion of nations after the flood, listing his descendants. The Book of Chronicles repeats exactly the same genealogical information, confirming his importance in the ancient history of peoples. These accounts establish Jokthan as a founding patriarch of significant Arab peoples mentioned elsewhere in the Bible, notably Sheba and Ophir.
H3355.portee: Jokthan reminds the reader that the Bible is concerned with all nations and their origins, not just Israel. His story shows how God guided the peopling of the earth after the flood and how the neighboring peoples of Israel descend from common ancestors. This perspective encourages humility: even the "other" peoples are part of God's divine history of the world.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the divided monarchy
H3356G.detail: Jakim is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:19. He is the son of Shimei and the brother of several other men: Zicri, Zabdi, Elienai, Zillethai, Eliel, Adaiah, Beriah, and Shimrath. His name means "He will raise" or "He will lift up," evoking the idea of elevation or restoration. He belongs to a genealogy of Benjaminites, the descendants of the tribe of Benjamin who survived after the kingdom split into Northern Israel and Southern Judah.
H3356G.origine: The name Jakim comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to raise" or "to lift up." It expresses the idea of a divine or human action that elevates, straightens, or establishes. In the Old Testament, this type of name was common: theophoric names (containing an allusion to God or a divine action) often expressed the hope or action of the parents and their faith in God.
H3356G.emploi: Jakim is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:19, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. He appears among the sons of Shimei, in a context that enumerates the Benjamite families surviving after the return from exile. This unique mention shows that he was a man of genealogical and familial importance, but whose individual life is not detailed in the Scriptures.

sens: Levitical priest during the time of David
Chief of a division of worship at the temple
H3356H.detail: Jakim is a Levitical priest who lived during the time of King David. He was responsible for the twelfth division (or "class") of priests assigned to service in the temple (1 Chronicles 24:12). Each division performed worship in turn; thus, Jakim led a group of priests assigned to this rotating service.
H3356H.origine: The name Jakim means "He will raise" or "He will establish," formed from the Hebrew root that expresses the action of raising, erecting, or constituting. This theophoric name (containing a divine action) was common among the priestly families of Israel.
H3356H.emploi: Jakim is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:12, in the list established by David of the twenty-four divisions of Levitical priests. This organization, documented at the time of the temple worship's organization, shows how religious service was structured and distributed among the priestly families. Jakim represents one of these families and his liturgical role.

sens: Precious, rare, of great value
Dear to someone, tenderly loved
Honored, esteemed, worthy of respect
H3357.detail: 1. The word primarily designates what is rare and of great value — something or someone that one possesses only once, which cannot be replaced. 2. It then describes what is dear to the heart, loved tenderly: in Jeremiah 31:20, God calls Ephraim "my beloved son," expressing a deep and personal love, almost maternal ("my heart is moved"). 3. The word can also mean "honored" or "esteemed," marking the dignity and respect one holds for someone.
H3357.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be rare" or "to be precious." There is an identical Aramaic form (yaq.qir) with the meaning "honorable." Rarity and preciousness underlie the idea of love: what is rare is dear, and what is dear deserves our respect and tenderness.
H3357.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 31:20.
