In this context, the prophet reports God's word: Ephraim (representing the ten northern tribes in exile) is called the "beloved son" of the Lord. The term here expresses God's inexhaustible love despite Israel's unfaithfulness. This uniqueness makes the word all the more moving: it is reserved for the moment when God affirms His unwavering attachment.
H3357.portee: This word reminds us that we are precious in God's eyes — not for our merits, but because He has chosen us and loves us as a father loves his only son. Jeremiah 31:20 shows that this love persists even when we stray: our hearts (the seat of our emotions) should be "moved" with the same tenderness towards the lost and the wayward.

sens: That requires a lot of effort, that is hard to accomplish
That is rare, precious, of great value
That is worthy of respect, honorable
H3358.detail:
1. The word primarily designates what requires great effort, what is arduous: in Daniel 2:11, the king of Babylon poses a riddle that no one can solve, and the magicians themselves confess that "what the king asks is difficult." It is a task that surpasses ordinary human strength.
2. By extension, it qualifies what is rare and precious, for what is hard to obtain or to do becomes valuable. In Ezra 4:10, the same word in its related form means rather "transported" — a less direct but related meaning: the idea of being elevated, distinguished, honored.
3. The word can also express what is noble or worthy of respect, what exceeds the ordinary. Effort and rarity confer a sort of dignity: only the gods can accomplish what is truly difficult.
H3358.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of "to harden" or "to be difficult." Words of the same family refer to what is hard, resistant, difficult to overcome or to traverse. The image is that of a compact, solid material that offers resistance. Over time, this notion has extended to what is rare, precious, and honorable, for what is hard to achieve deserves honor.
H3358.emploi: The word appears twice in the provided biblical usages. In Daniel 2:11, it describes an impossible task: the interpretation of the king's dream that only the gods can accomplish. In Ezra 4:10, it takes on a nuance related to honor or elevation — the peoples are "transported" by a great king, an action marked by importance. The context of prayer and divine miracle in Daniel shows that the word measures the gap between human limitation and divine power: only God can accomplish what is truly difficult.
H3358.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that certain trials or calls seem humanly impossible — this is normal. It is precisely there that God intervenes. Entrusting to God what is difficult is to acknowledge that His power infinitely surpasses ours. This invites prayer rather than anxiety, knowing that nothing is impossible for Him whose dwelling is in heaven.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah during the divided monarchy
H3359G.detail: Jekamja is a man of the tribe of Judah mentioned in the genealogy of Judah. He is the son of Shallum and the father of Elishama, integrated into the Davidic royal lineage (1 Chronicles 2:41). His name means "Jehovah raises" or "Jehovah exalts," expressing trust in God to uplift and establish the lineage.
H3359G.origine: The name Jekamja is composed of two Hebrew elements: "Jehovah" (the proper name of God) and a root meaning "to raise" or "to uplift." This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel to express a blessing or trust in God's action.
H3359G.emploi: Jekamja appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:41, in the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Judah. He is part of the lineage of Ahlai and represents a link in the transmission of the name and royal blessing through the Davidic lineage during a time marked by the division of the kingdom of Israel.
H3359G.portee: The name and presence of Jekamja in the royal genealogy remind us that God remains faithful to His promises to the house of David, even during political ruptures and dynastic crises. It is an invitation to recognize that God "raises" those He chooses and preserves His line of succession according to His purpose.

sens: son of Shealtiel, royal descendant of Judah
one of the seven children named in the Davidic succession
H3359H.detail:
1. Jekamia is a man of the people of Judah, son of Shealtiel. He appears in the royal genealogy of David, listed among the children of his father in the passage of 1 Chronicles 3:18.
2. He is one of the seven children who form an important branch of the royal descent, alongside his brothers Malkiram, Pedaiah, Shenazar, Hoshama, and Nedabiah. These seven sons illustrate the continuity of the Davidic royal line during the time of the Divided Monarchy.
H3359H.origine: The name Jekamia means "Jehovah raises" or "God uplifts." It is composed of theophoric elements revealing faith in God's protective action. This name appears only in the genealogies of the Book of Chronicles, which trace the continuity of the royal house of Judah through the generations.
H3359H.emploi: Jekamia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:18, where he is listed among the sons of Shealtiel. This genealogical list in the Book of Chronicles documents the continuity of the Davidic line, particularly after the Babylonian captivity. His inclusion in this official record shows that he played a role in preserving the royal succession of Judah, even though no specific details of his life are reported.

sens: Levite, son of Hebron and grandson of Kohath
H3360.detail: Jekameam is a Levite mentioned twice in the genealogical lists during the time of King David. He is the fourth son of Hebron, who is himself the son of Kohath. The two mentions (1 Chronicles 23:19 and 24:23) systematically place him fourth among the sons of Hebron, after Jeriah (the chief), Amariah, and Jahaziel.
H3360.origine: The name Jekameam literally means "let the people rise" or "let the people awaken." It is a theophoric Hebrew name — carrying a divine invocation — common in Levitical genealogies. It reflects a wish or parental blessing.
H3360.emploi: Jekameam appears only twice in the Bible, both in 1 Chronicles, in the genealogical records of the tribe of Levi established during David's reign. He is among the descendants of Kohath, an important branch of the Levitical priesthood. His name always appears in the same genealogical order: the fourth son of Hebron.

sens: City of refuge in the land of Israel
Fortified city assigned to the Levites of the tribe of Levi
H3361G.detail:
1. Jokmeam is a city in the region of Ephraim, mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Kings 4:12, where it appears as a geographical landmark. It was one of the cities of refuge established in Israel to provide protection for someone who had killed unintentionally.
2. This city was given to the Levites of the family of the Kohathites (descendants of Kohath, one of the priestly lines of Israel). It reflects how God provided for the housing and maintenance of the clergy: rather than owning a single piece of land, the Levites received several cities scattered throughout the territory of the twelve tribes.
H3361G.origine: The name Jokmeam literally means "gathered by the people" or "founded by the assembly" — it reflects its status as an important public place. The Bible sometimes mentions Jokneam (יׇקְנְעָם) as another name for this same city or a closely associated place. The name evokes a city that serves as a gathering point and refuge for the community.
H3361G.emploi: Jokmeam appears only once in the provided biblical usages, in 1 Kings 4:12, where it is cited as a geographical landmark in the list of the twelve administrative districts under the reign of Solomon. It is located in the district of Baana, son of Achilud, between Megiddo and Abel-Meholah, indicating its strategic position in the land of Israel. Its inclusion in this passage shows that it was significant enough and well-known to serve as a boundary marker delineating the borders of a royal administrative region.
H3361G.portee: Jokmeam reminds the reader that God established a system of cities of refuge to protect the innocent who had shed blood without intent. It also embodies divine providence toward the Levites, who had no territorial inheritance like the other tribes but received support and security from the people. It is a testimony to God's mercy and wise organization for His people.

sens: City of refuge in Ephraim, given to the Levites of the family of Kohath
H3361H.detail: Jokmeam is a city in Gilead, assigned to the Levites of the family of Kohath as a city of refuge according to the law of Moses (1 Chronicles 6:68). It is mentioned alongside Beth-Horon among the Levitical cities of Ephraim. Jokmeam has a second name, Kibzaim, and served as a place of asylum for someone who had committed unintentional homicide.
H3361H.origine: The name Jokmeam literally means "gathered by the people": it combines the idea of gathering and community. It is a city mentioned in the official lists of Levitical cities, which attests to its importance in the religious organization of Israel. It is identified at the same location as Kibzaim, showing that some places had multiple names.
H3361H.emploi: Jokmeam appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 6:68, in the list of cities of refuge given to the Levites of Kohath after the conquest of Canaan. This enumeration is part of the system established by Moses to ensure that each Levitical family had cities where they could exercise their ministry. The mention of its "suburbs" (the lands surrounding it) emphasizes that it was not isolated but integrated into an inhabited territory.
H3361H.portee: Jokmeam reminds us that God organized the territory of Israel to establish a holy people and places of refuge. The Levitical cities represented a fundamental principle: the equitable distribution of land and the protection of the innocent by the law. For the believer, it is a testimony to divine order and justice.

sens: City of Canaan located in Galilee, near Mount Carmel
City conquered by Joshua and integrated into the territory of Zebulun
City assigned to the Levites of the family of Merari
H3362.detail: 1. Jokneam is a city of Canaan located in the region of Mount Carmel, in northern Galilee. It is among the royal cities of Canaan that Joshua conquered at the head of Israel (Joshua 12:22). 2. This city marks the eastern boundary of the territory of Zebulun: "The boundary of their inheritance extended to Sarid. It went westward to Mareal, and touched Dabbesheth, then the torrent that flows before Jokneam" (Joshua 19:11). It thus served as a geographical landmark to delineate tribal possessions. 3. After the conquest, Jokneam was assigned to the Levites of the family of Merari as a city of refuge with its pastures (Joshua 21:34), in accordance with Moses' order regarding the Levitical cities.
H3362.origine: The name literally means "the people lament" in Hebrew. Jokneam also appears in the alternative form Jokmeam in 1 Chronicles 6:77, where it is referred to as Rimmono ("Pomegranate"), suggesting a change of name or two names for the same place.
H3362.emploi: Jokneam appears four times in the Bible. In Joshua 12:22, it is mentioned as one of the royal cities defeated by Joshua. In Joshua 19:11, it serves as a landmark for the boundaries of the territory of Zebulun. In Joshua 21:34, it is assigned to the Levites of Merari with its pastoral lands. In 1 Chronicles 6:77, the same passage is repeated but the city is called Rimmono, indicating a variation in the name or possibly a local distinction. These mentions highlight the importance of this city in the administrative and religious organization of Israel after the conquest.

sens: To be dislocated, dislocated (referring to a limb)
To be hanged, executed by hanging
To execute someone slowly, by exposure or impalement
To withdraw, detach, separate
H3363.detail:
1. The primary meaning is anatomical: a joint dislocates, becomes dislocated. In Genesis 32:25, Jacob's hip joint dislocates during his nighttime struggle with the angel — this is the only usage where the word refers to the body being mistreated.

2. The judicial and penal meaning is the most frequent: to hang someone means to execute them by exposing them, suspended. Numbers 25:4 commands to "hang the guilty before the Lord in the sight of the sun" to turn away divine anger. In 2 Samuel 21:6-9, the Gibeonites hang seven sons of Saul on the mountain. This punishment was a disgraceful one, often followed by exposure of the corpse.

3. In a related context, the word can mean to execute slowly by other means (impalement, prolonged exposure) — forms of horrific and degrading death intended to humiliate and warn.

4. Figuratively, in Jeremiah, the verb takes on the meaning of "to withdraw" or "to detach": God says "I do not withdraw from you" (Jeremiah 6:8), as if divine favor or presence were detaching from the unfaithful people.
H3363.origine: The Hebrew root יָקַע evokes first a brutal separation, a rupture or exclusion. The initial image is that of a joint dislocating — something being torn away, detached from the whole. From this comes the idea of public exposure and suspension: the one who is hanged is set apart from the community, rejected and made visible as punishment. The verb retains this ambivalence between bodily dislocation and social rejection.
H3363.emploi: The word appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated in two distinct areas. First, the judicial punishment of hanging: Numbers 25:4 and 2 Samuel 21 make it the primary usage, in a context of executing criminals or enemies, always publicly and before the Lord. The practice was disgraceful: the bodies remained suspended (2 Samuel 21:13 reports that they "gathered the bones of those who had been hanged"). Secondly, Jeremiah 6:8 transposes the verb figuratively: the Lord threatens to "withdraw" from Jerusalem, transferring the image of rejection and separation from the physical plane to the divine plane. The usages in Ezekiel (23:17-18) seem to fall under the same register of withdrawal or detachment.
H3363.portee: This word refers to one of the darkest forms of justice in the Old Testament: hanging as a disgraceful and public execution. For the Christian, it also evokes the suffering of the cross, which suspended the condemned between heaven and earth. But the word also teaches that the Lord can "withdraw" from His people when they reject Him — a threat that only repentance can avert. It is a reminder of the seriousness of sin and the cost of unfaithfulness.

sens: To come out of sleep, to regain consciousness after sleeping
To cease a stupor, to regain one's senses
To wake up from a dream or vision experience
To become active after a period of inactivity or forgetfulness
H3364.detail:
1. To awaken from sleep: the most direct and common meaning. It is to wake up after sleeping, like Noah who "awoke from his wine" (Genesis 9:24) or Jacob who "awoke from his sleep" upon recognizing the presence of God (Genesis 28:16). The verb describes the transition from sleep to a conscious state.
2. To wake up from a dream or vision: the word can also refer to the moment when someone comes out of a dream and realizes what has happened. Pharaoh "awoke" after his dreams of cows and ears of grain (Genesis 41:4, 7, 21) — he regains his senses, realizing it was just a dream but that it signifies something to him.
3. To wake up in an active and sudden manner: the verb can express a sudden and vigorous awakening. Samson "awoke from his sleep" and immediately "tore the pin from the loom" (Judges 16:14) — it is an awakening accompanied by immediate action.
4. In a figurative sense, to become active, to manifest: God "awakens" like a warrior who takes up arms (Psalms 78:65) — the image is that of a power that begins to move after silence.
H3364.origine: The Hebrew verb יָקַץ (yaqats) comes from a root that expresses the idea of rupture or separation. The word paints the image of someone who "detaches" or "separates" from sleep, who comes out of a state of drowsiness. The same root produces words that denote what cuts or breaks. It is therefore a very vivid verb: to awaken is like "detaching" oneself from the sleep that holds you.
H3364.emploi: The verb appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narratives of the Old Testament. It is first used in the literal sense: Noah wakes up, Jacob wakes up, Samson wakes up. But it also applies to dreams: Pharaoh "awakens" from his dreams, meaning he comes out of the dream vision and realizes he has dreamed. The verb can also apply to God: "The Lord awoke like a warrior who wakes from sleep" (Psalms 78:65) — the image is that of a power reclaiming its rights. In all cases, the word emphasizes the transition from a passive state to an active state, from unconsciousness to consciousness.
H3364.portee: This word reminds us that consciousness, the awakening of the heart and mind, is fundamental in biblical life. When Jacob awakens at Bethel, he recognizes the presence of God and his heart is transformed. Spiritual sleep — forgetfulness, indifference — is always a danger for the believer; to awaken is to become present again to the reality of God and His promises.

sens: To have value, to be deemed worthy of price
To be rare, difficult to obtain
To be dear to someone, to matter a lot to them
To become rare, to decrease in abundance
H3365.detail:
1. The word first denotes what has great value, what deserves to be appreciated and preserved. It is like saying that something is precious because it is deemed important. Saul says to David: "my life has been precious in your eyes" (1 Samuel 26:21), meaning that David values him enough to spare him.
2. Precious also means rare, difficult to find, because rare things are valuable. When Isaiah announces "I will make men more rare than fine gold" (Isaiah 13:12), the word expresses this rarity: men will become few in number, thus of great value.
3. To be precious to someone means that this person cherishes us, holds us in high esteem. The Lord says to His people: "you are precious in my eyes" (Isaiah 43:4), which means: you matter a lot to me, you are extremely dear to me.
4. The word can also mean to make rare or less frequent. "Do not frequently set foot in your neighbor's house" (Proverbs 25:17): in Hebrew, it is the same word that expresses the idea of becoming rare, thus coming less often.
H3365.origine: The Hebrew word יָקַר comes from a root that evokes the idea of what shines, what is visible and thus noticed. That is why it first denotes what is precious, rare, what attracts attention because it is valued. The same root is found in terms that speak of glory, honor, and weight (importance). Most neighboring Semitic languages use a similar root to express the idea of value and rarity.
H3365.emploi: This verb appears eleven times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives, Psalms, and Proverbs. In 1 Samuel 18 and 26, it describes the friendship between Saul and David: the life of one becomes precious in the eyes of the other. In the Psalms, the word denotes the priceless value of redemption (Psalms 49:9) or the value of someone we love (Psalms 139:17: "How precious to me are your thoughts"). Isaiah uses it more prophetically: men will become rare and thus precious (Isaiah 13:12), or God affirms that His people are precious in His eyes (Isaiah 43:4). Proverbs 25:17 plays on the sense of rarity: for your friend to appreciate you, become rare in his presence.
H3365.portee: This word reminds the believer that everything that is truly important in God's eyes — every person, every life — has immeasurable value. Knowing that we are precious in His eyes invites us to recognize ourselves as loved and valued by the Creator, not because of our merits, but because God cherishes us. It is also an invitation to sobriety and discretion in our relationships: true friendship is born when we become rare, available without overwhelming.

sens: What makes something or someone precious, worthy of esteem
The market value of something, its price
The respect, esteem one holds for someone
The brilliance, splendor, magnificence that impresses
The distinction, high rank in society
H3366.detail:
1. Preciousness or the quality of being precious: the word first denotes what has intrinsic value. Job 28:10 speaks of what is "precious" in the rocks — stones, gold, everything that sparkles and is worth something.
2. The price or market value: it is what one pays to obtain something. Zechariah 11:13 mentions the thirty pieces of silver, this price.
3. Respect and esteem: when one honors someone, one acknowledges their value. Esther 6:7-11 shows the king ordering great honor to be given to Mordecai by dressing him royally and parading him through the city for all to celebrate.
4. Brilliance and splendor: the word evokes visible magnificence. Esther 1:4 describes how the king displayed the "glorious" splendor of his greatness for one hundred eighty days — all that is dazzling and impressive in his palace.
5. Distinction and rank: the high status one acquires or receives. Esther 6:3 reports that Mordecai received a "mark of distinction and honor" from the king, who placed him above others.
H3366.origine: The word יְקָר comes from a Hebrew root that evokes what shines, what rises, what has weight and importance. It is from the same family as a word meaning "heavy" or "serious" — what is serious has weight, thus price, thus honor. The central idea is that of weight, importance: what truly matters. In Aramaic, the same word (יְקָר) also means "honor."
H3366.emploi: The word appears 15 times in biblical Hebrew, mainly in the wisdom books (Job, Psalms, Proverbs) and in the narrative of Esther. In Esther (about 6 occurrences), it regularly denotes the honor publicly rendered to the king or a minister: it is a visible act, a social distinction (clothing, procession, proclamation). In the Psalms and Proverbs, it takes on a broader hue: the honor of men, their esteem among others, or their apparent brilliance — which can be fragile or deceptive (Psalms 49:21: the honored man but without understanding is like the beasts). In Jeremiah and Ezekiel, the word denotes the riches and splendor of nations, often before their downfall.
H3366.portee: The term honor invites the reader to reflect on true value: what is really precious? Human honor, brilliance, wealth — all of this is visible and impressive, but the Bible suggests that it is only lasting if it rests on wisdom and justice. Esther shows that publicly rendered honor is legitimate when it rewards faithfulness (Mordecai). But the wise remind us that intelligence is worth more than reputation, and the fear of God above all distinction.

sens: Honor, dignity, consideration enjoyed by a person
Splendor, magnificence, brilliance surrounding power
Greatness, prestige attached to rank, authority
H3367.detail: 1. Glory is primarily the honor and esteem one receives: it is being recognized, valued, elevated in dignity. When King Nebuchadnezzar promises Daniel "great honors" (Daniel 2:6), he offers recognition and dignity. 2. It is also the visible splendor, the brilliance that shines around power and wealth: the "glory" of the king is his magnificence, his radiance (Daniel 4:30). 3. Finally, it is the very greatness of the reign: the empire, the power, the authority one possesses and from which one derives prestige. When Nebuchadnezzar is "deprived of his glory" (Daniel 5:20), he loses at once power, esteem, and brilliance.
H3367.origine: The Aramaic word יְקָר comes from a root that expresses the idea of weight, value, that which is precious. It is related to the Hebrew יְקָר (yéqar) which means exactly "preciousness" — that which has worth, value. This etymology shows that glory is fundamentally what has weight, value in the eyes of others.
H3367.emploi: This word appears only in the book of Daniel, in Aramaic, 7 times, exclusively to speak of the greatness of kings and their reign. It refers sometimes to the "honors" one can receive from a king (Daniel 2:6), sometimes to royal "glory" in the sense of visible splendor (Daniel 4:30: "for the glory of my magnificence"), and sometimes to the greatness of power itself (Daniel 2:37; 5:18: "the empire, the greatness, the glory"). The word marks that such glory is fragile and can be taken away: Nebuchadnezzar, in his pride, is "stripped" of it (Daniel 5:20), then it is "restored" to him (Daniel 4:36) when God restores him.
H3367.portee: In Daniel's eyes, human glory — power, wealth, the brilliance of a king — is never more than what God gives and can take away. It is not bad in itself, but it is fragile, and it becomes perilous as soon as man forgets it and becomes proud. It is a call to recognize that all authority comes from God alone.

sens: Having great material value, costly
Rare, difficult to find
Worthy of being valued, esteemed for its qualities
Magnificent, splendid, worthy of glory
(Figuratively) Having weight, influence, importance
H3368.detail:
1. A precious object is dear, costly, made of noble or rare material: the Queen of Sheba brings to Solomon "very great quantities of gold, and precious stones" (1 Kings 10:2), goods that are worth a lot and show her wealth.
2. What is rare is difficult to obtain, thus all the more valued: "The word of the Lord was rare in those days" (1 Samuel 3:1) — the revelations of God were lacking, which made them even more precious in the eyes of those who received one.
3. A precious person or quality deserves respect and honor because it is truly worth something: "How precious is your steadfast love, O God!" (Psalms 36:8) — divine goodness is a treasure that must be cherished and is indispensable.
4. What is magnificent or splendid shines with beauty and brilliance: the precious stones adorning the temple, the gold filling the palaces of kings embody glory and wealth.
5. In a figurative sense, a person or a word can be precious if it has weight and influence: one who knows how to hold their words is wise, and their rare words are of gold.
H3368.origine: The Hebrew word yakhar comes from a root that first evokes the idea of weighing, valuing — what is precious has weight in the literal sense (gold, stones) and in the figurative sense (importance, moral value). The family of the word includes "karod" (dignity, honor) and "kikar" (talent, balance). In the Greek of the Old Testament, this word is often translated as "timios" (precious, honored), which also carries the idea of a value that is respected.
H3368.emploi: The word appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Job), royal narratives (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), and the prophets. It primarily designates the material treasures of kings — gold, precious stones, rare woods of the temple — but gradually expands to spiritual and moral realities. In the prophets like Jeremiah, "precious" applies to the word of God or to faithful believers who must be separated from what is "worthless." In the Psalms and Proverbs, divine goodness, wisdom, and even life itself are described as precious. The word thus shifts registers without changing its essence: everything that is "precious" requires protection, cherishing, and not wasting.
H3368.portee: Understanding this word invites the believer to discern what truly has value: not primarily gold or stones, but the goodness of God, His word, wisdom, and life itself — so precious that God will redeem it at the cost of His Son's blood. It is also a call not to waste what is rare and valuable: our days, our strength, our words. The word teaches us that true wealth is not visible or measurable, but spiritual and moral.

sens: to set a trap, to lay a trap
to be ensnared, to be caught by a trap
one who sets traps, fowler
trap, net, bond that captures
H3369.detail:
1. The primary meaning is concrete: to set a trap for someone or an animal, like a fowler who lays his nets or snares to catch birds (Psalms 124:7). It is to put in place a hidden device aimed at capturing.

2. To be ensnared or caught means to fall into this trap, to be caught by the bond or net that has closed around oneself. The image is that of a prey that can no longer escape (Proverbs 6:2: "If you are ensnared by the words of your mouth," Ecclesiastes 9:12).

3. The fowler (participle) is one who makes and sets these traps to capture birds; it is the professional hunter who masters this art (Psalms 124:7).

4. The trap itself or the net, the bond that captures and holds; it can also figuratively be a hidden danger or a temptation that imprisons (Deuteronomy 7:25: idols become a "snare," Psalms 141:9).
H3369.origine: The Hebrew root יָקַשׁ carries the primitive image of stretching, binding, entwining. It evokes the action of the net closing or the cord entwining. The word first designates the concrete act of the trap — its installation and effect — and then expands to anything that captures, holds, or ensnares, in both a literal and figurative sense.
H3369.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Psalms) and in the prophetic writings. It always designates the action of capturing by a trap or being captured, and is used for both the capture of animals (the bird, the fish) and for misfortunes that surprise man. Figuratively, it evokes hidden dangers: words that ensnare (Proverbs 6:2), idols that become a snare (Deuteronomy 7:25), or the malicious plans of enemies (Psalms 141:9). The Bible uses it to show how sin or misfortune suddenly seizes one who does not protect themselves.
H3369.portee: This word invites the believer to be aware of the traps that await: seductions, bad words, idols, insidious compromises. It reminds us that sin functions like a hidden net that wraps around us if we are not careful. Spiritual vigilance becomes essential, and deliverance from the trap (as in Psalms 124:7) is a grace to ask of the Lord.

sens: Son of Abraham and Keturah
Father of Sheba and Dedan
Character from the patriarchal times
H3370.detail: 1. Jokschan is a son that Abraham had with Keturah, his second wife after Sarah's death. He is one of the six sons born from this union, alongside Zimran, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuach (Genesis 25:2). 2. Jokschan was the father of two sons: Sheba and Dedan, whose descendants will form peoples or clans of the ancient Near East (Genesis 25:3). 3. He lived during the time of the patriarchs and belongs to the lineage of Abraham, but he is not an ancestor of Israel: his descendants will follow a different story than that of God's people.
H3370.origine: The name Jokschan means "one who traps" or "snares" in English. It derives from the Hebrew root evoking the idea of capturing or trapping. Although the name is rarely used, it fits into Abraham's genealogy where each son represents a distinct family branch and different peoples.
H3370.emploi: Jokschan is mentioned three times in Scripture, all in genealogical context: twice in Genesis 25 (verses 2 and 3), where he is listed among the sons of Abraham and identified as the father of Sheba and Dedan, and once in 1 Chronicles 1:32, which repeats the same genealogy. He does not appear elsewhere in biblical narratives and plays no narrative role. His importance is purely genealogical: he represents a branch of Abraham's descendants that developed into peoples of the Arabian desert.

sens: City of low Judea mentioned in the enumeration of cities in the territory of Judah
H3371G.detail: Joktheel is a small city located in the Shephelah, the region of low hills between the Mediterranean coast and the heights of Judah. It is listed among the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the territory after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:38), situated near Lachish, a well-known fortress.
H3371G.origine: The name Joktheel literally means "the blessing of God" (from the verb "to establish, found" and the divine name Elohim). It expresses the hope that this city, like any establishment in the promised land, participates in the divine blessing granted to the people of Israel.
H3371G.emploi: Joktheel appears only once in the Bible, in the list of cities in the Shephelah of Judah (Joshua 15:38). Its precise geographical identity remains uncertain today, but it was significant enough to be included in the official inventory of the territory of Judah, alongside strongholds like Lachish.

sens: Fortress of Edom conquered by King Amaziah
Former name of Sela (Petra)
H3371H.detail:
1. Joktheel is the name given by King Amaziah of Judah to the fortress of Edom after conquering it. The king had defeated ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, then took this stronghold and renamed it Joktheel (2 Kings 14:7).
2. This place is another designation for Sela, the famous citadel of Edom built on rocky heights, which the Greeks would later call Petra. The name "Sela" literally means "the rock," which aptly describes the geographical nature of the site.
H3371H.origine: The Hebrew name Joktheel means "the blessing of God" or "the happiness of God." It is composed of two elements: "yoq" (happiness, blessing) and "theel" (God). By giving this name to the conquered fortress, King Amaziah acknowledged that his victory was a divine blessing. It is a typical example of renaming: when a king took an enemy city, he often gave it a new name that proclaimed his victory or piety.
H3371H.emploi: Joktheel appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 14:7, during the account of King Amaziah's military campaign against Edom. This passage recounts the capture of the strategic fortress and the imposition of the new name by the victorious king. The text specifies that this name "has remained to this day," indicating that, at the time the text was written, the site was still designated as such. Joktheel and Sela refer to the same place, a key strategic position in the mountains of Edom.
H3371H.portee: This name reminds us that Israel's military victories were never solely the work of human strength, but the result of divine blessing. The choice of a name that proclaims "the blessing of God" invites the believer to recognize that all success comes from God, and that true victory consists in remaining obedient to His commandments.

sens: To feel fear in the face of real or supposed danger
To respect someone or something with a kind of reverential fear
To dread the consequences of an action or word
To inspire fear, to frighten
H3372G.detail:
1. To feel fear in the face of real or supposed danger: this is immediate, visceral fear, the kind felt when confronted with something threatening. Adam was afraid when hiding naked in the garden (Genesis 3:10), and the Israelites were afraid before the Red Sea (Exodus 14:10). It is the raw emotion of one who feels threatened.

2. To respect someone or something with a kind of reverential fear: fear then becomes a mixture of respect and admiration mixed with fear. Exodus 20:20 says, "Do not be afraid: God has come to test you, and that His fear may be before your eyes" — here it is about respecting and revering God. It is an attitude of respectful submission rather than simple terror.

3. To dread the consequences of an action or word: this is anticipating misfortune. Saul feared David because the Lord was with him (1 Samuel 18:12) — he sensed an impending threat. It is the anxious calculation of one who sees a storm coming.

4. To inspire fear, to frighten: the word can describe the effect produced rather than the fear felt. Joshua did not need to fear that Jericho was formidable (Joshua 10:2), for God was with him — the city inspires fear, but not for one who relies on God.
H3372G.origine: The verb יָרֵא (yaré) comes from a root that first evokes trembling, shivering — this physical shiver one has in the face of danger or the sacred presence. In Hebrew, this word is linked to the idea of fear that raises the hair, that chills the blood. It is used for ordinary fear before an enemy, but also for religious fear, this reverence mixed with respect felt in the presence of the divine. The word can describe either the one who fears or what inspires fear.
H3372G.emploi: The verb יָרֵא is one of the most frequent words in the Old Testament, used over two hundred times. It denotes ordinary fear: Saul fears David (1 Samuel 18:12), the Israelites fear the enemy at the border (Deuteronomy 1:21). But it also denotes the fear of God, which is a central virtue in biblical faith: it is fear as respect and reverence (Exodus 20:20, Psalms 56:5). The same word thus covers both paralyzing fear in the face of danger and fear-respect in the face of the divine. Moses tells the Israelites, "Do not be afraid" when facing the enemy (Deuteronomy 1:29; Joshua 10:25), inviting them to replace fear with trust in God. The context determines whether it is a fear to be rejected or a fear to be cultivated.
H3372G.portee: This word teaches the reader that the true response to fear is not the absence of feelings, but the refocusing: replacing the fear of danger or man with the fear-respect of God. Everywhere, God tells His people "do not be afraid" not because danger does not exist, but because He is with them. Cultivating the fear of God thus becomes the way to be freed from other fears.

sens: To be afraid, to be frightened by a danger
To stand in awe before something great or powerful
To respect, honor someone by submitting to their authority
To revere God in obedience and worship
To be formidable, to inspire fear
H3372H.detail:
1. To be afraid means to feel fear in the face of a threat or peril: Genesis 28:17 shows Jacob who "was afraid" upon seeing the majesty of the place.
2. To stand in awe before greatness means to be seized by the power or splendor of something: the psalmist says, "All the inhabitants of the earth fear you" (Psalms 66:3), speaking of God's power that inspires respectful dread.
3. To respect someone means to recognize them for their status or authority and to obey them: Leviticus 19:3 commands to "fear" father and mother, which means to honor and respect them.
4. To revere God means to fear Him with a sincere fear that arises from love and trust in His goodness: Deuteronomy 6:2 calls to "fear the Lord" by keeping His commandments, which is the beginning of wisdom (Ecclesiastes 12:13).
5. To be formidable means to inspire fear through one's power or majesty: Psalms 68:36 proclaims that God is "formidable" in His sanctuary.
H3372H.origine: The Hebrew verb יָרֵא comes from a root that primarily expresses physical and sensible fear. In the Old Testament, it often designates the emotion in the face of the supernatural or the divine: the sacred fear inspired by the presence of God. The same root appears in names like יִרְאָה (fear) and combines with God in expressions like "the fear of the Lord." This word embodies the idea that a true relationship with God begins with a deep respect that combines fear and trust.
H3372H.emploi: This verb appears more than a hundred times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the Pentateuch, the Psalms, and the wisdom books. It primarily denotes ordinary fear in the face of danger (Exodus 1:17, the midwives who do not fear Pharaoh), but quickly takes on a religious and moral dimension. Fearing God becomes the fundamental principle of the law (Deuteronomy 6:2, 6:13), of wisdom (Job 1:9, Job 37:24), and of praise (Psalms 33:8, Psalms 111:9). The meaning refines: it can denote terror (Exodus 9:30), respect for parents (Leviticus 19:3), respect for others (Leviticus 19:14, Leviticus 25:17), or admiration for God's wonders (Psalms 65:9, Psalms 139:14).
H3372H.portee: Understanding this word is crucial for the Christian faith. The fear of God is not servile terror but the reverent love of a child for their father: it is the right posture before infinite holiness and goodness. It inspires obedience, wisdom, and trust. It begins by recognizing that He is great, powerful, and good, and that our lives belong to Him. This fear frees us from all other fears and elevates us toward praise.

sens: To be afraid of someone or something, to dread a danger
To respect someone, to show reverence mixed with fear
To revere God, to honor Him with a heart that respects and obeys Him
To manifest restraint, moral prudence in the face of evil
H3373.detail:
1. To feel physical or psychological fear: to experience fright in the face of danger. Abraham "fears" God to the point of not refusing his only son (Genesis 22:12), like someone who truly dreads disobeying the one who can do anything. Those who are afraid of battle are invited to leave (Judges 7:3).
2. To respect someone with a reverential fear: this is the attitude toward an authority, a king, or a master. Obadiah "greatly feared the Lord" (1 Kings 18:3), which means he respected Him deeply and refrained from disobeying Him.
3. To fear God in particular: this is the heart of biblical faith. Those who "fear the Lord" form a blessed community (Psalms 115:11, 118:4), heirs of divine mercy and His promises (Psalms 103:17). It is a spiritual attitude that combines filial respect, obedience, and trust.
4. To exercise moral restraint, prudence: "The wise has restraint and turns away from evil" (Proverbs 14:16). Fear becomes a safeguard against arrogance and insecurity of the heart.
H3373.origine: The verb יָרֵא comes from a root that designates the emotion of fear or terror. In ancient Hebrew, it primarily expresses the physical reaction to a real danger (trembling, retreating), then gradually rises to the moral and spiritual sense of respect and reverence. In the Greek Old Testament, this verb often translates the idea of "standing before" someone in a respectful and fearful manner. The family includes words like יִרְאָה (the fear itself, the emotion).
H3373.emploi: This verb is one of the most important in biblical theology: it appears 63 times in the provided usages, mainly in the Psalms (over 30 occurrences) and in Proverbs, but also in historical narratives (Genesis, Kings, Samuel). Two dominant usages emerge: first, physical or psychological fear in the face of a threat (fear of death, fear of the enemy, Genesis 32:11, Exodus 9:20). Then and especially, "fearing the Lord" becomes the classic expression of biblical piety (Job 1:1, Psalms 15:4, Proverbs 14:2): it is a respect that encompasses obedience, trust, and love. The fear of God produces life, wisdom, and blessing. An important nuance: unlike ordinary fear, the fear of God calms and strengthens those who enjoy it (Psalms 34:8).
H3373.portee: Understanding this word transforms the Christian vision of faith. "Fearing God" is not synonymous with servile terror, but with a conscious filial respect that recognizes God's greatness and justice. It is the posture of the heart that says "yes" to His will, like Abraham with his son. For today's believer, it is a call to step out of arrogance and indifference, and to live in a holy moral restraint. This fear brings peace, for it places life under the protection of the one who is sovereign and merciful.

sens: Intense fear, terror in the face of a real or perceived danger
Respect mixed with fear towards an authority, a power
Religious feeling of reverence and submission towards God
Respectful obedience and fear of divine judgment
H3374.detail:
1. Fear is primarily a concrete fear, a terror in the face of danger: Abraham fears being killed because of his wife (Genesis 20:11), and the sailors of Jonah tremble upon seeing the storm unleashed by God (Jonah 1:10). It is the physical emotion of being frightened.

2. This fear also extends to a fearful respect in the presence of what is powerful or impressive: fear inspires obedience, as when one dreads the judgment of a king or authority. Job asks if there is anything to fear in virtue, showing that fear can also arise from the awareness of good (Job 4:6).

3. In the relationship with God, fear becomes the heart of religious wisdom: "The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom" (Proverbs 1:7, Proverbs 9:10). It is not panic terror, but respectful reverence and conscious submission to God, mixed with trust. It is an attitude of the heart.

4. This fear of God produces practical fruits: it protects ("The fear of the Lord prolongs days," Proverbs 10:27), it purifies the heart, it supports hope (Job 4:6), and it engenders justice and piety (Isaiah 11:2).
H3374.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of fearing or dreading. It primarily denotes the visceral emotional reaction to threat or the mysterious. When used for God, it takes on this imagery — one cannot dominate God, one can only fear Him and bow down — but transforms it into a moral and religious posture: that of the heart recognizing its Creator and dependence. The word appears mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Job, Psalms), where it is the first step towards true knowledge.
H3374.emploi: This word is used 45 times in the Old Testament, very often in relation to God. It first appears to express a real physical fear (fear of death, of the enemy), particularly in Genesis and Exodus. But quickly, especially from the Psalms and Proverbs, it becomes the key term to designate religious respect towards God and the obedience that flows from it. It is also encountered for the reverential fear before divine judgment or the manifestation of His power (Ezekiel 1:18, Jonah 1:16). The nuance is constant: it is a fear that does not crush, but leads to wisdom, justice, and life.
H3374.portee: The fear of God is never presented in the Bible as an overwhelming servitude, but as the joyful foundation of wisdom and a good life. It teaches the Christian that respecting God — fearing Him, recognizing His absolute authority — is not the opposite of faith and love, but their condition. It is accepting our smallness before the infinite, and finding in this humility our true freedom and security.

sens: City in the territory of Naphtali
Biblical locality assigned to the tribe of Naphtali
H3375.detail: Jireon is a city that was assigned to the tribe of Naphtali during the division of the Promised Land. It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of cities in the territory of Naphtali in Joshua 19:38, among other localities such as Migdal-El, Horem, Beth-Anath, and Beth-Shemesh.
H3375.origine: The name Jireon comes from the Hebrew yir'on, which means "he who fears" or "fear." This name likely reflects a religious or moral significance, like many place names in Israel, although the exact meaning of the connection between the name and the city remains uncertain. It is a specific geographical location in the northern part of the Israelite territory.
H3375.emploi: Jireon is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in Joshua 19:38, in the context of the division of the territory among the twelve tribes of Israel. It appears in the enumeration of cities assigned to the tribe of Naphtali, indicating its importance as a geographical reference point during the distribution of the Promised Land to the tribes of Jacob after the conquest.

sens: Officer of the royal guard during the divided kingdom
The one who arrested the prophet Jeremiah
H3376.detail: Jireija is a military leader, commander of the guard, who appears during the arrest of the prophet Jeremiah in Jerusalem. In Jeremiah 37:13, he is at the Benjamin Gate and arrests Jeremiah, falsely accusing him of wanting to defect to the Chaldeans. Although Jeremiah protests his innocence (Jeremiah 37:14), Jireija refuses to listen to him and forcibly brings him before the leaders of Jerusalem to be judged. He represents the opposition of civil and military authorities to the prophet's message.
H3376.origine: His Hebrew name means "Jehovah sees me" or "God sees me," composed of the verb "to see" and the name of God. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, affirming that God watches over the one who bears it. He is the son of Shelemiah, who is himself the son of Hananiah.
H3376.emploi: Jireija appears only twice in the Bible, both in Jeremiah 37, during the siege of Jerusalem by the Babylonians. At this time, Jeremiah is moving about the city and advising surrender to Jehovah, which the authorities interpret as treason. Jireija, as an officer of the guard, feels compelled to arrest the prophet. These two verses show a man fulfilling his duties without discerning that the one he is imprisoning is a messenger of God. His role underscores the resistance of earthly powers to the prophetic word.
H3376.portee: The figure of Jireija reminds us that opposition to God and His messengers can come from ordinary people who carry out their responsibilities without considering the spiritual consequences. For the Christian reader, it invites us to examine whether we are merely serving our structures or truly listening to the voice of God, even when it disturbs our certainties.

sens: Nickname of the Assyrian king Tiglath-Pileser III
A title meaning "he who contends" or "the great contention"
H3377.detail:
1. Jareb is a nickname or title given to the Assyrian king of the time. The term specifically refers to Tiglath-Pileser III, the powerful Assyrian monarch of the 8th century BC. It is under this nickname that biblical texts mention him when they speak of the king to whom Ephraim (the northern kingdom) turns for help.
2. The name literally means "he who contends" or "he who disputes" — an image of strength, combat power, and authority. This title suits a feared warrior king well. It expresses the idea of a formidable adversary, a great contention between powers. In Hosea 5:13, Ephraim, wounded and sick, goes to this king hoping to be healed, but the prophet announces that King Jareb can do nothing for him.
H3377.origine: The Hebrew name יָרֵב (Jareb) comes from a root meaning "to contend, dispute, lawsuit." It is a title given to the king of Assyria to express his authority and power of domination. In reality, this nickname or epithet was applied to Tiglath-Pileser III (also called Tiglath-Pileser in other biblical texts), the great Assyrian conqueror. Historians and biblical scholars consider that "Jareb" is a veiled or symbolic way of referring to this feared king.
H3377.emploi: Jareb appears twice in the book of the prophet Hosea, in chapters 5 and 10, always at the moment when the northern kingdom of Israel turns away from God to seek help from the king of Assyria. In Hosea 5:13, Ephraim, aware of his sickness and wounds, goes to Assyria and addresses King Jareb, hoping to be healed; but the prophet warns that this king can neither heal nor save him. In Hosea 10:6, the prophet announces that the idols of Israel will be carried to Assyria as tribute offered to King Jareb. In these two passages, Jareb embodies the foreign power on which Israel vainly places its hope instead of turning to God.
H3377.portee: These verses show the vain recourse of unfaithful kingdoms to human alliances and earthly power instead of returning to God. For the Christian reader, Jareb symbolizes all worldly power in which one places trust instead of trusting in the Lord. The lesson of Hosea remains current: seeking salvation elsewhere than in God can only lead to disappointment.

sens: Another name for Gideon, the military leader who freed Israel from Midianite oppression
Nickname given to Gideon after he destroyed the altar of the god Baal
Literally means 'let Baal plead' or 'let Baal contend'
H3378.detail: 1. Jerubbaal is the second name of Gideon, a warrior who became a judge of Israel before the establishment of the monarchy. This name was given to him by his father Joash after an act of defiance against idolatry. 2. The nickname commemorates the moment when Gideon overturned the altar of the god Baal and destroyed the idol that was there (Judges 6:32). His father gave him this provocative name to symbolically challenge the false god: 'let Baal plead against him, since he has overturned his altar' (Judges 6:32). It was a way of saying that if Baal was truly a god, he would take his own vengeance. 3. The name literally means 'let Baal contend' or 'let Baal plead', an expression of challenge directed at the god of the Canaanites. This name reveals Gideon's spiritual courage, as he did not hesitate to openly confront the idolatry of his people. He continued to be referred to by this name throughout his life and in his military exploits against Midian.
H3378.origine: The Hebrew name יְרֻבַּעַל (Yerubbaal) consists of two elements: יְרוּ (yeru, 'let') and בַּעַל (Baal, the name of the Canaanite god of fertility and storm). The structure of the name expresses a wish or a challenge: 'let Baal plead' or 'let Baal contend'. It is a theophoric name (containing a divine name) characteristic of the period of the judges. Gideon's father chose this name to express his challenge against the idolatry that dominated Israel at that time. Gideon himself also bears the Hebrew name Gideon (גִּדְעוֹן), which means 'hewer' or 'destroyer'.
H3378.emploi: Jerubbaal appears 13 times in the Bible, always referring to Gideon. The name is used primarily in the book of Judges (chapters 6 to 9) and once in 1 Samuel 12:11. The name is first attributed to Gideon in Judges 6:32, immediately after he overturned the altar of Baal. It is then used to identify Gideon in the context of his military exploits against the Midianites (Judges 7 and 8), and to name him in the family and political relations of his time. The name appears particularly in the account of his son Abimelech who massacred the children of Jerubbaal (Judges 9), showing how the nickname remained attached to Gideon even when speaking of his descendants. Most uses serve to identify Gideon in historical or genealogical contexts.
H3378.portee: This name reminds us that God uses those who dare to break with idolatry, even at the risk of challenging the established religious powers of their time. Jerubbaal symbolizes spiritual courage: Gideon not only fought the external enemies of Israel, but also confronted the religious waywardness of his own people by overturning the altar of Baal. His nickname speaks to the trust in God alone, as he thus challenged a false god, convinced that God was the true protector of Israel. It is an invitation for Christians to stand firmly in the truth, without fear of the idols of their time.

sens: The first king of the northern kingdom of Israel after the division
The eighth king of the northern kingdom of Israel, son of Joash
H3379G.detail: 1. Jeroboam was the first king of northern Israel when the united kingdom of Solomon divided at his death. The ten northern tribes broke away from Judah and Benjamin to follow him, rather than Rehoboam, the son of Solomon. From the beginning of his reign, he introduced idolatry by creating shrines on the high places and establishing non-Levitical priests (1 Kings 12:25-33; 13:33). His reign became a biblical reference point for the sin of Israel: subsequent kings are judged based on whether they deviated from 'the sins of Jeroboam'. 2. A second Jeroboam, son of Joash, was the eighth king of northern Israel, four generations after the first. Under his reign, he repelled Syrian invaders and restored the ancient borders of Israel; however, he maintained the idolatry introduced by his ancestor (2 Kings 14:23-29). Like the first, he is remembered in history as a king who prospered militarily but left the nation in religious sin.
H3379G.origine: The name Jeroboam means 'the people will contend' or 'the people will rise'. It comes from two Hebrew elements: 'people' and a verb meaning 'to raise, to contend'. It is a significant royal name given to two important rulers of the northern kingdom of Israel.
H3379G.emploi: Jeroboam appears 84 times in the Bible, primarily in 1 Kings and 2 Kings, as well as in 2 Chronicles. The first Jeroboam (1 Kings 11:26-14:20) is introduced as a servant of Solomon who received a prophecy from Ahijah before fleeing to Egypt, then returning to receive the ten tribes at Solomon's death. His reign is marked by the establishment of idol worship with the golden calves, an act condemned from its first mention (1 Kings 13:33). The second Jeroboam (2 Kings 14:23-29) is evaluated by the same criterion: he did not turn away from the sins of the first. Throughout Scripture, the name 'Jeroboam' becomes synonymous with institutionalized sin and deviant worship that contaminates the kingdom.

sens: King of northern Israel, son of Joash
Eighth monarch of the northern kingdom after the division
Ruler under whom the borders of Israel were restored
H3379H.detail: Jeroboam is the son of King Joash and the eighth king of the northern kingdom of Israel. He reigned for forty-one years in Samaria, starting from the fifteenth year of King Amaziah of Judah (2 Kings 14:23). During his reign, he repelled Syrian invasions and restored the borders of Israel to Damascus and Hamath, which had once belonged to the kingdom of Judah (2 Kings 14:28). However, despite these military and political successes, Jeroboam maintained the idolatry that characterized the northern kingdom. The prophet Amos criticized him for this religious practice (Amos 7:9-11), and his words were spoken during Jeroboam's time (Amos 1:1).
H3379H.origine: The name means 'the people would plead' or 'the people would contend', formed from the Hebrew 'am' (people) and 'rib' (to contend, dispute). It is a theophoric name that expresses the relationship of the people with God. There was a first Jeroboam, the founder of the northern kingdom at the time of the division of the empire (1 Kings 11-12), and this Jeroboam II mentioned here, the most powerful king of the North after the dynasty of Jehu.
H3379H.emploi: Jeroboam II (son of Joash) reigns over the northern kingdom of Israel in the 8th century BCE. Mentioned 14 times in the Segond, he appears primarily in 2 Kings 14-15 (his victories and reign) and in the prophets Amos, Hosea, and 1 Chronicles. The texts present him as a militarily victorious king, who repelled the Syrians and restored the borders of the kingdom; however, they emphasize that this political power coexisted with the maintenance of idolatry. The prophets Amos and Hosea, who preached during his time, denounced this contradiction: material prosperity and military success, but religious unfaithfulness.
H3379H.portee: The reign of Jeroboam II shows how power and material prosperity can mask spiritual unfaithfulness. Although the kingdom regained its military and economic strength, Jeroboam did not return to the true worship of God. It is a warning for believers: temporal success does not mean divine favor if it is accompanied by a departure from the truth.

sens: another name for the warrior and judge Gideon
H3380.detail: Jerubbeshath is an alternative name given to Gideon. This name literally means "the shame will contend" or "the shame will fight": it was formed by replacing the word "Baal" (a pagan god) with the Hebrew word meaning "shame," to avoid pronouncing the name of the false god. Gideon received this nickname after his victories against the Midianites and other enemies of Israel. The only mention of this name in the Bible occurs when David, speaking to his messenger Uriah, inquires about the fate of Abimelech, son of Jerubbeshath, who died at Thebez (2 Samuel 11:21).
H3380.origine: Jerubbeshath is a voluntary nickname given to Gideon. His real name was Gideon (in Hebrew Gid'on). But after his military exploits, he was also called Jerubbaal (יְרֻבַּעַל), which means "let Baal contend." The name Jerubbeshath is a respectful variant of Jerubbaal: the scribes replaced "Baal" with "shet" (shame) to honor the God of Israel and avoid any confusion with the worship of the pagan god Baal. This shows how biblical writers sometimes modified names to express their monotheistic faith.
H3380.emploi: Jerubbeshath appears only once in the entire Bible, in 2 Samuel 11:21. In this verse, King David speaks of Abimelech, the son of Jerubbeshath (that is, the son of Gideon), who was killed at Thebez when a woman threw a millstone on his head from the top of the walls. David uses this name as an example of an ignoble death in wartime. While the name Jerubbaal recurs regularly in the Book of Judges to refer to the same man during his battles against the Midianites, Jerubbeshath is used only here, presumably to respect the divine name in place of a name containing that of an idol.

sens: To go or come down, from a high place to a lower place
To enter a country or region, especially Egypt
To sink in water, to drown
To lose one's position, to be lowered or fallen
To intervene, to manifest visibly or actively
To reside, to settle in a place
H3381.detail:
1. To go or come down means to physically move from a high place to a lower place: Samson goes down to Timnah (Judges 14:1), a young woman goes down to the spring to fill her jar (Genesis 24:16), and the Lord descends to see the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:5).
2. Entering Egypt or a strange land is an important nuance of the word: Jacob and his sons go down to Egypt to stay there (Genesis 46:3, Isaiah 52:4), marking a major change in situation.
3. To sink in water or to drown describes what happens to Pharaoh's horses and riders: they go down to the depths of the sea (Exodus 15:5).
4. To lose one's position or authority: when Moses comes down from the mountain with the tablets of the Law, the people have already lowered themselves by worshiping a golden calf (Exodus 32:1, 32:15).
5. To intervene or manifest with power: the Lord descends to speak to Moses and promises to descend on Sinai (Numbers 11:17, Exodus 19:11, 19:20).
6. To reside or settle somewhere: Judah goes down from his father’s house to the Timnite (Genesis 38:1).
H3381.origine: The Hebrew root yd fundamentally means "to go down." It is a very common verb in the Old Testament, used in both a literal sense (downward physical movement) and a figurative sense (decline, humiliation, divine intervention). The word contrasts with "to ascend" (alah). It appears in the Qal (simple form, meaning "to descend"), the Hiphil (causative form, meaning "to cause to descend, to lower"), and the Hophal (passive form, meaning "to be lowered"). The word family includes terms denoting the bottom, the depth, and lowering.
H3381.emploi: This verb is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (346 occurrences). It appears mainly in Genesis and Exodus to describe the movements of the patriarchs: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob go down to Egypt, Samson goes down to Timnah. In the story of the Exodus, it also depicts God's action: the Lord descends from heaven to see, speak, give the Law, manifest. The meaning varies according to the context: to go down to a well (practical action), to go down to Egypt (changing region and condition), to come down from the mountain (returning from a divine encounter), or to be lowered (passive or figurative meaning). In the prophets, it often characterizes the decline or lowering of a nation.
H3381.portee: For the biblical reader, this verb reveals the humility of a God who descends from heaven to meet men, not from afar but by coming close to them. It also shows how the patriarchs move under God's guidance, each descent marking a decisive step in His plan. Understanding when and why one "descends" helps grasp the spiritual stakes of a passage: a descent is rarely neutral in the Bible; it signifies a change of state, an encounter, or a consequence.

sens: Antediluvian man, son of Mahalalel and father of Enoch
Descendant of Judah and father of Gedor
H3382G.detail:
1. Jared is a man who lived before the Flood, listed in the genealogy descending from Seth. He is the son of Mahalalel and the father of the prophet Enoch, famous for having "walked with God" and being taken up to heaven without experiencing death. According to Genesis 5:18-20, Jared lived 962 years in total, making him one of the oldest men in history according to the biblical text.
2. A second character bears the same name: he is a descendant of the tribe of Judah, mentioned in 1 Chronicles 1:2 as the father of Gedor.
H3382G.origine: The name Jared means "descent." In Hebrew, it comes from a root that evokes the idea of descending or falling. This meaning aligns with Jared's position in human history: he lived just before Enoch, who will ascend to heaven, and his time precedes the Flood, that great judgment which will mark a "descent" of humanity. The name also appears in Greek in the New Testament as Iared (Ἰάρεδ).
H3382G.emploi: Jared is mentioned six times in the Bible. First, in Genesis 5:15-20, he is an essential link in the genealogical chain before the Flood: son of Mahalalel, father of Enoch. These verses detail his longevity and confirm that he had other children. Then, 1 Chronicles 1:2 reiterates this same genealogy as a reminder in the genealogical records of Israel. Jared embodies the continuity of the divine plan through the antediluvian generations.

sens: man of the tribe of Judah living during the divided monarchy
H3382H.detail: Jared is a minor character in the Old Testament, mentioned only once in the genealogies of the tribe of Judah. He is the son of Mered and Jehoiada (a Jewish woman), and the father of Gedor. His name means "descent" in Hebrew.
H3382H.origine: The name Jared comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to descend." It is the same name as that of Jared, ancestor of Enoch in the antediluvian genealogy (Genesis 5), although these are two distinct characters in biblical history. The root evokes the idea of descent or lineage.
H3382H.emploi: Jared appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:18, in a genealogical list of the tribe of Judah. He is presented as the son of Mered and Jehoiada (daughter of Pharaoh according to a tradition), and the father of Gedor. This passage is part of the complex genealogies of Judah, where the descendants and family alliances of this tribe are enumerated. His role is limited to his place in this genealogical chain.

sens: the great river of Palestine that flows from Lebanon to the Dead Sea
H3383.detail: 1. The Jordan is the main watercourse of Palestine. Its name in Hebrew means "the one who descends" because it flows from the springs of Lebanon (Anti-Lebanon) to the Dead Sea, over approximately 320 kilometers, following a deep geographical fault line. The Jordan plain was known to be extremely fertile: Lot saw "the whole plain of the Jordan, which was well watered... like the garden of the Lord, like the land of Egypt" (Genesis 13:10). 2. The Jordan serves as a natural border between the lands to the east (Transjordan) and Canaan to the west. Moses remained "on this side of the Jordan, toward the sunrise" and did not cross the river (Deuteronomy 1:5; 4:46). Crossing the Jordan meant leaving the desert and entering the promised land: this is why Joshua was commanded to cross the Jordan to conquer Canaan (Joshua 1:2, 1:11). 3. The crossing of the Jordan under Joshua's leadership remains one of God's great acts: the waters stopped and the people crossed on dry ground (Joshua 3:14-17). This event marked the fulfillment of the promise made to the patriarchs and the people's definitive entry into possession of the land (Joshua 24:11).
H3383.origine: The name "Jordan" comes from the Hebrew "Yardèn," which literally means "the one who descends" or "the descender," from the root "yarad" (to descend). This etymology perfectly evokes the nature of the river: its sources are located at a very high altitude (at the roots of Lebanon) and the water constantly descends toward the lowest point, the Dead Sea. The Greek word "Iordanēs" captures this same reality, and in the Greek biblical texts, it designates exactly the same river.
H3383.emploi: The Jordan appears 181 times in the Segond 1910, almost exclusively in the Old Testament (Genesis, Numbers, Deuteronomy, and Joshua). In Genesis and Exodus, it marks the eastern boundary of the promised land that Abraham and his descendants are to inhabit. In Deuteronomy, Moses constantly reminds the people that they must cross the Jordan to enter into possession of the land, but he himself will not enter (Deuteronomy 1:5, 3:20-27, 4:22). The book of Joshua is dominated by the crossing of the Jordan: the account of the miracle of the stopping waters occupies three entire chapters (Joshua 3-4) and remains the founding event of the occupation of Canaan (Joshua 24:11). After the conquest, the Jordan continues to designate the borders of Canaan and the cities of refuge established on either side of the river (Numbers 35:10-14).
H3383.portee: The Jordan is never just a geographical marker: it represents the boundary between slavery and freedom, between the desert and the promised rest. For Israel, crossing it was an act of faith, as the waters only parted when the priests stepped into them (Joshua 3:15-17). This river teaches Christians that possessing God's promise requires entering into a territory of obedience, even in the face of seemingly insurmountable obstacles. The crossing of the Jordan signifies the people's definitive commitment to their God and entry into the prepared inheritance.

sens: To launch an arrow using a bow
To throw or project something with force
To send water or rain
To strike or wound by shooting
H3384A.detail:
1. To shoot with a bow: to launch an arrow using the tension of a string. This is the most concrete and common meaning. David says to Jonathan: "I will shoot three arrows to the side of the stone" (1 Samuel 20:20) to communicate secretly.
2. To throw or project: to send something with force from one place to another, like Pharaoh who "threw" his chariots into the Red Sea (Exodus 15:4). The word applies to any projectile, not just arrows.
3. To water or pour water: the verb also describes the action of making water flow onto the ground. In Proverbs 11:25, "he who waters will himself be watered" uses this verb to speak of generosity that returns as a blessing.
4. To wound or hit: when the shot reaches its target and causes harm, like the archers who struck King Saul (1 Chronicles 10:3). The verb then encompasses the effect of the shot: the wound.
H3384A.origine: The Hebrew verb yara comes from a root that evokes the idea of projecting, sending far away. It has given rise in Hebrew to several words of the same family: yorer (the one who shoots, the archer) and yarah (to show, to teach – perhaps because to show is to "point" at something). The primitive meaning is that of the gesture of projection: to launch something forcefully from one place to another.
H3384A.emploi: This verb appears 25 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is very common in war and hunting narratives: it is found in the stories of David (1 Samuel 20-31), in the battles of the kings of Judah, and in siege descriptions (2 Samuel 11, 2 Kings 13 and 19). The military context dominates: shooting arrows, projectiles from the top of a wall, or projectiles in battle. But the verb extends to other projections: throwing water (Proverbs 11:25), rain (Hosea 6:3). In Job 38:6, God "lays" the cornerstone of the earth, as one places a foundation solidly. The word maintains a fairly concrete and physical meaning throughout.
H3384A.portee: This verb reminds the reader that human actions – whether of violence, generosity, or labor – have visible and lasting effects. Notably in Proverbs 11:25, the image of shooting becomes that of circular blessing: "he who waters will be watered." This teaches that generosity returns to the one who practices it, like an arrow returning to its shooter. It is an invitation to trust in God and in the balance He establishes.

sens: To show, indicate by pointing or gesture
To transmit knowledge, understanding, or practice
To instruct someone in the right way, justice, or wisdom
To direct, guide someone towards an action or understanding
H3384B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to show concretely: to point something out to draw attention. In Genesis 31:51, Laban "raises" a monument between himself and Jacob, meaning he shows it as a visible testimony. It is the action of making something clearly seen.

2. The word then designates the act of transmitting knowledge or technique. In Exodus 35:34, God "taught" workers how to shape wood and metals for the tabernacle. It is to instruct someone in a concrete art or practice.

3. It takes on a moral sense when it comes to making known the law, justice, or divine wisdom. Leviticus 10:11 asks the priests to "teach" the children of Israel the laws that the Lord has given. It is to guide towards what is right and honest.

4. The word broadens to encompass any act of spiritual direction or guidance. When Psalm 27:11 says, "Lord! teach me your way," it means: lead me, show me how to live according to your will. Teaching becomes a matter of inner orientation towards God.
H3384B.origine: The Hebrew root יָרָה evokes the idea of extending, showing, hence the gesture of pointing with a finger or arm. It is related to the image of "drawing" (this root is found in the word for "arrow"). The verb initially meant "to point out," and then expanded to designate any act of knowledge transmission. The family of this word includes terms for "instruction" and "doctrine." It is a very ancient verb that expresses the fundamental idea of making visible or known.
H3384B.emploi: This verb appears 47 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the pedagogical and legislative books (Deuteronomy, Psalms, Proverbs, Leviticus). It is one of the preferred verbs to describe divine teaching: God "teaches" through Moses (Exodus 4:12 and 4:15), the priests "teach" the law (Leviticus 10:11), and the believer implores, "Lord, teach me" (Psalms 27:11, 119:33). The context oscillates between practical instruction (trades, rituals) and moral or spiritual guidance. In Proverbs (4:11), it is wisdom that "shows" the way. In the Prophets (Isaiah 2:3, Micah 4:2), it is the Word of the Lord that "teaches." The word always emphasizes the idea that knowledge, direction, or a standard is made clear and transmissible.
H3384B.portee: For the Christian reader, this verb expresses a dynamic relationship: God does not merely give a written law; He "teaches," meaning He guides, directs, opens eyes. That is why Psalm 119:102 says, "I have not forsaken your teachings": learning from God is not about accumulating information; it is about being led towards justice and life. This word reminds us that faith is a continuous learning process, trusting in the one who "shows the way."

sens: Place in the southern desert of Judah
H3385.detail: Jeruel is a location in the southern desert of the territory of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. The prophet Elijah indicates it to King Jehoshaphat as the point where his soldiers will meet the enemy army (2 Chronicles 20:16). It is a geographical landmark located at the end of a valley, accessible by the hill of Ziz.
H3385.origine: The Hebrew name Jeruel literally means "taught by God" or "founded by God" (from "Jah" = God and "ruel" = taught). This uncommon name could also be an ancient form of topography. It is a place in the desert of Judah that the Bible locates with natural landmarks.
H3385.emploi: Jeruel appears only once in the Bible, at the moment when the prophet Elijah tells Jehoshaphat where to find the enemies coming against Judah. It is a concrete and precise geographical detail in the story of this king. The context shows that it is a real and strategically important place, situated between the valley and the desert.

sens: Man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H3386.detail: Jaroach is a chief of the tribe of Gad mentioned only once in the genealogy of the clan of Gad (1 Chronicles 5:14). He is the son of Gilead and the father of Huri, occupying his place in the lineage that establishes his authority and importance among the elders of Gad.
H3386.origine: His name means "new moon" in Hebrew, an image that evokes youth or renewal. It is a name particular to the context of the tribe of Gad during the period when Israel was divided into two kingdoms.
H3386.emploi: Jaroach appears only once in the Bible, in the genealogical role of 1 Chronicles 5:14. He is listed among the mighty men and chiefs of the tribe of Gad, indicating that he was a man of importance and influence in his time. This brief mention situates him during the divided monarchy, when the tribes of Israel were fragmented.

sens: Of the color green
Fresh and green plant or grass
That which is new, young, full of vigor
H3387.detail:
1. The word designates the color green itself, that of healthy and living vegetation. In Job 39:11, the author describes the horse seeking its food: it roams the mountains "in search of everything that is green," meaning the grasses and green plants that feed the animals.
2. More broadly, the word evokes everything that is green in a botanical sense — the grasses, young shoots, fresh greenery. It is the tender and nutritious grass that herbivores eat, a sign of fertility and life.
3. By extension, it can evoke that which is new and full of strength, as a green plant is full of sap. Green symbolizes life, youth, and vigor.
H3387.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of greenness and freshness. It is related to the image of the living plant, full of sap and color. Ancient Hebrew saw in the color green a sign of life in full bloom.
H3387.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 39:11. In this poetic context, it describes what the horse seeks to eat in nature — the greenery of the mountains. It is a concrete word used to talk about the food of beasts. Its meaning remains simple and descriptive: it refers to the color and biological reality of what is green and living.
H3387.portee: This word reminds us that God provides for all the needs of animals, including the powerful horse. The greenery that the horse seeks is a sign of the Creator's generosity, who makes plants grow to feed His creatures. It is also an invitation to see in the green color of nature a testimony of life and divine protection.

sens: woman of Judah during the divided monarchy
wife of King Uzziah
mother of King Jotham
H3388.detail: Jeruscha is a woman of Judah mentioned as the wife of King Uzziah and mother of King Jotham. She is the daughter of Zadok. Her name appears twice in the Bible, always at the time of her son Jotham's accession to the throne: she is identified as the mother of the king (2 Kings 15:33 and 2 Chronicles 27:1), which was important for establishing royal legitimacy in Jerusalem.
H3388.origine: The name Jeruscha literally means "she who dispossesses" or "she who would inherit." It is formed from the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of taking possession or inheriting. This name was borne by a woman of the royal house of Judah during the period when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah coexisted separately.
H3388.emploi: Jeruscha appears twice in Scripture, in the same two parallel passages: 2 Kings 15:33 and 2 Chronicles 27:1. These two accounts report her role as the mother of Jotham at the time of his accession to the throne. She was the daughter of Zadok, which shows an important alliance between the royal family and a priestly or high-ranking family. The Bible mentions her briefly but sufficiently to establish the legitimate royal succession in Judah.

sens: the historical capital of Israel, fortified city of Judah
the political and religious center of the kingdom of Judah after the division
the place of God's dwelling among His people
H3389.detail:
1. Jerusalem is the royal city where the kings of Israel and then Judah reign.
