David makes it his capital (2 Samuel 5:6-9), and it is here that the major events of the Kingdom take place: inaugurations, wars, alliances (Joshua 10:1 mentions Adoni-Zedek, king of Jerusalem; 1 Kings 2:11 confirms that David reigns there). The kings reside there, govern there, and are buried there — it is the political heart of Israel.
2. Jerusalem is also the religious center, as the House of the Lord stands there (1 Kings 8:1 reports the dedication of the Temple). It is the unique place where God establishes His presence among His people, where sacrifices and worship according to the Law take place, and where the faithful gather for the great feasts.
3. In the prophets, Jerusalem becomes the symbol of hope and restoration: Isaiah 65:18 announces that God will create "Jerusalem" for gladness and His people for joy, expressing the messianic promise of a future of peace and happiness beyond captivity.
H3389.origine: The Hebrew name literally means "city of peace" or "foundation of peace" (from yru "he sees" or "he founds" and shalom "peace"). It is a very ancient city, probably founded by the Jebusites before the conquest of Israel. David takes it from the Jebusites and makes it the political and religious capital of the united kingdom, transforming what was a small fortified outpost into the metropolis of God's people.
H3389.emploi: Jerusalem appears more than 600 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the historical books (Samuel, Kings, Chronicles), the Psalms, and the prophets. It is mentioned as early as Joshua 10:1 during the conquests of Canaan, and then becomes the permanent seat of Davidic royalty starting from 2 Samuel 5. It is the stage for dynastic intrigues (the revolt of Absalom in 2 Samuel 15-16), cultic reforms (Josiah in 2 Kings 22), sieges (Sennacherib, then Nebuchadnezzar), and reconstruction efforts (Nehemiah 3:8). In prophetic preaching, Jerusalem embodies both the sin and unfaithfulness of the people and the messianic hope and promise of future restoration.
H3389.portee: Jerusalem reminds the believer that God chooses a city, a people, a concrete place for His dwelling and action in history. It shows that the Gospel is rooted in a geographical and political reality, not in the abstract. For the New Testament reader, Jerusalem remains the center of the Passover event and the starting point of the Good News proclaimed to the world.

sens: The capital of Judah and the united kingdom of Israel
The city where the temple of God stands
The place of worship and government of the kings
The spiritual center of the people of Israel
H3390.detail:
1. Jerusalem is the great city, capital of the kingdom of Judah. After the Babylonian captivity, Ezra obtains from King Artaxerxes the authorization to bring back the exiles to rebuild the city and its temple (Ezra 7:13-14).
2. It is primarily the city of the temple, the house of God. The sacred utensils taken by Nebuchadnezzar must be brought back and "placed in the house of God in Jerusalem" (Ezra 6:5).
3. Jerusalem is the seat of political and religious power: the governor administers there, the temple altar receives offerings there (Ezra 7:17), and the people who want to serve God must go there.
4. In the eyes of the Hebrew believer, this city embodies the covenant between God and His people: it is where God dwells among His own through His presence in the temple.
H3390.origine: The name means "teaching of peace" or "foundation of peace" in Hebrew-Aramaic. The city has borne this name for centuries as the religious center of Israel. In the books of Ezra and Daniel, the word is used in Aramaic (the language spoken in Babylon and under the Persian empire), showing how the exiled Jews continued to speak of their holy city even under foreign domination.
H3390.emploi: Jerusalem appears 25 times in the provided passages, almost exclusively in the books of Ezra and Daniel, which recount the return from exile in the 6th century BC. It systematically designates the city that needs to be rebuilt: the Persian authorities issue orders there (Ezra 4:8), the exiles gather there to rebuild the temple (Ezra 5:15), and the sacred utensils must be returned there (Ezra 6:5). The context is almost always that of restoration: restoration of the wall, the temple, the worship. It is the city of return, a symbol of renewal after exile.
H3390.portee: For the people of Israel, Jerusalem is not just a simple political capital: it is the place where God has chosen to place His name, where He dwells among His people. The return to Jerusalem signifies the return to the broken relationship with God, the restoration of the covenant. What this name evokes for the believer is the hope of forgiveness and restoration after the fall.

sens: Period of approximately thirty days, corresponding to the lunar cycle
Division of the annual calendar, called by a specific name according to the Hebrew system
Indeterminate period of time to measure any duration
H3391.detail:
1. The month is originally a natural period defined by the moon: a complete lunar cycle lasts about 29 or 30 days. It is the oldest and most visible unit of time in the sky. The Hebrew calendar is based on these lunar cycles (Exodus 2:2).

2. In the official Israelite system, each month has a proper name (Bul, Abib, etc.) and occupies a fixed place in the liturgical and civil year. The first three months of the year are celebrated for the great feasts, and years are counted in "sabbatical" years of seven (1 Kings 6:38).

3. Figuratively, the word simply denotes a period of time: Job speaks of "months of pain" (Job 7:3) as one would say "weeks of trials," without specifying an exact duration, just a succession of difficult days.
H3391.origine: The Hebrew word יֶרַח (yerach) is related to the root יָרַח which means "to mark with the lunar crescent." Its Aramaic equivalent retains the same form and meaning. In the Greek Old Testament, it is generally translated as μήν (mèn). The notion is universal: a month is literally "the time of a moon."
H3391.emploi: The word "month" appears twelve times in the provided Old Testament, mostly to count durations and mark key moments in sacred history. It is found as early as the story of Moses (Exodus 2:2, where Moses' mother hides him for three months), and then very often in the accounts of the kings to date events: Solomon takes seven years (84 months) to build the Temple (1 Kings 6:38), Shallum reigns for only one month (2 Kings 15:13). The wisdom books use it to express lasting emotional states: Job laments having "months of pain" to share (Job 7:3). It is thus a practical and universal word, never speculative.
H3391.portee: This word reminds us that human life flows according to natural rhythms established by God. Months mark the seasons, feasts, mourning, births: they measure the time of our lives. Recognizing the month is to accept that time passes and that each period — whether happy or painful — has a limit. For the believer, this invites seeking wisdom in every season: neither to be discouraged when a month of pain comes, nor to forget God in the abundance of good months.

sens: Son of Joktan, ancestor of an Arab tribe
H3392.detail: Jerach is a figure from the patriarchal era, son of Joktan (Genesis 10:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:20). His name means "new moon" in Hebrew, reflecting the importance of astronomy and the lunar calendar in ancient Semitic culture. He is presented as the ancestor of an Arab tribe and appears in the genealogy of the descendants of Shem, alongside his brothers Almodad, Sheleph, Hazarmaveth, and others.
H3392.origine: The name Jerach comes from the Hebrew יֶרַח (yeraḥ), which literally means "moon" or "month" (since the month was defined by the lunar cycle). It is a simple and natural image: the new moon marked the beginning of a new month in the calendar of ancient Middle Eastern peoples. The same Hebrew word appears in the Bible to denote the month or the moon itself.
H3392.emploi: Jerach appears only twice in the Bible: in Genesis 10:26 and 1 Chronicles 1:20, where he is listed among the sons of Joktan. These two passages are the same genealogy reproduced in the historical books of the Old Testament. It is simply his insertion into the family tree that establishes the origins of the Arab peoples according to biblical tradition. His role is purely genealogical: ancestor of a lineage.

sens: Division of time, defined by the lunar cycle
Period of about thirty days, twelfth part of the year
H3393.detail:
1. The word designates a unit of time linked to lunar phases: this is why the Hebrew calendar counts twelve months corresponding to the revolutions of the moon. In Ezra 6:15, it specifies "the third day of the month of Adar" to pinpoint exactly when the house of the Lord was completed: the month is the reference unit for dating important events.
2. More broadly, a month is a period of about thirty days. In Daniel 4:29, "at the end of twelve months" means a full year: King Nebuchadnezzar had this vision, and after a complete year of prosperity, he began to walk in his palace, unaware that his trial was approaching.
H3393.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "moon": it is the moon that marks time and seasons in the Eastern Mediterranean and ancient Near East. The same word (יֶרַח) exists in classical Hebrew (H3391). The Aramaic form here follows the same etymology, as Aramaic and Hebrew are sister languages and share common roots.
H3393.emploi: The word appears only once in Aramaic in the Bible (Daniel 4:29) and once in this passage from Ezra. In the Aramaic Old Testament, it is an administrative and historical term: it is used to precisely date events of the Persian period, such as the completion of the Temple's reconstruction or key moments in Nebuchadnezzar's reign. These two occurrences show it in a historical and official context, without particular religious connotation.
H3393.portee: Understanding that the month is the biblical temporal unit reminds the reader of the importance of time in Providence: God reigns over the seasons, the years, and the details of history. That the Temple was completed in a specific month, that the king's dream occurred exactly after twelve months, shows that nothing escapes God's calendar.

sens: night celestial body that illuminates the night
satellite that measures months and seasons
object of idolatrous worship
light that governs the night
witness of God's wonders
H3394.detail:
1. The moon is the celestial body that shines at night in the sky and provides natural light to the earth during hours of darkness. In Joshua 10:13, God stops the moon in the middle of its course to prolong daylight and allow Israel to defeat its enemies.

2. The moon serves to mark times and seasons: it determines the months of the year and helps calculate religious festivals. Psalm 104:19 explains that God created the moon "to mark the times," thus establishing a celestial calendar visible to all.

3. In many cultures, the moon was worshiped as a god. The Bible condemns this idolatry: Deuteronomy 4:19 and Jeremiah 8:2 show that some Israelites bowed down to it and served it, which constitutes a serious rebellion against God.

4. The moon is associated with the night and the governance of the night, in contrast to the sun which governs the day. It participates in the marvelous order of creation, illuminating creation during dark hours.

5. The moon is a visible testimony to God's creative wisdom and power. Psalm 8:4 invites the believer to contemplate it among the works of the Lord and to be filled with awe before divine greatness.
H3394.origine: The Hebrew word יָרֵחַ (yaréach) designates the moon, this celestial body that appears every night. Its etymology suggests a link with cyclical renewal: the moon changes appearance each month, going from crescent to full moon and back to nothingness, symbolizing the perpetual movement of time. This same word is the origin of the term "month" (חֹדֶשׁ, 'hodesh) in Hebrew, since each lunar month corresponds to a complete cycle of the moon. The moon was well known in the ancient Near East as a major natural phenomenon and as an object of religious observation.
H3394.emploi: The word moon appears 27 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the Psalms, the prophets, and the historical books. In the narratives, the moon is often mentioned alongside the sun and stars as part of divine creation (Psalms 8:4, 148:3). It occupies an important place in the biblical time system: Psalms 104:19 emphasizes its role as a marker of times and seasons. A notable usage concerns eschatological passages, where the darkening of the moon heralds catastrophic events or the end of times (Isaiah 13:10, Joel 2:10, 2:31). Finally, the moon appears in condemnations of idolatry, as some peoples and even Israelites worshiped it as a deity (Deuteronomy 4:19, Jeremiah 8:2).
H3394.portee: The moon reminds the believer that God has established a marvelous order in creation, where each celestial body has a specific function in service to life on earth. It invites praise for the Creator rather than the creature, which protects the heart from idolatry. For the Christian, contemplating the moon is an opportunity to meditate on God's faithfulness: it returns every night according to an unchanging cycle, testifying to divine constancy toward His people.

sens: ancestor of the prophet Samuel in the lineage of Levi
H3395G.detail: Jeroham is a Levite who appears in the genealogy leading to the prophet Samuel. He is the son of Elihu and the father of Elkanah (father of Samuel) — he is seen in the genealogy of 1 Chronicles 6:27, where he is listed in the lineage of Levi, or in 1 Samuel 1:1 where Elkanah is presented as "son of Jeroham." His name means "he who shows mercy," suggesting a divine blessing. Thus, he represents an important link in the genealogical chain leading to one of Israel's greatest prophets.
H3395G.origine: The name Jeroham carries the Hebrew root meaning "to have mercy, to show compassion." It is a theophoric name, that is, one bearing spiritual significance, very common in the Bible where names recall divine qualities or the hopes of parents. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, all from important families: Levites, Benjamites, priests, and warriors.
H3395G.emploi: Jeroham is mentioned three times in the Bible, each time in a genealogical context. In 1 Samuel 1:1, he is presented as the father of Elkanah, who himself will be the father of the prophet Samuel — this is the anchor point of the narrative introducing Samuel. In 1 Chronicles 6:27 and 6:34, he appears in two listings of the Levitical genealogy, confirming his belonging to the tribe of Levi and his role as an ancestor in this prestigious lineage. These three occurrences are all genealogical: none report specific actions, but they establish the lineage.

sens: Benjamite from the time of the Divided Monarchy
father or descendant and ancestor of several Israelite families
H3395H.detail:
1. Jerocham is a man from the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the period of the Divided Monarchy in Israel. He is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8:27 as the father of several sons: Jaaréschia, Élija, and Zicri, which shows that he had an important lineage among the Benjamites.
2. The name Jerocham means "showing mercy" or "compassionate." He is a founding ancestor in the genealogy of the Benjamite families, serving to identify and classify the groups of this tribe throughout the history of Israel.
H3395H.origine: The name Jerocham comes from Hebrew and carries the meaning of "showing mercy" or "merciful." This name reflects an important value in Israelite culture, that of compassion and kindness. The root of the name suggests the divine idea of showing grace and mercy to others, a characteristic often associated with God Himself in the Old Testament.
H3395H.emploi: Jerocham appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:27, where he is presented as the father of three Benjamite sons: Jaaréschia, Élija, and Zicri. This verse is part of the detailed genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin at the time of the return from exile. Jerocham was part of the important families of Benjamin that survived and reestablished themselves in Judah after the Babylonian captivity. His unique mention in the Scriptures highlights his role as a founding ancestor of a recognized Benjamite lineage.
H3395H.portee: The name Jerocham, meaning "showing mercy," reminds believers of the importance of compassion in their lives. Although he is mentioned only once, his place in the genealogy of Benjamin shows how God preserved and restored His people after exile, through families like that of Jerocham.

sens: Man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogies of the return from exile
Father of Ibneija, one of the family leaders established in Jerusalem after the exile
H3395I.detail: 1. Jérocham is a Benjamite whose name appears in the list of ancestors of those who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is found in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 9:8, where he is presented as the father of Ibneija, who himself was recognized with an honorable place among the family leaders who returned. This context shows that Jérocham represents a respectable and established lineage at the return of the people. 2. The name Jérocham literally means "one who shows mercy" or "one who has compassion." In this context of the return from exile, his name carries symbolic significance: it expresses the divine idea of compassion towards His people who returned from captivity. His appearance in the genealogies emphasizes that God had not forgotten these families during the exile.
H3395I.origine: The name Jérocham comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to have pity, to show compassion." This type of theophoric name (containing a divine idea) was common in Israel: it reflects the belief that God acts with mercy towards His people. The name thus expresses a divine virtue rather than a simple description of the person, which was common to honor ancestors whose faith was to be highlighted.
H3395I.emploi: Jérocham is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:8, where he appears exclusively in a genealogy listing the family leaders of Benjamin who returned from the Babylonian exile. In this context, he is identified as the father of Ibneija. These genealogical lists served to establish the legitimacy and identity of the families resettling in Jerusalem and rebuilding the community life of God's people. The fact that he is mentioned, even briefly, indicates his importance as an ancestor of a family deemed worthy.

sens: Man from the tribe of Levi living during the Exile and Return
Father of Adaja, priest from the family of Immer
H3395J.detail: Jerocham is a character name that designates several men in the Old Testament, but the two uses provided refer to the same man: a Levite and priest from the family of Immer, a descendant of Paschhur. He is presented as the father of Adaja in two genealogies of the return from exile (1 Chronicles 9:12 and Nehemiah 11:12), suggesting that he was an important figure in the restored worship in Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile.
H3395J.origine: The name Jerocham literally means "[God] shows mercy" or "[God] had mercy" in Hebrew, formed from the root that expresses divine compassion. It is a theophoric name, meaning a name that contains the name or idea of God, common among Levites and priests. Several other biblical characters bear this name, indicating its popularity in priestly circles.
H3395J.emploi: Jerocham here designates a Levite priest from the lineage of Immer, living at the time of the return from the Babylonian exile (end of the 6th century B.C.). The two biblical references mention him only in genealogical lists that enumerate the priests and Levites who returned to Jerusalem and were engaged in the service of the restored Temple. He is primarily known as the father of Adaja, who was also a man of quality and responsibility in worship.

sens: Man from the tribe of Benjamin who lived during the time of the divided monarchy
Father of valiant warriors who joined David
H3395K.detail:
1. Jerocham is a Benjamite mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when David was gathering his troops. He is the father of Joéla and Zebadia, two warriors from Guedor who came to join David in his early days (1 Chronicles 12:7). His name means "showing mercy" or "compassionate," which recalls kindness.
2. These sons of Jerocham are cited among the valiant warriors who recognized David while he was fleeing from King Saul, which shows that Jerocham was a man of value whose lineage produced courageous men in service to the future king of Israel.
H3395K.origine: The name Jerocham carries the idea of compassion or mercy. In the Hebrew Old Testament, several men bear this name, indicating that it was a common name among the Israelites, particularly among the Levites and Benjamites. The Bible mentions several Jerocham from different families and eras, but all are presented as men of rank or responsibility.
H3395K.emploi: Jerocham is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:7, where he is designated as the father of two warriors who united with David. This passage situates the character at the time when David was gathering his men before becoming king. The Bible provides no further details about his life or personal deeds, but the mere fact that his sons are listed among David's valiant men suggests that he was a respected man of good reputation in the Benjamite clan of Guedor.
H3395K.portee: This brief passage reminds the reader that biblical history is often constructed through lineages and families. Jerocham and his sons illustrate how ordinary men from distant provinces recognized and supported God's plan by rallying to David. It is a silent invitation to consider how each person, regardless of their obscurity, can participate in God's work.

sens: Man of the time of the Divided Monarchy, father of Azareel
Name meaning 'showing mercy'
H3395L.detail:
1. Jerocham is a man living during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided into two rival kingdoms, Judah and Israel. He appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:22, where he is presented as the father of Azareel, chief of the tribe of Dan. This is why he is mainly known through his familial connection to his son.
2. His Hebrew name literally means 'showing mercy' or 'full of compassion' — an important virtue in biblical tradition, reflecting God's mercy towards His creatures.
H3395L.origine: The name Jerocham comes from a Hebrew root that evokes mercy and compassion. It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries a religious idea, common in the Old Testament. The name suggests a character of kindness and clemency, values that parents wished to impart to their child by naming him this way.
H3395L.emploi: Jerocham appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 27:22. This verse lists the leaders of the twelve tribes of Israel during the time of King David. Azareel, son of Jerocham, is named there as chief of the tribe of Dan. The genealogies in 1 Chronicles show that several men bore this name at different times, including an ancestor of the prophet Samuel and several Levites and priests. However, only the Jerocham who is the father of Azareel is mentioned in this passage.

sens: Character from the divided kingdom of Israel and Judah
H3395M.detail: Jerocham is a name borne by several men in the history of Israel during the time of the Kings. The only one explicitly mentioned in the Segond text is the father of Azariah, one of the military leaders who allied with Jehoiada to overthrow Queen Athaliah and restore the young king Joash (2 Chronicles 23:1). His name means 'showing mercy' or 'having compassion', which reflects a particular piety in this ancestor of the lineage of leaders.
H3395M.origine: The name Jerocham (יְרֹחָם) is composed of the root meaning 'to have compassion' or 'to show mercy' — a cardinal virtue in Israelite spirituality. The biblical chronicles attest to several characters bearing this name, including an ancestor of the prophet Samuel and various members of the priestly and warrior families of Israel.
H3395M.emploi: Jerocham appears only once in the Segond 1910 text, in 2 Chronicles 23:1, where he is presented as the father of Azariah. The latter is one of the seven military leaders who formed an alliance with the high priest Jehoiada to restore the worship of the true God and place the legitimate heir on the throne. This event takes place during the time of Queen Athaliah, who had usurped power after the death of her son King Ahaziah. Jerocham's appearance in this context highlights the importance of his lineage in the decisive events of the Kingdom of Judah.

sens: Eldest son of Hezron, himself son of Perez and descendant of Judah
Ancestor and founder of the Jerachmeelite clan
Officer of King Jehoiakim sent to arrest the prophet Baruch
Levite from the family of Merari, representative of the clan of Kish
H3396G.detail:
1. Jerachmeel is an important figure in the genealogy of Judah: he is the first son of Hezron, who himself descends from Perez and Judah. He thus belongs to the noble lineages of the Hebrew people.
2. He is the founder and ancestor of the Jerachmeelite clan, a family or social group recognized in Israel before the monarchy. His children (Ram, Buna, Oren, Otsem, and Onam) are listed in detail in 1 Chronicles 2:25-27, showing the importance of his descendants.
3. An officer bearing this name was sent by King Jehoiakim to arrest Baruch, the secretary of the prophet Jeremiah, indicating that the name was held by other important figures.
4. There is also a Jerachmeel Levite, belonging to the family of Merari, who represents the clan of Kish among the ministers of worship.
H3396G.origine: The name Jerachmeel means 'may God have mercy' or 'God will have mercy'. It combines two Hebrew elements: the divine name (El) and a verb meaning 'to have compassion'. It is a typical theophoric name in the Old Testament, expressing a blessing or a request for divine mercy. The derived word 'Jerachmeelite' (יְרַחְמְאֵלִי) designates the members of the clan founded by Jerachmeel.
H3396G.emploi: Jerachmeel is primarily mentioned in 1 Chronicles 2, where the genealogies of Judah are listed. He is the first son of Hezron and the founding ancestor of a recognized family. His direct descendants and grandchildren are named, highlighting the importance of this lineage in the tribal structure of Israel before the monarchy. The name also appears in other contexts (the officer of Jehoiakim, the Levite), indicating that it was held by several personalities at different times. These occurrences show that Jerachmeel was a name of honor among the people of Israel.

sens: Levite from the family of Kish, living during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H3396H.detail: 1. Jerachmeel is a Levite from the tribe of Levi, a member of the family of Kish. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:29, during the enumeration of the Levitical families at the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the North and the South. His name means 'may God have mercy'.
H3396H.origine: The name Jerachmeel comes from Hebrew and literally means 'may God have mercy' or 'God will have mercy'. It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains an invocation to the name of God. This type of name was common among the Levites and priestly families of Israel, expressing trust in divine benevolence.
H3396H.emploi: Jerachmeel is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 24:29. He represents the family of Kish among the Levites, and he is cited in the context of the classification of Levitical families responsible for the service of the Temple. This passage is part of an administrative list of the descendants of Levi during the time of King David.

sens: Officer of King Jehoiakim of Judah tasked with arresting the prophet Jeremiah and his secretary Baruch
H3396I.detail: Jerachmeel is a historical figure from the kingdom of Judah during the time of the divided monarchy. He appears in Jeremiah 36:26 as one of the three officers sent by King Jehoiakim to arrest the prophet Jeremiah and Baruch, his secretary. This mission fails, as the Lord hides the prophet and the one who transcribed his words. Jerachmeel acts on royal orders during a period of tension between the king and God's prophets.
H3396I.origine: The name Jerachmeel means 'may God have mercy' or 'God will have mercy'. It is composed of two elements: Yah (a contraction of the divine name) and raham (to have mercy, to show compassion). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing a prayer or blessing. The historical text designates him as a son of the king, integrated into the royal court and executing Jehoiakim's orders.
H3396I.emploi: Jerachmeel appears only once in the provided usages, in Jeremiah 36:26. He is named as 'son of the king' — not a direct son of Jehoiakim, but a member of the royal family with authority. The king sends him with two other officers (Seraiah and Shelemiah) to capture Jeremiah and Baruch after the prophet dictated his written oracles to his secretary. This episode occurs in the context of the scroll burned by Jehoiakim (Jeremiah 36): the king rejects the word of God and seeks to eliminate those who bear it. The failure of this mission illustrates divine protection over the prophet.
H3396I.portee: Jerachmeel embodies the opposition of political powers to the prophetic word. His appearance reminds us that even court personalities, vested with authority, cannot stop or silence the message that God entrusts to His messengers. His failure to capture Jeremiah illustrates the biblical certainty: no earthly power has the final word against the will of the Lord.

sens: Esclave égyptien au service de Schéschan
H3398.detail: Jarchah is a man of Egyptian origin who lived during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel. He was a slave in the service of Sheshan, a man from the tribe of Judah (1 Chronicles 2:34). Since Sheshan had only daughters and no sons to continue his lineage, he gave his daughter in marriage to Jarchah. From this union was born Attai, who thus became the heir of the family line (1 Chronicles 2:35). This event shows how a foreigner, even a slave, could be integrated into an Israelite family and participate in its genealogical continuity.
H3398.origine: The name literally means "the month of sweeping" in Hebrew. Although Jarchah is an Egyptian name, its bearer was inserted into the genealogy of Israel through marriage. His story illustrates how God's providence sometimes acted beyond ethnic and social boundaries.
H3398.emploi: Jarchah appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 2 of the book of Chronicles, where he is mentioned in the genealogy of the house of Judah. These two consecutive verses (1 Chronicles 2:34-35) constitute the only biblical account concerning him. He is presented solely as "the Egyptian slave" of Sheshan and as the husband of his daughter, a key role since he ensures the transmission of the name and family heritage. His unique example shows how, in Israel, the law allowed a master to give his daughter to his slave, establishing a form of legal and social filiation.

sens: to leap forward impetuously
to lead someone to a disastrous outcome
to act hastily and dangerously
H3399A.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of launching oneself violently and without thought, like someone rushing into the void. It is an inconsiderate race, a hasty movement forward without measure.
2. Figuratively, it means to lead someone to their ruin or misfortune. Balaam was on a "path of destruction": he was rushing toward a situation that could have destroyed him if he had continued in that direction (Numbers 22:32).
3. The underlying idea is that of an action done with haste and recklessness, without regard for the consequences — it is to act blindly and with impetuosity.
H3399A.origine: The Hebrew root expresses the idea of pushing, chasing, or forcefully advancing. It carries the image of a brutal push that strips away reason and discernment. The word appears rarely in the Bible, which underscores its particular force: it designates not just simple movement, but perilous movement, the kind that leads to ruin.
H3399A.emploi: This verb appears only once in the biblical text, in Numbers 22:32. Balaam, the diviner hired to curse Israel, rides his donkey. The animal stops three times, and Balaam strikes it in anger. The angel of the Lord reproaches him for this violence: he did not see the angel and was literally rushing on the path of destruction. This passage illustrates how the verb describes both Balaam's impetuosity and the destructive trajectory he was embarking upon.
H3399A.portee: This word reminds the reader that impatience and haste can blind us and lead us down paths that lead to our destruction. Balaam did not see the danger; he acted on impulse. For the believer, it serves as a warning against unthoughtful action and uncontrolled passion — God intervenes even when our animal (the donkey) tries to stop us.

sens: to express a liquid by twisting
to pour out, to let flow abundantly
Figuratively: to deliver, to hand over to someone else
H3399B.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a physical twisting: to twist something (like a wet cloth) to extract water from it. The image is that of a violent pressure that causes a liquid to flow.

2. By extension, the verb designates the pouring out or abundant flowing of a liquid, as if one were pouring or "twisting" a liquid substance.

3. Figuratively and in a context of misfortune, "to twist" or "to rush" means to deliver someone, to hand them over to a third party — often to an enemy. In Job 16:11, Job cries that God has "cast him" into the hands of the wicked: the image of twisting becomes that of a violent projection, an abandonment without defense.
H3399B.origine: The Hebrew verb רָטָה (ratah) is infrequent and its root evokes the idea of pressing, twisting, or pouring. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words revolving around the action of mistreating or mishandling something by force. The underlying imagery is that of a violent twisting, like one twists a fabric to expel water.
H3399B.emploi: This verb appears very rarely in the Hebrew Bible — only one certified use. In Job 16:11, it expresses the protest of a man unjustly treated, who accuses God of having delivered him into the hands of the wicked. The context of the Book of Job (dialogue on just suffering) sheds light on the meaning: Job is not speaking of a material twisting, but of a total deliverance, an abandonment without help at the mercy of his enemies. The verb, though rare, carries a strong emotional charge.
H3399B.portee: This word highlights Job's sincere distress in the face of unexplained suffering. For the reader, it underscores how God's faithful can feel — rightly or wrongly — abandoned or "delivered" to their adversaries. It is a raw expression of anguish, inviting us to listen to the complaint of one who suffers without understanding and to recognize the depth of desolation.

sens: To shape, give form to something
To conceive a plan, develop a project
To prepare in advance, organize
To predestine, fix in advance
H3335I.detail:
1. To form means to give shape to a material, to mold it. It is the idea of a potter creating an object, or an artisan working with creation. In Isaiah 46:11, God "conceives" a plan as one conceives a work in the mind.
2. To conceive a plan means to imagine something in one's mind and resolve it: it is the thought before action. In Psalms 94:20, the wicked "form wicked plans" — they devise malicious schemes in secret.
3. To prepare in advance means to organize something long before it happens. In Isaiah 37:26, God has "prepared these things from afar" and has "resolved them from ancient times" — it is a plan matured over a long time.
4. To predestine means to decide in advance the fate of something or someone. In Jeremiah 18:11, God "prepares" a calamity against Judah — He has determined this judgment even before it comes to pass.
H3335I.origine: The Hebrew verb יָצַר comes from a root that evokes the idea of molding, shaping. The word recalls the image of the potter (יֹצֵר, "yotser") who works the clay. The basic form suggests creation through the work of hands. In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this verb is often rendered as "plassein" (to shape) when it concerns concrete creation, and by "bouleuesthai" or "diatithemai" when it expresses a divine design.
H3335I.emploi: The verb יָצַר appears 6 times in the provided passages, mainly in the prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah) and the Psalms. It primarily expresses an act of creation or formation: God "forms" His plans from afar (Isaiah 37:26). It also describes human thoughts — the "wicked plans" of the wicked (Psalms 94:20). The word carries a nuance of thoughtful intention: it is not an impulsive action, but a project elaborated in advance, carefully considered. In Jeremiah 18:11, it is a calamity that God "prepares" — a judgment that proceeds from His sovereign decision.
H3335I.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the sovereignty of God: He does not improvise; He forms His designs from afar. This offers comfort — events are not random, but orchestrated by prior wisdom. But it also invites fear: our own plans and thoughts are transparent before God who "forms" and knows the intentions of the heart. It is a call to submit our designs to His.

sens: What is formed, shaped, molded (like pottery or an image)
The structure, framework, the outline of something
The intention, design, project that one conceives
Imagination, reasoning, thoughts that arise from the heart
Inclination, inner disposition, natural tendency
H3336.detail:
1. The word first designates what has been formed, shaped — like pottery from the hands of the potter, or a carved image. In Psalms 103:14, the Lord knows "what we are formed from," which refers to the human body shaped by God, created like clay: it is the original formation.
2. By extension, it means the framework, the internal structure of something — its basic plan, its mental architecture.
3. The meaning becomes more intellectual with "design" or "intention": it is what one conceives, what one proposes to do. In 1 Chronicles 28:9, the Lord "penetrates all designs" — the hidden plans of the heart.
4. It is also imagination and thought in the sense of "what happens in the mind." In Genesis 6:5, all the "thoughts" of the hearts of men are inclined toward evil — it is the constant activity of their spirit.
5. Finally, the word takes on a moral hue of "inclination" or "disposition": it is the natural bent of the heart, the deep orientation of a person. In Deuteronomy 31:21, the Lord knows the "dispositions" of Israel — what their hearts naturally tend toward.
H3336.origine: The word comes from the root "to form, to shape, to mold," as a potter works the clay. The basic image is tactile and creative: giving shape to formless material. It then extends to the mind: to form a thought is to give it shape, as an artist gives form to his material. The Hebrew word is also used to describe the formation of the human body in the womb, and the formation of the images we create mentally.
H3336.emploi: The word appears nine times in the Hebrew Bible. It is particularly frequent in the narratives of Genesis and the Psalms, where it speaks of the thoughts of the human heart. In Genesis 6:5 and 8:21, it designates the thoughts of the heart of humanity — thoughts inclined toward evil from youth, which explains the Flood. In wisdom texts like Chronicles, it takes on the meaning of "design" or "inner disposition" that God knows and probes: it is the hidden fabric of intention. In Psalms 103:14, it returns to its concrete meaning: that of "given form," the formation of the human body. The word can thus move from the concrete (what has been formed) to the abstract (what one thinks, imagines, projects).
H3336.portee: This word reminds us that our thoughts, intentions, and inclinations are not trivial: they reveal the true structure of our heart, and God has total knowledge of it. It invites vigilance over the direction our thoughts take — for they are never neutral; they show where our heart leads us. At the same time, it emphasizes that we are a creation formed by the hand of God: our thoughts are not all bad because we come from Him.

sens: Son of Naphtali
Founder of the family of the Jitsrites
H3337.detail:
1. Jetser is the third son of Naphtali, mentioned for the first time when Jacob and his family go down to Egypt (Genesis 46:24). He also appears in 1 Chronicles 7:13 among the sons of Naphtali.
2. Jetser is the founder of the family of the Jitsrites, a tribal branch that bears his name. This family is counted during the second census in Numbers 26:49, where it states "of Jetser, the family of the Jitsrites." Thus, his name is perpetuated through his descendants.
H3337.origine: The name Jetser comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to form" or "to shape." This image of formation or creation is particular to the names of the family of Naphtali. The name Jitsrite, which designates the members of his family, comes directly from Jetser and shows how, in ancient Israel, families bore the name of their founding ancestor.
H3337.emploi: Jetser is mentioned three times in the Hebrew Bible. First in Genesis 46:24, he is listed among the sons of Naphtali who go down to Egypt with Jacob. Then in Numbers 26:49, during the counting of the second generation in the wilderness, his family, the Jitsrites, is officially counted as a branch of the tribe of Naphtali. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 7:13, he is again listed in the genealogy of the sons of Naphtali. These three occurrences show that Jetser was an important man of his time, whose descendants were followed through generations and key events in the history of Israel.
H3337.portee: Jetser reminds the believer that every individual, even minor in the biblical narrative, has a place in the genealogy of God's people. His name and descendants are preserved, emphasizing that God knows and recognizes every family and tribe in His covenant with Israel.
